How RustStream is built, and what its design costs a service.
The tasks a running service holds, the way one delivery passes through them, and the order a shutdown stops them in.
What RustStream costs on every message: throughput against each broker's raw client, and instructions and allocations of its own code.
How every RustStream crate measures itself: the three loops, the run, the report and the code measurement.
What each published benchmark number measures, and which numbers can be compared with each other.
How a crate publishes its benchmark results: one JSON document at a stable path that the Benchmarks page reads.
What the framework's own code costs per message, measured in instructions and allocations, and where the cost goes.
The core knows no broker: a broker crate implements its traits and owns every broker-specific setting.
Mistakes that do not compile, and the error the compiler prints for each.
A broker's states are types: a configuration, a connection and a closed connection, each reached by a call that consumes the one before.
The stages one delivery passes, from the broker's stream to its settlement, in the order the runtime runs them.
How a delivery is settled: what the handler returns, what a failure policy decides, and where a retry ends.
Every broker RustStream runs on: the in-memory broker of the core and one crate per external broker, each with its own documentation.
MemoryBroker is a complete broker inside the service's process: it needs no server and comes with the memory feature of ruststream.
The building blocks of a RustStream service, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to.
A RustStream value names the service, holds its brokers and mounts each handler on the broker it subscribes to.
The attribute turns a builder function into the service's main: a binary that runs the service or prints its AsyncAPI document.
The ruststream command runs a service and prints its AsyncAPI document through cargo run; cargo generate scaffolds a new one.
Four hooks run around the brokers' connection: on_startup, after_startup, on_shutdown and after_shutdown.
A service runs until a signal, until a future of yours, or beside another server that owns the process.
health hands out a HealthProbe that reports whether a started service is running, stopping, stopped or failed, and how many of its subscriptions consume.
An HTTP server owns the process and the service runs beside it: started before the server, stopped after it.
run starts the service and serves until SIGINT or SIGTERM, then shuts it down gracefully.
shutdown stops a started service gracefully: hooks, subscriptions, running handlers, then the brokers.
start brings the service up and returns a RunningApp, so the caller owns the process and decides when it stops.
run_until serves until a future of yours resolves, then shuts the service down gracefully.
Shared state is one value built at startup that every handler reads, as a State<T> parameter or through a dependency-injection container.
on_startup builds one value of any type; a handler takes any of its fields as a State<T> parameter.
froodi is a dependency-injection container whose ruststream feature builds a handler's dependencies per delivery, as Inject parameters.
shaku is a dependency-injection container with no RustStream support; the service builds it in on_startup and a handler resolves from it.
TestApp runs a service's production app in process, drives its brokers and asserts on what its handlers received and published.
How a test publishes to a broker of the app and moves the app forward: settling deliveries and advancing time.
TestApp::advance lets a delay pass, fires the delayed redeliveries now due, and drives their reaction to a standstill.
TestApp::broker_named addresses a broker by the label it was registered under, which tells apart two brokers of one type.
TestApp::broker addresses one broker of the app by its production type, for publishing to it and reading its records.
TestApp::drain waits for the post-settle continuations of everything settled so far, for a test that asserts on their effects.
message(&v) starts an input with the publish builder the service itself publishes through: destination, headers and codec.
TestApp::publish and BrokerHandle::publish send any serde value to a named destination in one call; publish_with_headers adds headers.
publish() sends the input onto the broker and returns once the whole reaction to it has settled, so the next line can assert.
TestApp::settle drives a reaction the test started without the harness to a standstill, without publishing anything new.
Assertions on what was published to one destination: how many messages, their payloads, headers and per-message settings.
assert_called_once checks that exactly one message was published to the destination.
assert_called(n) checks that exactly n messages were published to the destination.
assert_not_called checks that nothing was published to the destination.
assert_options_default checks that the latest recorded publish carried no per-message settings, so the publish policy's defaults applied.
decoded_as::<U>() re-types a record, so its payload assertions decode to U.
decoded returns every payload published to the destination as a value; decoded_with names the codec.
messages returns every message published to the destination, with its name, headers and payload, for checks of your own.
with_header checks one header of the latest message published to the destination, such as one a transform or a publish layer added.
with_options checks the per-message settings the latest recorded publish carried, the value a builder step set.
with_raw checks the bytes of the latest payload published to the destination.
with checks that the latest payload published to the destination decodes to a value; with_codec names the codec.
The records a test reads: what one subscriber received, what was published to a destination, and what went through an Out slot.
TestApp::out opens the record of one Out slot: every message the handler sent through it, on whichever broker it went.
BrokerHandle::published opens the record of one destination on a broker: every message published there, with its name and headers.
BrokerHandle::subscriber opens the record of one subscription: what its handler received and how each delivery settled.
How a test checks whether the app is still running or has shut down, and how its run ended.
TestApp::assert_running asserts the service is still up: no fail-fast failure has shut it down.
TestApp::assert_shut_down asserts a fail-fast failure has shut the service down, as a handler panic does under the default policy.
TestApp::run_result returns what the service run would return now: Ok while it is healthy, an error once a fail-fast failure stopped it.
How a test starts the production app, gives it state, and shuts it down.
TestApp::shutdown tears the service down the way the service does, hooks included, and returns what run would return, so a fail-fast failure fails the test.
start_live connects the brokers of the same app to a running stand, so one test body checks the service against the real broker.
TestApp::start runs the app main builds, unchanged, with every broker connected in process and no server.
TestApp::with_state starts the app with a state the test builds in place of on_startup, wired to the brokers of the app.
Assertions on one subscriber: how often it ran, what it received and how each delivery was settled.
assert_batch_sizes(&[..]) checks how a subscriber's deliveries were cut into handler calls.
assert_called_once checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly once: one delivery, or one batch.
assert_called(n) checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly n times, counting a batch as one call.
assert_last_failed_to_decode() checks that the latest delivery did not decode into the handler's input type.
assert_not_called checks that a subscriber's handler never ran.
assert_outcome(..) checks the latest handler call by its classified Outcome, failures included.
batches_raw() returns the bytes a batch handler received, one list per call.
batches::<T>() returns what a batch handler received, one decoded list per call.
outcomes() returns how every handler call settled, in call order.
panicked() checks that the handler panicked on its latest call.
received_raw() returns the bytes of every payload a subscriber received, in delivery order.
received_values::<T>() returns every value a subscriber's deliveries lent its handler, batch elements included.
received::<T>() returns every payload a subscriber received, decoded with the default codec, for a check of your own.
settled(outcome) checks how the latest handler call settled, against the HandlerOutcome a handler returns.
with_raw(bytes) checks the exact bytes of the latest handler call, before any decoding.
with_value(&value) checks the value the latest delivery lent its handler, on a broker whose deliveries already hold one.
with(&value) checks that the latest handler call received this value, decoded with the default codec.
The asyncapi feature generates the AsyncAPI 3.1 document of a service from its app value, with build_spec.
How the document is produced, serialized and served, and where its payload schemas come from.
build_spec reads the AsyncAPI document of a service from its app value, the same value main runs.
asyncapi gen prints the document of a service from the main that #[ruststream::app] generates.
.describe(text) gives a manual registration the operation description the attribute takes from the handler's doc comment.
MessageInfo names the component of a message in the document and describes it, whatever the Rust type is called.
messages_without_schema lists the messages the document describes with no payload schema, for a check to fail on.
A message type that derives JsonSchema gives its message a payload schema in the document.
to_json and to_yaml serialize the document in the two formats AsyncAPI tools read.
.undocumented() takes the schemas of one manual registration out of the document and lifts its JsonSchema demand.
render_viewer_html returns a self-contained HTML page that renders the document with the AsyncAPI React component.
What the document says about a service beyond its channels: replies, channel parameters, headers, content types and retries.
A destination declared as a name template becomes a channel whose address keeps its placeholders, each one declared as a parameter.
Each message names the media type of the codec that reads or writes it; the root defaultContentType appears only when all of them agree.
A header contract becomes the headers schema of its message, from a Headers<T> parameter or from #[outgoing(headers = ..)].
A reply is the reply of the receive operation it answers: the document names its channel and its message.
The attempt cap and the dead-letter destination of a registration appear on its receive operation as the x-ruststream-retry extension.
The servers section: the brokers a service connects to, how clients authenticate, and the protocol bindings.
Bindings carry what one protocol says about a server, a channel, an operation or a message, in that protocol's AsyncAPI vocabulary.
ServerSpec::security attaches a SecurityScheme that says how clients authenticate; each scheme becomes a component the server references.
RustStream::server declares a server the document lists, from a ServerSpec that says how clients reach the broker.
with_broker_labeled registers a broker under a label that is its server name in the document, and the broker describes the server.
The info section: what the service is, who owns it and under which license.
AppId is the identifier of the service at the root of the document, a URI parsed when it is built.
AppInfo is the info section of the document: the title and the version, a description and the terms of service.
Contact names who answers for the service: a person or a team, a URL and an e-mail address, each optional.
ExternalDocs points at documentation kept outside the document: a URL and what the reader finds there.
License names the license the service is published under, with an optional URL of its text.
A Tag is a label that groups the service among its neighbours, with an optional description and link.
MemoryBroker is a complete broker inside the service's process, and the reference implementation of the broker contract.
A MemoryPattern subscription reads every name its pattern matches, and the broker's Routing decides who receives a shared match.
A retaining MemoryBroker keeps the newest messages of every name within a bound, and its subscriptions replay over them.
Logs, metrics and traces of a running service: each comes from a layer on the app and a feature that exports it.
The logging feature prints the service's tracing events on the console, colored, at the verbosity RUST_LOG sets.
The metrics feature counts and times deliveries and counts publishes in a Prometheus registry that the service serves on /metrics.
Otel sends the service's spans and metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector over OTLP, the dispatch metrics included.
The otel feature carries the W3C trace context from a delivery to its replies and opens a span for every delivery.
TracingLayer logs every delivery and its outcome as tracing events, so handlers hold no logging code of their own.
#[subscriber] turns an async fn over a reference to the message into a handler that include mounts on a broker.
A handler over &[T] runs once per batch the broker delivers; the mount site names the batch size, and the body settles the batch or each element.
A codec turns a payload into a message type and back; it is a compile-time type, chosen at the mount site, and JSON is the default.
A handler that reads the delivery's bytes as they arrived, and a reply that leaves as the bytes it holds, skip the codec.
CborCodec reads and writes CBOR through ciborium, a compact binary format with the data model of JSON; it is on with the cbor feature.
A codec of your own implements the Codec trait over any serde format and mounts wherever a built-in codec does.
JsonCodec reads and writes JSON through serde_json; it is the default codec, on with the json feature.
MsgpackCodec reads and writes MessagePack through rmp-serde; a struct travels as an array of its field values. It is on with the msgpack feature.
A message generated by prost carries its own bytes with #[wire(prost)]: no serde, no codec feature, encoded once into the buffer that leaves.
A handler's parameters after the message: the per-delivery Context and the values extracted from it.
Ctx<K> passes one field of the broker's per-delivery context to the handler as a parameter.
Context carries one delivery's channel, headers, state and broker fields to the middleware and the handler.
A type that implements FromContext becomes a handler parameter, resolved from the delivery before the body runs.
How many deliveries of one subscription run at once, and on which threads.
The poll-diagnostics feature times the polls of every handler and names the handlers that compute on the app's runtime.
threads(n) gives a subscription n threads of its own, so a handler that computes leaves the app's runtime free for I/O.
workers(n) handles up to n deliveries of one subscription at once; workers(n, by_key) keeps the deliveries of one key in order.
What a subscriber does when its handler panics or a payload cannot decode, set per subscriber with on_failure.
What a handler returns settles its delivery: ack, retry, retry after a delay, or drop, as a HandlerOutcome.
and_after attaches a continuation to an outcome: work that runs on a task of its own once the delivery is settled.
What the handler body returns settles the delivery: a HandlerOutcome, nothing at all, or a Result.
A post-settle hook registered on the context runs once the delivery is settled, only for the settlement it names.
retry_after(delay) asks for the delivery back no sooner than the delay, for a condition that will pass.
Layers wrap handlers and publishes: app-wide, per router or per registration.
A DynStack is a handler middleware chain assembled when the app starts, mounted on one registration as one layer.
A layer wraps handlers in code of your own: every handler of the app, every handler of a router, or one registration.
A PublishDynStack is a publish middleware chain assembled when the app starts, added to the app as one publish layer.
A publish layer wraps every message the app's handlers publish: it changes the message, observes the send, or refuses it.
Settings the attribute leaves open are chained where the handler is mounted: name, workers, failure policy, batch size and start position.
How a handler answers a message and publishes to other destinations.
A handler consumes from one broker and publishes through another, named by a token the target broker mints before registration.
An Out slot hands a handler a live publisher as a parameter: one marker per slot, bound to a publish policy at the mount site.
A message type declares where it goes: a fixed name, a name template with a setter per placeholder, or no name, left to the call.
One builder publishes every message: message(&value), the positions its type leaves open, then publish().
A broker's per-message settings, such as a priority, a QoS or a key: defaulted by the publish policy, set per publish by the broker's own steps.
The publisher capabilities a broker offers, one trait each, starting with Publisher.
OwnedTransactions opens independent transactions that own their buffers, so a handler keeps several open on one slot at once.
Publisher is the capability every slot names; a publish policy at the mount site becomes one when startup pairs it with the connected broker.
RequestReply sends a request from a handler and awaits the correlated answer, on a broker that correlates replies natively.
TransactionalPublisher puts several publishes in one broker transaction: every reply of a batch, or a scope a handler opens on its slot.
A handler answers a message by returning a value; the reply type or the mount site says where the answer goes.
A publish transform changes an outgoing message at one publish position, before it reaches the publisher.
A batch publish transform is a step on the replies of a batch handler: each reply passes it on its own, with the batch's context.
A naming transform sets the destination of each message, on a position where nothing else declared it: a reply to the inbox a request named.
A publish transform is a static step on one publish position: it reads the delivery or the slot, and changes the outgoing message.
A subscription over a replayable log opens at a position of your choice, and its handler can move it.
A handler moves its own subscription to another position of the log through the broker's seek handle.
start_at opens a replayable subscription at a position: the start of the log, a sequence number, or the tip.
max_attempts(n) ends a message that keeps coming back, and dead_letter(name) is where it goes then.
The Retry slot is the publisher a copy of a delivery leaves through; out_retry replaces it and to(name) names its destination.
A Router groups one module's handlers with their own middleware and codec, and include_router mounts the group on a broker.
A [subscriber](./index.md) reads a subscription named by a string or by the broker's descriptor, fixed in the attribute or left to the mount site.
A serde struct is the header contract a handler reads and a publish writes, checked in both directions.
insert_typed writes a header contract into a header map, the way a publish transform stamps every message of a slot.
Message<H, T> hands a handler the decoded payload and its parsed header contract as one input.
A message type names its header contract, so publishing it does not compile without the headers.

This section describes how RustStream is built and what its design costs a service.

The tasks a running service holds, the way one delivery passes through them, and the order a shutdown stops them in. The tasks of each dispatch form on the app runtime, and the dedicated threads beside itpoll_nextsendpushpopspawnApp runtime: Tokio, multi-thread by defaultSubscription streams of the connected brokersdefaultone task runsevery stepworkers(n)one loop taskhands them outthreads(n)one feeder taskfills the ringsn worker tasksan inbox of onen ringsof eight slotsTracked tasks: and_after,hooks, retry_after timersn OS threadsa Tokio runtimeon each The diagram as text App runtime: Tokio, multi-thread by default: default one task runs every step; workers(n) one loop task hands them out; threads(n) one feeder task fills the rings; n worker tasks an inbox of one; n rings of eight slots; Tracked tasks: and_after, hooks, retry_after timers Subscription streams of the connected brokers → default one task runs every step: poll_next Subscription streams of the connected brokers → workers(n) one loop task hands them out Subscription streams of the connected brokers → threads(n) one feeder task fills the rings workers(n) one loop task hands them out → n worker tasks an inbox of one: send threads(n) one feeder task fills the rings → n rings of eight slots: push n rings of eight slots → n OS threads a Tokio runtime on each: pop default one task runs every step → Tracked tasks: and_after, hooks, retry_after timers: spawn n worker tasks an inbox of one → Tracked tasks: and_after, hooks, retry_after timers The service runs on Tokio. #[ruststream::app] builds a multi-thread runtime. flavor = "current_thread" picks a single-threaded one, and worker_threads = n sets the number of threads. A subscriber is a Stream of deliveries, and back-pressure comes from polling it. The default loop polls for the next delivery once the previous one is settled. workers(n) keeps at most n deliveries in flight. workers(n, by_key) sends every delivery of one key to the same worker, so one key keeps its order. threads(n) reads ahead at most n × 9 deliveries: one in the hands of each thread and eight in its ring. A dedicated thread runs the whole delivery, from decode to settlement, on its own current-thread runtime. Work the handler hands to MainRuntime, taken as Ctx<MainRuntime>, runs back on the app runtime.

One delivery, step by step, in the column of the task that runs each stepLoop taskHandling taskLater, trackednext turnspawnpoll thestreambuild thecontextconsumelayersdecodehandlerbodypublishthe replysettlepoll thenext onecontinuationsand timers The diagram as text Loop task: poll the stream; poll the next one Handling task: build the context; consume layers; decode; handler body; publish the reply; settle Later, tracked: continuations and timers poll the stream → build the context build the context → consume layers consume layers → decode decode → handler body handler body → publish the reply publish the reply → settle settle → poll the next one: next turn settle → continuations and timers: spawn The handling task is the loop task itself by default, a worker task under workers(n), and a dedicated thread under threads(n). An and_after continuation, a post-settle hook and a retry_after timer run after the settlement, as tasks the app tracks. They run at most once: the delivery is already settled.

What a graceful shutdown does, in orderA signal, a fail-fastor RunningApp::shutdownon_shutdown hooks runwhile the brokers are connectedThe loops stoptaking new deliveriesDeliveries in handare handled and settledTracked continuationsand retry timers finishBrokers shut downin reverse registration orderafter_shutdown hooks runwith the brokers closed The diagram as text A signal, a fail-fast or RunningApp::shutdown → on_shutdown hooks run while the brokers are connected on_shutdown hooks run while the brokers are connected → The loops stop taking new deliveries The loops stop taking new deliveries → Deliveries in hand are handled and settled Deliveries in hand are handled and settled → Tracked continuations and retry timers finish Tracked continuations and retry timers finish → Brokers shut down in reverse registration order Brokers shut down in reverse registration order → after_shutdown hooks run with the brokers closed A shutdown timeout bounds the wait. When it expires, loops still running are aborted, and tracked tasks still pending are left to finish on their own. Without a timeout, a shutdown waits for all of them. A task spawned with plain tokio::spawn on a dedicated thread is not tracked and ends with its thread.

What RustStream costs on every message, measured against each broker's raw client and as the cost of its own code. A framework between the broker client and your handler costs time on every message: the subscription stream, the decode, the dispatch, the ack. This page publishes that cost twice, as two measurements that answer different questions. The first is throughput against the raw client, on a real broker, doing the same work on the same machine. It says what a deployed service pays. The second is the cost of the code: instructions and allocations per message. In ruststream it is the framework's own code, with no broker in the number. It says what changed when the code changed, and it is precise enough to fail a pull request that makes a message more expensive. Each crate measures itself by one methodology and publishes its own numbers. This page loads them from the main branch of each crate's repository and shows each crate in a tab of its own. A new measurement appears in its tab as soon as it is merged. What the numbers allow you to conclude, and what they do not, is on the Numbers page.

The first chart of a broker's tab is its comparison. Each scenario draws three loops of three interleaved rounds against the raw client's best round, the zero of its axis. A loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. A dot right of zero is slower than the raw client. The best round is the closest to the undisturbed cost, and the median is the one a rerun typically repeats. The shaded band around zero is what the runtime's indistinguishable verdict rests on: the spread from the best round to the worst. A best round inside it cannot be told from the raw client. A hollow dot marks every loop the crate judged indistinguishable, and the verdicts beside a row are the ones the crate published. A row shows its numbers on hover or focus, and the table under the chart lists them all: the best round, with the median in parentheses. Broker crate is the crate's own consumer and publisher driven without the runtime, so the two differences read apart: what the crate costs over the client it wraps, and what the runtime costs on top of that. A crate that ships a plugin draws the plugin's scenarios on a chart of their own, on an axis of its own. Its three loops are one app: without the plugin, with the plugin written by hand, and with the crate's plugin. The plugin's table and the verdict beside the crate's plugin also show its overhead over the plugin written by hand.

The cost chart closes every tab, and it is the core's only chart. It shows instructions and allocations per message in the steady state. These are absolute figures, not a comparison: what the framework costs over a broker's own client is the comparison. ruststream measures its own code on the in-process transport. A broker crate measures over its real transport, and its benchmarks page says what its number covers. Each crate has an axis of its own, because a broker crate counts its client's work too. Cold start is what starting the service and handling the first delivery cost together, instructions and allocations, and a service pays it once rather than per message. A row shows it on hover or focus, and the table under the chart lists it. The line above a crate's chart is the machine the run was taken on, down to the memory, then the versions of the crate and of ruststream it counted and the date it ran: an instruction count is comparable across machines only once you know they ran the same code.

How every RustStream crate measures itself, so a number published for one broker means the same thing as a number published for another. Every broker crate follows the procedure below. A broker that departs from it says so on its own page.

A run measures the same scenario three times over, and the three differ in exactly one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. The broker's own client, driven directly. Broker crate. The crate's own consumer and publisher - its subscription source, the subscriber stream it yields, its acknowledgement, its publisher - driven by a loop in the benchmark, with no runtime above them. RustStream. The whole service a user writes: the handler, the app, the dispatch. The first difference is what a broker crate costs over the client it wraps, which is the crate's own responsibility. The second is what the runtime costs on top, over that broker in particular - and it is published per broker because the crates meet the runtime differently: how a stream yields, whether deliveries arrive in batches, how back-pressure reaches the consumer. Same client, same client configuration. Prefetch, ack mode, consumer group, durability, connection count and any broker-specific tuning are identical on both sides. The framework side configures the broker through RustStream, and the resulting client settings still have to match. Same ack position. RustStream acks after the handler returns, so the other two loops ack in the same place. Batching acks at the end of the raw run measures a different protocol, not a different framework. Same decode into the same type. The loops without a handler deserialize the payload into the same struct with the same codec and touches a field through std::hint::black_box. Skipping this is the easiest way to produce a wrong number: the optimizer removes a decode whose result is unused, and the raw side silently stops decoding. Same payload, byte for byte. One generator produces the bodies every loop consumes. Same runtime. The tokio flavor, the worker thread count and the number of messages processed at once are the same everywhere. Same build. Profile, RUSTFLAGS and the allocator match, and the observability features (logging, metrics, otel) are enabled for every loop or for none. A machine with -C target-cpu=native in the environment produces numbers another machine cannot reproduce. The flags are therefore published with the results.

The consumer is attached before the first message is published. Otherwise one side works through a backlog the broker already holds, and the other receives messages as they are published. In most brokers those are two different paths. Every run gets its own names. A fresh subject, queue, stream or consumer group per run, so run N never sees what run N-1 left behind. The window starts at the first message received and ends at the ack of the last one. A calibration run precedes the measured ones and its result is discarded. Connection setup, consumer registration and the first allocations are startup cost, not per-message cost. The message count makes a run last at least five seconds, so startup transients and timer resolution stay inside the noise. The loops are interleaved, not blocked. Raw, crate, framework, raw, crate, framework and so on, for three rounds. Running one loop to the end and then the next attributes every drift of the machine (thermal, background load, page cache) to whichever ran last.

Every loop reports three rounds: its best, its median and its worst. Noise on the machine only ever slows a run down, so the fastest round is the closest to the undisturbed cost, the median is the round a rerun typically repeats, and the slowest says how far from quiet the machine was. A single number from a single run is not a result. The table prints the best round with the median in parentheses. The worst round stays in the document and out of the cell, because what it is there for is the spread: the distance from the best round to the worst. A difference smaller than that spread is published as indistinguishable, never as a percentage: a figure below the run-to-run noise reads as precision that was never measured. A saturated consumer is flagged. When the raw side spends the run waiting on the broker, the row is marked broker-bound. The environment is published with the numbers: CPU and core count, kernel, how the broker was started (image, container, host), the rustc version, the crate versions, the build profile and the flags. Without them a number cannot be reproduced or declared out of date.

Each crate produces its cost chart with a benchmark recipe of its own, which its benchmarks page names: just bench in ruststream. The recipe needs valgrind and the benchmark runner pinned to the version the crate depends on. just bench 5000 measures every scenario of ruststream over five thousand deliveries instead of a thousand: a steadier number for a longer run, while the published document stays at the default. Every scenario is the service a user writes, started through the real runtime with the test harness compiled out, so what is measured is the code that ships. The numbers are absolute, and in ruststream they are the framework's own cost. The comparison against a client someone else wrote is the comparison chart, and the broker crates produce it. In ruststream the transport is in process. The framework's own code is the subject, so the numbers must not move with a socket, a server's load or a network. Both halves pay the same transport cost anyway, and it cancels in the difference. A broker crate measures over its real transport, and its benchmarks page says what that adds to the number. The queue is filled before the measured region opens. What a scenario measures is steady-state delivery, never the connect, the subscription open or the first allocation behind them. Collection covers the measured region and nothing around it. Setup and teardown run in the same process and through the same framework code, so a measurement that counted them would report the queue being filled as the cost of draining it. Three runs per scenario, and what they are for. One delivery, then two longer runs, the second twice the first: a thousand and two thousand deliveries in ruststream, and the counts a broker crate's benchmarks page gives. The difference between the last two is what a message costs once the service is running; the single delivery is the cold start. Nothing has to be switched off part way through a run, which is what makes this work for the allocation counter, whose counting cannot be toggled at all. Two numbers per scenario. Instructions from callgrind, which is exact and compared; allocations from DHAT, which is exact and held to the floor the scenario declares. In ruststream, a separate benchmark measures wall time on scenarios of its own. just bench prints those times, which are noisy and informational. A comparison, not a threshold. Run with --baseline=main, the recipe measures a branch against the same benchmarks run on the branch it targets, and fails when a scenario's instructions grow past the crate's own limit: two percent in ruststream, and in a broker crate the limit its benchmarks page states. The limit is relative, so it applies only against a baseline. Allocations are held to what the scenario declares on every run, with a baseline or without. The author of a pull request runs the comparison and cites its numbers, and a change that lowers a scenario lowers its declared floor in the same pull request. The same rules apply to the cold start.
What each published number measures, and which numbers can be compared with each other.

Each row was measured by whoever maintains that broker crate, on their own machine, against a broker on localhost. Rows are therefore not comparable with each other: the absolute throughput of one says nothing about another. Only the loops inside a row are comparable, and that is the comparison the results exist for. A broker on localhost is the harshest setting for the framework. There is no network latency here, so the same absolute cost per message comes out as a larger percentage than it would against a broker across a real network. Read the percentage as an upper bound on what a deployed service pays, not as a typical figure. The broker-bound mark means the raw client spent most of the run waiting on the socket. The framework does its work inside that wait, and the measured difference comes out near zero. For that workload it is a real result: this is what a saturated consumer looks like. But the number is a lower bound on the cost of dispatch, not a measurement of it, and you cannot read it as "free".
documents.s: The comparison against a raw client

documents.t: An instruction count is exact. In ruststream two runs of the same binary give the same number, and a machine twice as fast gives the same number too, so its rows are comparable with each other and with the same row measured on another machine. What a count does not tell you is time: the same count costs more where it misses the cache. In ruststream the number is the crate's own work and nothing else: the service a user writes, over the in-process queue, decoding the payload into a type, reading a field and settling the delivery. No broker is in it, so the figure moves when the framework's code moves and at no other time, which is what lets two percent count as a defect rather than as noise. Every per-message figure is the steady state. Starting a service costs what it costs once - the connect, the subscription, the first allocations behind them - and dividing that over the messages of a run would publish it as a price per message it is not. So a scenario is measured over two runs, the second twice as long as the first, and what a message costs is the difference between them; the cold start is measured on its own, over a single delivery. In ruststream the two runs are a thousand deliveries and two thousand. Allocations are counted per message. In ruststream the figure on the delivery path is zero: once the service is running, a message goes from the queue to the handler body without the framework asking the allocator for anything. On its publish path the figure is what the broker takes to own the message it is handed, and nothing above it. A broker crate measures over its real transport, which in most crates is the broker in its compose file, so its number also holds the client's work and moves a little from run to run. Its benchmarks page says what the number covers, how far it moves, which delivery counts it uses and which limit it is held to.

How a crate publishes its benchmark results: one JSON document at a stable path, which the Benchmarks page reads. A broker crate runs its own harness with just bench against the broker in its compose file. It commits the outcome to its repository: a page a reader can follow, and one JSON document the Benchmarks page reads.

The file lives at docs/benchmarks/results.json in the broker repository, next to the page that explains it. The Benchmarks page reads it from main, so a measurement shows as soon as it is merged. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/powersemmi/<crate>/main/docs/benchmarks/results.json

schema is the version of the document: 3 reports each loop as three rounds (best, median and worst), 2 added the code section, and a schema 1 document carried a median with its extremes. The table prints best with median in parentheses. worst is read rather than printed: the verdict rule rests on the distance between the best round and the worst. A schema 3 document without median keeps the worst round in parentheses, which is what it printed before the field existed. unit is a short label rendered next to every value in the row, not a sentence. verdict is measured or indistinguishable, decided by the spread rule; overhead_percent is recorded either way and displayed only when the verdict is measured. It is the framework against the raw client, end to end. adapter and adapter_overhead_percent are the crate's own consumer and publisher against the same client, measured without the runtime, and adapter_verdict applies the spread rule to that difference the way verdict applies it to the other - and where a crate leaves it out, the page applies the same rule to the spreads it did publish, so the two columns of a row never disagree about what is visible. A crate that publishes none of them leaves the middle column empty. environment may carry round_trip, the probe the broker_bound arithmetic rests on, so a reader can redo the sum. broker_bound marks a run the broker paced rather than the consumer. environment describes the machine and the build. cpu, architecture, cpu_frequency, cores, memory and memory_speed are the machine; profile and features are what the benchmarks were built with. A field the machine does not publish is written as unknown rather than guessed: memory speed comes from the DMI tables, which most systems only let root read. Everything but cpu, os and rustc is optional, so a schema 1 document stays readable. code feeds the cost chart, one entry per scenario. framework is per message in the steady state; cold is the whole cost of starting the service and taking the first delivery, not divided by anything. gated says whether a regression in it fails the crate's benchmark recipe. A crate that publishes scenarios alone declares schema 1 and shows its comparison only. A crate that measures no broker of its own leaves scenarios out instead of publishing it empty, and shows a cost chart only. A crate that measures its code apart from the comparison records that run in code_measured: its measured_at, crate_version and core_version. The line above the cost chart takes its date and versions from there, and from the top-level fields in a document without it. A document that does not load, or that declares a schema the Benchmarks page does not know, leaves its tab with the "no results published yet" line. A broken publish is visible instead of silently missing. { "schema": 3, "crate": "ruststream-nats", "crate_version": "0.7.0", "core_version": "0.7.0", "measured_at": "2026-08-20", "environment": { "cpu": "AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor", "architecture": "x86_64 (x86-64-v3)", "cpu_frequency": "base 3400 MHz, max 4900 MHz", "cores": "16 physical, 32 logical", "memory": "62.7 GiB", "memory_speed": "DDR4, 3600 MT/s", "os": "Linux 6.16.7", "broker": "nats:2.10-alpine in Docker on localhost", "rustc": "1.90.0", "valgrind": "3.25.1", "profile": "bench, inheriting release (opt-level = 3, lto = false, codegen-units = 16)", "features": "--no-default-features --features memory,macros,json", "rustflags": "-C target-cpu=native" }, "scenarios": [ { "name": "core NATS, 512 B JSON, ack each", "unit": "msg/s", "messages": 200000, "pairs": 3, "raw": { "best": 129604, "median": 128470, "worst": 126980 }, "adapter": { "best": 129310, "median": 128040, "worst": 126700 }, "framework": { "best": 129020, "median": 127640, "worst": 126100 }, "overhead_percent": 0.4, "adapter_overhead_percent": 0.3, "adapter_verdict": "indistinguishable", "verdict": "indistinguishable", "broker_bound": true } ], "code": [ { "name": "consume, JSON decode into a small struct", "messages": 1000, "framework": { "instructions": 2839.8, "allocations": 0.0 }, "cold": { "instructions": 19219, "allocations": 26 }, "gated": true } ] }

broker 3,157.7 0 16,662 / 26 The numbers are the steady state per message, on the in-process broker, so no transport is in them. A row shows its cold start on hover or focus: what starting the service and handling the first delivery cost together, paid once. Taking a delivery allocates nothing. The loop keeps one slot for the delivery and one encode buffer, and every stage is a generic type resolved at compile time, with no dynamic call on the way. A DynStack of layers chosen at run time costs one boxed future per layer per message. An and_after continuation is one boxed future, paid only by the delivery that sets it. A reply allocates nothing when the broker's client only reads the bytes: it is lent the loop's buffer. The in-process broker keeps what it is handed, so its reply costs the buffer the codec wrote. The other publish rows allocate what the in-process broker keeps of each message, and what the scenario builds itself: a header value, or a request's single-use inbox. The payload's size is the expensive part of a decode: compare the 1 KB body with the small struct. The benchmarks publish every scenario with its method, against each broker's raw client too.

The core knows no broker: a broker crate implements its traits and owns every broker-specific setting. The service, the broker-agnostic core, and broker crates that plug into its traitsmounted onimplementsimplementswrapswrapsYour serviceruststreamBroker crates#[subscriber]handlers#[ruststream::app]builderruntime: routing, dispatch,settlement, publishingcodecs: JSON, CBOR,MessagePack, or nonechosen at compile timefeatures: memory broker,AsyncAPI, metrics,OpenTelemetry, testingBroker, Subscriber,Publisher, sources,policiescapabilities: batches,transactions, requestand reply, seekingruststream-natssubjects, streams,policies, options,mount stepsruststream-rdkafkatopics, groups,policies, options,mount stepsasync-natsrdkafka The diagram as text Your service: #[subscriber] handlers; #[ruststream::app] builder ruststream: runtime: routing, dispatch, settlement, publishing; codecs: JSON, CBOR, MessagePack, or none chosen at compile time; features: memory broker, AsyncAPI, metrics, OpenTelemetry, testing; Broker, Subscriber, Publisher, sources, policies; capabilities: batches, transactions, request and reply, seeking Broker crates: ruststream-nats subjects, streams, policies, options, mount steps; ruststream-rdkafka topics, groups, policies, options, mount steps #[subscriber] handlers → runtime: routing, dispatch, settlement, publishing: mounted on ruststream-nats subjects, streams, policies, options, mount steps → Broker, Subscriber, Publisher, sources, policies: implements ruststream-rdkafka topics, groups, policies, options, mount steps → capabilities: batches, transactions, request and reply, seeking: implements ruststream-nats subjects, streams, policies, options, mount steps → async-nats: wraps ruststream-rdkafka topics, groups, policies, options, mount steps → rdkafka: wraps The core depends on no broker client. Its required traits are the lifecycle of a connection, a subscriber that is a Stream of deliveries, and a publisher. Batches, transactions, request and reply, seeking and values a delivery already holds are capability traits a broker implements only when its client has them. A broker crate owns its vocabulary. The descriptor of a subscription form, the policy of a publisher, the per-message settings a publish carries and the mount steps that read the chain's settings all live there. The core has no broker-specific setting and no default for one. The codec is a type: the codec a mounting names, or the default one the enabled feature selects. A service without a codec feature has no default, and a mounting that needs one does not compile. Everything beyond the traits and the runtime is a cargo feature of the one crate: the memory broker, AsyncAPI, metrics, logging, OpenTelemetry, testing and the command line. Features only add, and none of them changes what another one does.

A check per message would cost every delivery, and a check at startup finds the mistake only where the service first runs. Each error names the type or the step at fault. Each row is a reply, transform, codec, publisher capability, dispatch, publish and typed header rule, in that order. A setting fixed once on a mount chain cannot be fixed again, and a capability the broker lacks is a missing method or an unmet bound. The lifecycle is typed too: a broker that is not connected has no method to subscribe or publish with, and a closed one has been consumed.

A broker's states are types: a configuration, a connection and a closed connection, each reached by a call that consumes the one before. The broker's states as types, and the app steps that move it from one to the nextconnect(self)shutdown(self)start()shutdown()BrokerAppB::new(config)sync, no I/OB::Connectedsubscribe, publishClosedteardown reportThe builderregisters brokersand handlersRunningAppconnected, loopsrunningStoppedloops drained,brokers closedA publisher that outlives its broker's connectionanswers with an error, never with a silent success The diagram as text Broker: B::new(config) sync, no I/O; B::Connected subscribe, publish; Closed teardown report App: The builder registers brokers and handlers; RunningApp connected, loops running; Stopped loops drained, brokers closed B::new(config) sync, no I/O → B::Connected subscribe, publish: connect(self) B::Connected subscribe, publish → Closed teardown report: shutdown(self) The builder registers brokers and handlers → RunningApp connected, loops running: start() RunningApp connected, loops running → Stopped loops drained, brokers closed: shutdown() A publisher that outlives its broker's connection answers with an error, never with a silent success A broker is built without I/O, so the #[ruststream::app] builder stays synchronous whatever the broker. Every network call waits for start(). Subscribing and publishing are methods of the connected form only. Code that holds a broker before connect has nothing to subscribe with, and shutdown consumes the connection it closes, so these mistakes do not compile. start() connects the brokers in the order they were registered, opens every subscription against its connected broker and runs the after_startup hooks. A failure on the way closes what is already open, in reverse order. shutdown() stops the loops, drains them and closes the brokers in reverse registration order. Where each hook runs is drawn on Async. A publisher handed out earlier can outlive the connection. Using it after shutdown returns an error. The conformance suite holds every broker crate to this rule.

The stages one delivery passes, from the broker's stream to its settlement, in the order the runtime runs them. The path of a delivery that is answered, from the broker's stream to its settlementSubscription streamopened once, at startupDispatch loopthe delivery in a reused slotConsume layersthe first one added is outermostDecodethe mounting's codec, or the bytesHandlerasync fn under #[subscriber]Replyencoded into the loop's bufferPublish transformsin the order the chain names themPublish layersaround every publishPublishersends the reply to the brokerSettlementack, or retry if the reply failed The diagram as text Subscription stream opened once, at startup → Dispatch loop the delivery in a reused slot Dispatch loop the delivery in a reused slot → Consume layers the first one added is outermost Consume layers the first one added is outermost → Decode the mounting's codec, or the bytes Decode the mounting's codec, or the bytes → Handler async fn under #[subscriber] Handler async fn under #[subscriber] → Reply encoded into the loop's buffer Reply encoded into the loop's buffer → Publish transforms in the order the chain names them Publish transforms in the order the chain names them → Publish layers around every publish Publish layers around every publish → Publisher sends the reply to the broker Publisher sends the reply to the broker → Settlement ack, or retry if the reply failed The subscription and the reply's publisher are resolved once, when the app starts, against the connected broker. Nothing on this path looks a subscription or a publisher up per message. Consume layers wrap the decode, so a layer sees a delivery even when its payload does not decode. A payload that does not decode never reaches the handler: the failure policy settles it. A handler with no reply settles right after its body. A handler that returns an error outcome skips the reply. A reply that fails to publish settles the delivery with a retry, so the request is not lost. The reply goes where its type declares. A publisher that only reads the bytes is lent the dispatch loop's own buffer, so a reply allocates nothing. A publisher that keeps the bytes gets a buffer of its own.

How a delivery is settled: what the handler returns, what a failure policy decides, and where a retry ends. From a delivery to its settlement: decode, handler, outcome, retry and dead letterdecodedreturnsother policiesA deliveryDecodethe payloadHandlerrunsOutcomewhat the body returnedDoes not decode:drop by defaultPanics:fail_fast by default,the service stopsack()acknowledgeddrop()rejectedretry()nowretry_afterlaterThe attempt cap is checked firstBelow the cap:requeued, or acopy to theretry addressAt the cap:a copy to thedead letterAt the cap,no dead letter:rejectedAfter settling:and_after and hooks run The diagram as text A delivery → Decode the payload Decode the payload → Handler runs: decoded Decode the payload → Does not decode: drop by default Handler runs → Outcome what the body returned: returns Handler runs → Panics: fail_fast by default, the service stops Does not decode: drop by default → Outcome what the body returned Panics: fail_fast by default, the service stops → Outcome what the body returned: other policies Outcome what the body returned → ack() acknowledged Outcome what the body returned → drop() rejected Outcome what the body returned → retry() now Outcome what the body returned → retry_after later retry() now → The attempt cap is checked first retry_after later → The attempt cap is checked first The attempt cap is checked first → Below the cap: requeued, or a copy to the retry address The attempt cap is checked first → At the cap: a copy to the dead letter The attempt cap is checked first → At the cap, no dead letter: rejected After settling: and_after and hooks run A handler's outcome is a value. Ok acknowledges, and an error outcome says how to settle. A plain Result<(), E> that fails is dropped, not retried. A payload that does not decode and a handler that panics go through the failure policy. A policy other than fail_fast settles the delivery like the outcome of the same name, and skip acknowledges it. fail_fast stops the service and leaves the delivery unsettled, so a broker that redelivers hands it back after the restart. An immediate retry() with no attempt cap and no dead letter declared is the broker's own requeue. Under a declaration, a broker that counts its redeliveries still requeues, and the count is the broker's. On a broker that counts nothing, the runtime publishes a copy to the subscription's retry address instead and drops the original. The copy carries its attempt count in a header. A delayed retry_after waits on the broker's own delayed redelivery where it has one. Elsewhere the runtime publishes the copy after the delay, with or without a declaration. A declared cap is checked before either retry. At the cap, a delivery with a declared dead letter is copied there, and one without is rejected. A broker that moves a spent delivery itself receives the declaration at startup and applies it on its own. A settlement that the broker refuses is logged, and the loop moves on.

Handlers, routers, codecs, and middleware are broker-agnostic. You can move a service to another broker by changing one line at with_broker. The framework ships a full in-memory broker for queues that stay inside a single application. Brokers backed by an external service are separate crates you add as a dependency. Each broker crate has its own documentation site, linked in the Docs column and from the Brokers menu. Every broker is constructed synchronously. The runtime connects it when the application starts. The examples below differ only in the line that constructs the broker. Memory NATS Redis RabbitMQ Kafka use ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker; use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include_router(routes::orders())) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_nats::NatsBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_fred::RedisBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_lapin::LapinBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_rdkafka::KafkaBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }, ) } Each broker crate documents its own connection options. When a subscription needs broker-specific options (consumer groups, durable names), you can write that broker's descriptor in the #[subscriber(..)] attribute; see broker-specific descriptors.

MemoryBroker is a complete broker that runs inside the service's process. It comes with the memory feature of ruststream and needs no server, so it suits a queue that belongs to one application. The default cargo generate template starts on it. ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } How to use it is in the Memory broker components: the broker and its prelude, a retaining log to replay, and pattern subscriptions.
The building blocks of a RustStream service, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to.

A RustStream value names the service, holds its brokers and mounts each handler on the broker it subscribes to. AppInfo holds the service's title and version, and AppInfo::new takes them. They name the service in its logs and in its AsyncAPI document. with_broker registers one broker and mounts handlers on it inside the closure, a BrokerScope. A service with several brokers calls it once per broker. A broker constructor does no I/O: the application connects every broker when it starts. Handlers mounted with b.include(..) decode with the default codec; with_broker_codec names another one for the whole scope. register_broker adds a broker that only publishes and has no handlers. A builder function returns impl App, so its signature stays the same as layers and state are added.

Macros Manual examples/quickstart.rs #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "got order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/quickstart.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(handle); }) } examples/manual/quickstart.rs #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, } /// The handler: `#[subscriber("orders")]` generates this type and this impl. Every axis of the /// form - the reply, the injections, the broker context, the application state - is a defaulted /// parameter of `Handle`, so a plain body names none of them. struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "got order"); ready(Ok(())) } } examples/manual/quickstart.rs fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

The #[ruststream::app] attribute turns a builder function into the service's main: a binary that runs the service or prints its AsyncAPI document. The attribute keeps the function and adds a main that hands it to run_main. The function is synchronous, takes no arguments and returns impl App or a RustStream; any other signature is a compile error. The function is the application builder, unchanged. The binary reads its first argument as a command, the same commands the CLI drives through cargo run. run, or no argument, runs the service until SIGINT or SIGTERM. asyncapi gen prints the AsyncAPI document; -o <file> writes it to a file and --yaml switches the format from JSON. asyncapi gen needs the crate's asyncapi feature. With the logging feature, run installs the console logger first, unless the service installed a subscriber of its own. An error is printed to stderr and the process exits with a failure code. The attribute takes the runtime arguments of #[tokio::main]: flavor = "current_thread" and worker_threads = n. The default is a multi-threaded runtime with one worker per core. A hand-written main calls run_main_on to choose the runtime as an AppRuntime value. A test runs the same builder function on TestApp, as the example does.

Macros Manual examples/app_macro.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } examples/manual/app_macro.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); }) } // What `#[ruststream::app]` writes: the command line (`run`, `asyncapi gen`) on a multi-threaded // Tokio runtime. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

The ruststream command runs a service and prints its AsyncAPI document through cargo run; cargo generate scaffolds a new one. ruststream run executes cargo run -- run against the crate's Cargo.toml, and ruststream asyncapi gen executes cargo run -- asyncapi gen. The service's own binary does the work: the main that #[ruststream::app] generates understands both commands. That main hands the commands to run_main, and the runtime::cli module documents them. cargo run -- run and cargo run -- asyncapi gen therefore give the same result without the command installed. The same run is one call from code. -p points at another crate or its Cargo.toml, and --release builds in release mode. asyncapi gen needs the service crate's asyncapi feature; the starter template enables it. The template's console logs come from its logging feature. cargo generate comes from the cargo-generate project; a broker crate ships templates of its own for its transport.

Install the command: cargo install ruststream --features cli Scaffold a service from the in-memory starter template: cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream templates/memory --name my-service cd my-service The template writes a crate whose main is generated by #[ruststream::app]: Cargo.toml src/main.rs src/orders.rs src/routes.rs Run it; Ctrl+C stops it gracefully: ruststream run Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.02s Running `target/debug/my-service run` 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254761Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle starting service service=my-service version=0.1.0 brokers=1 subscribers=2 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254790Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle broker connected broker="ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254844Z INFO ruststream::dispatch subscriber started subscriber=orders input="my_service::orders::Order" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254854Z INFO ruststream::dispatch subscriber started subscriber=cancellations input="my_service::orders::Order" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254859Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle service running subscribers=2 2026-10-16T07:50:00.281593Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle shutdown signal received 2026-10-16T07:50:00.281755Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle service stopped Print the AsyncAPI document: ruststream asyncapi gen Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.02s Running `target/debug/my-service asyncapi gen` { "asyncapi": "3.1.0", "info": { "title": "my-service", "version": "0.1.0" }, "defaultContentType": "application/json", "channels": { "cancellations": { "address": "cancellations", ... Write it as YAML, to a file, or for a crate in another directory: ruststream asyncapi gen --yaml ruststream asyncapi gen -o asyncapi.json ruststream asyncapi gen -p ../my-service

Four hooks run around the brokers' connection: on_startup, after_startup, on_shutdown and after_shutdown. on_startup runs before any broker connects. The value it returns becomes the application state, and its error aborts startup with no broker dialled. on_startup comes first in the builder: a hook registered before it makes the builder panic. after_startup runs once every subscription is open; its error aborts startup and shuts down the brokers that connected. on_shutdown runs when shutdown begins, while the brokers are still connected. after_shutdown runs after the brokers have shut down. The shutdown hooks' errors are logged and do not stop the shutdown. Every hook after on_startup receives the state as Arc<State>. shutdown_timeout bounds how long shutdown waits for handlers still running; past it, they are aborted. Without it, shutdown waits for them indefinitely. A broker scope's after_startup receives a live publisher of that broker, paired from the policy it names. TestApp runs every hook in the service's order: the startup hooks on start, the shutdown hooks on shutdown.

pool.record("open"); pool } fn record(&self, event: &'static str) { if let Ok(mut log) = self.log.lock() { log.push(event); } } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); Macros Manual examples/app_lifecycle.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "services.started")] struct Started { service: String, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); // Runs once the subscriptions are open, with a publisher of this broker. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }) } examples/manual/app_lifecycle.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Started { service: String, } // `#[outgoing(name = "services.started")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Started { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "services.started"; } impl MessageHeaders for Started { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); // Runs once the subscriptions are open, with a publisher of this broker. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }) }
A service runs until a signal, until a future of yours, or beside another server that owns the process.

health hands out a HealthProbe that reports whether a started service is running, stopping, stopped or failed, and how many of its subscriptions consume. The probe is a cheap clone, so each task that reports health holds its own. Its state is a HealthState: Running, ShuttingDown, Stopped or Failed with the fail-fast diagnostic. The probe outlives shutdown and keeps reporting the final state. stopping resolves when the service tears itself down after a fail-fast failure, so a server beside it can stop with it, as the HTTP page shows. subscriptions returns a SubscriptionCount: the subscriptions that consume and the subscriptions the service started. A subscription counts once, whatever its number of workers. The count changes only when a subscription starts or stops, so a delivery pays nothing for it.

examples/http_outbox.rs /// The liveness endpoint: the probe outlives `shutdown`, so this route reports the terminal /// state for as long as requests still reach it. Here that window is the graceful drain: a /// fail-fast also resolves the `stopping()` future below and stops the HTTP server. A host /// that should keep serving after the messaging side dies would omit that select arm. /// /// This service is unhealthy once a subscription stops consuming, even though the rest of it /// still runs: the orders it no longer reads would wait unanswered. async fn healthz(State(health): State<HealthProbe>) -> (StatusCode, String) { let count = health.subscriptions(); match health.state() { HealthState::Running if count.active == count.started => { (StatusCode::OK, "running".to_owned()) } HealthState::Running => ( StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, format!( "{} of {} subscriptions consuming", count.active, count.started ), ), state => (StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, format!("{state:?}")), } }

A subscription's stream can end while the service runs: the server cancels a consumer when its queue is deleted, or the broker gives up reconnecting. By default the subscription logs the end and stops, and the rest of the service runs on. The probe still reports Running and counts one subscription fewer, and the service decides whether that is healthy. on_subscription_end with SubscriptionEnd::FailFast makes the end a fail-fast failure instead. The service then shuts down gracefully, run returns an error that names the subscription, and the probe reports Failed. An end during shutdown is part of the shutdown and is never reported. examples/app_running.rs /// The service exists to answer orders, so a subscription whose stream ends while the /// service runs stops the service. fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_subscription_end(SubscriptionEnd::FailFast) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(issue_receipt).out_reply(Publish); }) }

An HTTP server owns the process and the service runs beside it: started before the server, stopped after it. The service starts with start before the server accepts traffic, so a startup failure stops the process early. publisher pairs a bound token with its connected broker, for a task beside the service that publishes. The example's relay task publishes the orders an HTTP request stored in a transactional outbox. The server stops on Ctrl+C, or when stopping reports a fail-fast failure of the service. The service then drains with shutdown.

Macros Manual examples/http_outbox.rs #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); // A token, not a publisher: minted before registration, paired after start. let egress = broker.bind(Publish); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(fulfil); }); // The messaging side starts in the background; a startup failure (a broker refusing to // connect, a subscription failing to open) surfaces here, before HTTP accepts traffic. let running = app.start().await?; // The handle existing witnesses that startup connected the broker, so the relay task gets a // live publisher, never a "not connected" state. let egress = running.publisher(egress).await?; let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Store::default())); tokio::spawn(relay_outbox(store.clone(), egress)); let router = Router::new() .route("/orders", post(place_order)) .with_state(store) // The health probe is `Clone` and outlives the app handle; /healthz flips to 503 the // moment the messaging side fail-fasts, answering through the graceful drain below. .route("/healthz", get(healthz).with_state(running.health())); let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?; tracing::info!("orders API on http://127.0.0.1:8080/orders"); // The host owns the signals.
