run starts the service and serves until SIGINT or SIGTERM, then shuts it down gracefully. run is the whole process: it connects the brokers, opens the subscriptions and runs the startup hooks, then waits for a signal. A startup failure is the error it returns. A signal starts the same shutdown a started service gets. A subscriber that fails fast tears the service down, and run returns that failure as its error. A subscription whose stream ends while the service runs does the same under SubscriptionEnd::FailFast. The main that #[ruststream::app] generates calls run.

examples/app_running.rs /// Runs the service until `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, then shuts it down gracefully. async fn serve_forever(broker: MemoryBroker) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { app(broker).run().await?; Ok(()) }

shutdown stops a started service gracefully: hooks, subscriptions, running handlers, then the brokers. shutdown runs on_shutdown, stops the subscriptions and waits for the handlers still running. It then shuts the brokers down in reverse order of registration and runs after_shutdown. The lifecycle page shows the hooks, and shutdown_timeout there bounds the wait for running handlers. A service that already tore itself down after a fail-fast failure returns that failure from shutdown. Dropping a RunningApp without shutdown detaches the service with no graceful shutdown.

examples/app_running.rs /// Stops a started service: the shutdown hooks run and the handlers in flight finish first. async fn stop(running: RunningApp) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let health = running.health(); running.shutdown().await?; tracing::info!(state = ?health.state(), "stopped"); Ok(()) }

start brings the service up and returns a RunningApp, so the caller owns the process and decides when it stops. start connects the brokers, opens the subscriptions and runs the startup hooks, then returns. A startup failure is the error start returns, before the caller accepts its own traffic. start installs no signal handlers: the caller stops the service with shutdown. The RunningApp also hands out the service's health and publishers for tasks beside it, as the HTTP page shows.

examples/app_running.rs /// Starts the service beside other work of the process, and stops it once that work is done. async fn serve( broker: MemoryBroker, work: impl Future<Output = ()> + Send, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // `start` returns once every subscription is open. let running = app(broker).start().await?; work.await; running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

run_until serves until a future of yours resolves, then shuts the service down gracefully. It starts the service the way run does, and installs no signal handlers. The future starts once the service has started, so it may publish to the service and wait for the answer. A subscriber that fails fast ends the run before the future resolves, and run_until returns that failure as its error.

examples/app_running.rs /// Runs the service until `work` resolves; `work` starts once the service has started. async fn serve_until( broker: MemoryBroker, work: impl Future<Output = ()> + Send, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { app(broker).run_until(work).await?; Ok(()) }
Shared state is one value built at startup that every handler reads, as a State<T> parameter or through a dependency-injection container.

on_startup builds one value of any type; a handler takes any of its fields as a State<T> parameter. on_startup runs once, before any broker connects, and its value becomes the application state. Its future can await: open a pool, connect a client, read a file. on_startup comes before with_broker, because it fixes the state type every handler is checked against. The lifecycle hooks after it receive the same state. #[derive(FromRef)] writes one FromRef impl per field, each cloning that field. A handler parameter State(prices): State<Prices> resolves through that impl before the body runs. A field that is expensive to clone goes behind an Arc, so a delivery pays one reference count. A handler can also borrow the whole state with ctx.state() from its &mut Context<'_, (), AppState> parameter, with no clone. A hand-written FromRef impl builds a value from several fields. A dependency-injection container fills the same role: froodi with RustStream support, or shaku wired by hand.

Macros Manual examples/app_state.rs /// A price list, loaded once at startup. #[derive(Clone)] struct Prices { per_item: u64, } /// The application state: each field is available to a handler as `State<FieldType>`. #[derive(FromRef)] struct AppState { prices: Prices, } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order, State(prices): State<Prices>) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: order.items * prices.per_item, } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { prices: Prices { per_item: 25 }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(price).out_reply(Publish); }) } examples/manual/app_state.rs /// A price list, loaded once at startup. #[derive(Clone)] struct Prices { per_item: u64, } /// The application state. struct AppState { prices: Prices, } // What `#[derive(FromRef)]` writes for each field: `State<Prices>` resolves through it. impl FromRef<AppState> for Prices { fn from_ref(state: &AppState) -> Self { state.prices.clone() } } struct Price; // The state type is the last parameter of `Handle`; the mount checks it against the app's. impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), (), AppState> for Price { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let prices = Prices::from_ref(ctx.state()); ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: order.items * prices.per_item, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { prices: Prices { per_item: 25 }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); }) }

froodi (crates.io, docs.rs, GitHub) is a dependency-injection container whose ruststream feature builds a handler's dependencies per delivery, as Inject parameters. The registry declares each dependency with the scope it lives in. Config lives in the App scope, as long as the container. Pricing lives in the Request scope and is built from Config by its factory. ContainerLayer is a middleware, mounted with RustStream::layer: for every delivery it enters a child Request scope, runs the handler inside it and closes the scope once the handler has answered. Closing the scope runs the finalizers of what it built before the message is settled. Inject<Pricing> is a FromContext extractor that resolves from that child scope, so two parameters of one delivery share an instance. InjectTransient<T> builds a fresh instance for each parameter instead. A dependency the container cannot resolve drops the delivery and logs the channel and the type. A handler that takes Inject in a service with no ContainerLayer drops every delivery the same way. The layer builds a child container for every delivery, which allocates; dependencies in the App scope are built once. With froodi's async feature, AsyncContainerLayer holds a container whose factories and finalizers can await.

Macros Manual Cargo.toml [dependencies] froodi = { version = "1.0.0-beta.19", features = ["ruststream"] } ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } src/lib.rs use froodi::ruststream::ContainerLayer; use froodi::{Container, DefaultScope, Inject, instance, registry}; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] pub struct Order { pub id: u64, pub items: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] pub struct Receipt { pub order_id: u64, pub total: u64, } /// Lives as long as the application. #[derive(Clone)] pub struct Config { pub price_per_item: u64, } /// Built for every delivery from the configuration. pub struct Pricing { per_item: u64, } impl Pricing { fn total(&self, order: &Order) -> u64 { order.items * self.per_item } } fn container(config: Config) -> Container { Container::new(registry! { provide(DefaultScope::App, instance(config)), scope(DefaultScope::Request) [ provide(|Inject(config): Inject<Config>| Ok(Pricing { per_item: config.price_per_item, })), ], }) } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order, Inject(pricing): Inject<Pricing>) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: pricing.total(order), } } pub fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(ContainerLayer::new(container(Config { price_per_item: 25, }))) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(price).out_reply(Publish); }) } Cargo.toml [dependencies] froodi = { version = "1.0.0-beta.19", features = ["ruststream"] } ruststream = { version = "0.7", default-features = false, features = ["memory", "json"] } schemars = "1" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } src/lib.rs use froodi::ruststream::ContainerLayer; use froodi::{Container, DefaultScope, Inject, instance, registry}; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use schemars::JsonSchema; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub struct Order { pub id: u64, pub items: u64, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the call site names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub struct Receipt { pub order_id: u64, pub total: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "receipts")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// Lives as long as the application. #[derive(Clone)] pub struct Config { pub price_per_item: u64, } /// Built for every delivery from the configuration. pub struct Pricing { per_item: u64, } impl Pricing { fn total(&self, order: &Order) -> u64 { order.items * self.per_item } } fn container(config: Config) -> Container { Container::new(registry! { provide(DefaultScope::App, instance(config)), scope(DefaultScope::Request) [ provide(|Inject(config): Inject<Config>| Ok(Pricing { per_item: config.price_per_item, })), ], }) } struct Price; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Price { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { // What the attribute emits for `Inject(pricing): Inject<Pricing>`: a failed resolution // settles the delivery by its outcome and the body does not run. let Inject(pricing) = <Inject<Pricing> as FromContext>::from_context(ctx) .await .map_err(HandlerOutcome::from)?; Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: pricing.total(order), }) } } pub fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(ContainerLayer::new(container(Config { price_per_item: 25, }))) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); }) }

shaku (crates.io, docs.rs, GitHub) is a dependency-injection container with no RustStream support; the service builds it in on_startup and a handler resolves from it. A shaku module is the container: module! lists its components, and each component implements an interface trait. on_startup builds the module with the components' parameters, and the module becomes the application state. A FromRef impl from the module to Arc<dyn Pricing> lets a handler take State<Arc<dyn Pricing>>, as for any struct as state. The module resolves a component as a clone of its Arc, so each delivery pays one reference count and the calls go through dyn Pricing. A handler that reads ctx.state().resolve_ref() borrows the component instead, with no reference count. Components are singletons of the module and are Send + Sync, so every handler on every worker shares them. An interface method that awaits needs a dyn-compatible form, such as one returning a boxed future.

Macros Manual Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } shaku = "0.6" src/lib.rs use std::convert::Infallible; use std::sync::Arc; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; use shaku::{Component, HasComponent, Interface, module}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] pub struct Order { pub id: u64, pub items: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] pub struct Receipt { pub order_id: u64, pub total: u64, } /// The service a handler asks the container for. pub trait Pricing: Interface { fn total(&self, order: &Order) -> u64; } #[derive(Component)] #[shaku(interface = Pricing)] struct FlatPricing { per_item: u64, } impl Pricing for FlatPricing { fn total(&self, order: &Order) -> u64 { order.items * self.per_item } } module! { OrdersModule { components = [FlatPricing], providers = [] } } // The bridge from the container to `State<T>`: a handler that takes `State<Arc<dyn Pricing>>` // gets the component the module resolves. impl FromRef<OrdersModule> for Arc<dyn Pricing> { fn from_ref(module: &OrdersModule) -> Self { module.resolve() } } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order, State(pricing): State<Arc<dyn Pricing>>) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: pricing.total(order), } } pub fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // The container is built once, before the brokers connect, and becomes the app state. .on_startup(async move |()| { let module = OrdersModule::builder() .with_component_parameters::<FlatPricing>(FlatPricingParameters { per_item: 25 }) .build(); Ok::<_, Infallible>(module) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(price).out_reply(Publish); }) } Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", default-features = false, features = ["memory", "json"] } schemars = "1" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } shaku = "0.6" src/lib.rs use std::convert::Infallible; TestApp runs a service's production app in process, drives its brokers and asserts on what its handlers received and published.
How a test publishes to a broker of the app and moves the app forward: settling deliveries and advancing time.

TestApp::advance lets a delay pass, fires the delayed redeliveries now due, and drives their reaction to a standstill. A handler that answers retry_after(delay) settles at once, and the publish returns with the delivery pending. advance(delay) then delivers the message again, by a broker's native delayed redelivery or by the runtime's deferred copy. In process it moves the paused clock, so the test starts paused with #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]. On a running clock the in-process advance panics. In a start_live test it lets the time pass for real, because the delay is the broker's own timer. A copy the runtime publishes for a zero delay arrives in the same reaction, without advance. settle drives a reaction without moving the clock.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn an_uncleared_payment_is_checked_again_later() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 7, cleared: false, }; tb.message(&payment).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK)); tb.advance(RECHECK).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&payment); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn an_uncleared_payment_is_checked_again_later() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 7, cleared: false, }; tb.message(&payment).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK)); tb.advance(RECHECK).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&payment); Ok(()) }

TestApp::broker_named addresses a broker by the label it was registered under, which tells apart two brokers of one type. The label is the one with_broker_labeled gives the broker in the app. The handle is the one broker::<B>() returns: it publishes onto that broker and reads its records, such as subscriber(name). A publish onto one broker reaches only that broker's subscriptions. In the example with shows which handler received the value. broker_named panics when no broker carries the label.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_stays_in_its_region() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker_named("eu") .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker_named("eu") .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); tb.broker_named("us") .subscriber("orders") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_stays_in_its_region() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker_named("eu") .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker_named("eu") .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); tb.broker_named("us") .subscriber("orders") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) }

TestApp::broker addresses one broker of the app by its production type, for publishing to it and reading its records. B is the type the app registered, so MemoryBroker and MemoryBroker<Retaining> are two different brokers. The BrokerHandle it returns publishes onto that broker with message(&v) and opens its records: subscriber(name) and published::<T>(name). A subscription name is local to its broker: the "orders" of one broker is not the "orders" of the other. broker panics when the app has no broker of type B or more than one; two brokers of one type are addressed by label with broker_named. In live mode the test's input reaches the broker through its connected form's default publish policy.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn each_broker_is_addressed_by_its_type() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker<Retaining>>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker<Retaining>>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once(); tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn each_broker_is_addressed_by_its_type() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker<Retaining>>() .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker<Retaining>>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once(); tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) }

TestApp::drain waits for the post-settle continuations of everything settled so far, for a test that asserts on their effects. A continuation is work a handler attaches to its outcome, ack().and_after(..), or to its context with after(..) or after_settle(..). It runs on its own task after the delivery settles, so a publish can return before it has finished. A settlement registers its continuations before it releases the delivery, so drain after a publish finds them all. An effect of the handler body itself needs no drain: the publish has already settled it. In the example the test builds the state with with_state to read the mail client's record afterwards. shutdown waits for continuations too.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_confirmation_follows_the_ack() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mailer = Arc::new(Mailer::default()); let tb = TestApp::with_state(app(), |_| Arc::clone(&mailer)).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.drain().await; let sent = mailer.sent.lock().map_err(|_| "a confirmation panicked")?; assert_eq!(*sent, [7]); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_confirmation_follows_the_ack() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mailer = Arc::new(Mailer::default()); let tb = TestApp::with_state(app(), |_| Arc::clone(&mailer)).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.drain().await; let sent = mailer.sent.lock().map_err(|_| "a confirmation panicked")?; assert_eq!(*sent, [7]); Ok(()) }

message(&v) starts an input with the publish builder the service itself publishes through: destination, headers and codec. The value is an Outgoing type, and the type decides whether the builder still asks for a destination. A type that names its destination publishes there; a type that names none takes to(name). with_headers(&meta) adds a typed header contract, and with_codec(codec) encodes with another codec than the default one. publish() sends the input and drives the reaction, and with checks the value the handler received. TestApp::message publishes onto the app's only broker. With more than one broker it has no single target, so the publish fails with TestError::Ambiguous. tb.broker::<B>().message(..), the BrokerHandle::message of a broker chosen with broker::<B>() or broker_named, publishes onto that broker. A value whose type the test does not own goes through the shortcuts.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn inputs_are_built_like_the_service_builds_its_own() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .message(&Refund { order_id: 7 }) .to("refunds") .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); broker .subscriber("refunds") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refund { order_id: 7 }); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn inputs_are_built_like_the_service_builds_its_own() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .message(&Refund { order_id: 7 }) .to("refunds") .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); broker .subscriber("refunds") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refund { order_id: 7 }); Ok(()) }

TestApp::publish and BrokerHandle::publish send any serde value to a named destination in one call; publish_with_headers adds headers. They are for a value whose type the test does not own, such as a serde_json::Value. The builder of message(&v) needs the type to declare a destination, and the orphan rule keeps a foreign type from declaring one. The value is encoded with the default codec and sent to name; the call then drives the reaction like publish(). publish_with_headers serializes a typed header contract into the delivery's headers, the input a Message<H, P> or Headers<H> handler reads. TestApp::publish needs a single broker and fails with TestError::Ambiguous otherwise. A value that does not encode fails the call with TestError::Encode.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn any_serde_value_can_be_published() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.publish("orders", &json!({ "id": 7 })).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .publish_with_headers( "tenant-orders", &json!({ "id": 8 }), &Tenant { tenant: "acme".to_owned(), }, ) .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); broker .subscriber("tenant-orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn any_serde_value_can_be_published() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.publish("orders", &json!({ "id": 7 })).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .publish_with_headers( "tenant-orders", &json!({ "id": 8 }), &Tenant { tenant: "acme".to_owned(), }, ) .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&Order { id: 7 }); broker .subscriber("tenant-orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) }

publish() sends the input onto the broker and returns once the whole reaction to it has settled, so the next line can assert. The input, built with message(&v), enters the broker the way an external producer's message would. The reaction covers the handlers it reaches, their replies and slot publishes, and the handlers those reach, across brokers. In the example the receipt the first handler replies with is filed before publish returns, and with reads the value the handler received. A reaction that does not settle within 10,000 dispatched deliveries fails the publish with TestError::NotQuiescent, which catches an endless requeue. A publish after a fail-fast failure stopped the TestApp fails with TestError::ShutDown. settle drives a reaction the test started some other way, and advance lets a delayed redelivery come due.

Macros Manual examples/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_whole_reaction_is_over_when_publish_returns() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order_id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_driving.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_whole_reaction_is_over_when_publish_returns() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&Order { id: 7 }).publish().await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { order_id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) }

TestApp::settle drives a reaction the test started without the harness to a standstill, without publishing anything new. A publish through the harness settles for you; settle is for input that arrived some other way, such as a bare publisher of the broker. A batch handler needs it: each harness publish settles alone, so the batch it reaches holds one message. Two messages sent through a bare publisher wait together, and settle delivers them as one batch, which assert_batch_sizes reads back. In process settle waits until the transports report nothing in flight. In live mode it waits until every subscription has handled what the harness saw published to it, up to the deadline of start_live. advance settles after a delay has passed.

Per-message settings are the broker's Publisher::Options; the memory broker's publisher has none, so the example wraps it with a priority, as a networked broker ships one. The harness records the settings with every publish the runtime makes (a reply, a slot publish, a retry copy), on the broker it went to. Both records read them: a slot record, out::<M>(), and a destination record, published::<T>(name). A message the test publishes itself carries no recorded settings. The assertion names the broker's own type and panics when the latest publish carried no settings, carried another type, or carried a different value. It also panics when it cannot tell which settings the latest publish carried: another publish to the destination had the same payload, and either their order is unknown or the harness never saw that publish. assert_options_default checks that no step set any.

The records a test reads: what one subscriber received, what was published to a destination, and what went through an Out slot.

out::<M>() opens the record of one Out slot: every message the handler sent through it, on whichever broker it went. M is the slot's marker type, the one the handler names in Out<impl Publisher, M>, and it implements OutSlot. The record is attributed by slot, not by destination, so it shows which slot sent a message when two slots share a destination. published::<T>(name) is the record of one destination on one broker. Each entry keeps the destination name, the headers and the per-message settings of the publish, which with_options checks. The record is untyped: decoded_as::<U>() turns it into one that decodes to U. messages returns every entry for checks of your own. A publish made outside the handler task, such as a spawned task, is not attributed to the slot.

published::<T>(name) opens the record of one destination on a broker: every message published there, with its name and headers. T is the payload type that with and decoded decode to; the count and raw assertions ignore it. The assertions are those of PublishedAssertions, such as assert_called_once. In process the record is the broker's own publish log, so it holds replies, Out slot publishes, retry copies and the test's own publishes. out::<M>() shows what left through one slot, across brokers, and subscriber(name) is the record of a handler. Against a running stand it holds the test's publishes and everything a publisher wired by the runtime sent. The record is a snapshot taken when the method is called: call it after the publish that drives the reaction.

How a test starts the production app, gives it state, and shuts it down.

TestApp::shutdown tears the service down gracefully and returns what run would return, so a fail-fast failure fails the test. It is the service's own shutdown, step for step. It runs on_shutdown, stops the dispatch loops, and waits for in-flight handlers and post-settle continuations. It then shuts the brokers down in reverse order of registration and runs after_shutdown. The wait for handlers and continuations is bounded by the app's shutdown timeout. A failing shutdown hook is logged, and the shutdown goes on, as in the service. The result is Ok for a healthy run and RustStreamError::Dispatch after a fail-fast failure, such as a handler panic under the default policy. A broker that fails to shut down returns the service's error for it too. run_result gives the same result while the harness is still running, and assert_shut_down asserts the failure. shutdown takes the harness by value, so nothing can be published after it.

start_live connects the brokers of the same app to a running stand, so one test body checks the service against the real broker. It is for a stand of a networked broker: a Kafka or NATS server the test suite starts beside the tests. Each broker connects through its ordinary connect, and the rest of startup is the production one. The test body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs from TestApp::start. MemoryBroker connects without a server, so the example runs in process in every mode. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most; start_live_within sets another bound, and past it the call fails with TestError::NotSettled naming the subscription. A live test runs on the real clock: start_live on a paused clock fails with TestError::PausedClock. The test's input reaches the broker through its connected form's default publish policy.

TestApp::start runs the app main builds, unchanged, with every broker connected in process and no server. The harness starts the app in the service's own order: on_startup, then each broker's connect, then the subscriptions, then after_startup. Each broker connects through its in-process transition, which performs no I/O and yields the broker's production connected form. MemoryBroker has no server, so its in-process mode is its ordinary connect. A networked broker provides the in-process mode under its crate's testing feature, which a service enables in [dev-dependencies]. A broker without it makes start fail with TestError::NoTransport naming the broker. A failing on_startup fails start with TestError::Startup before any broker connects. start_live runs the same app against a running stand, and with_state starts it with a state the test builds. A test ends with shutdown.

TestApp::with_state starts the app with a state the test builds in place of on_startup, wired to the brokers of the app. It is for a state that reaches outside the service: a catalog, a database, a mail client the test cannot or should not call. The harness connects each broker in process first, then calls the builder, so the state's publishers pair against connected brokers. TestBrokers::broker::<B>() returns the connected form of the app's broker of type B. A publisher built from it publishes onto the bus the assertions read, such as published::<T>(name) and its with. The app's on_startup does not run; after_startup and everything else of startup do, as in TestApp::start. TestBrokers::broker panics when the app has no broker of type B or more than one.

Assertions on one subscriber: how often it ran, what it received and how each delivery was settled.

assert_batch_sizes(&[..]) checks how a subscriber's deliveries were cut into handler calls. Each number is the size of one call, in call order. The mount names the largest size, batch(nonzero!(2)); the broker builds the batches, and this reads back what it built. One batch is one call, so five orders in batches of two make assert_called(3). A single-message handler is called per delivery, so three deliveries read [1, 1, 1]. The batches come from a replayed log, as on the batches page. A batch built from a bare publisher is driven with settle.

assert_called_once checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly once: one delivery, or one batch. It counts handler calls in the record, subscriber(name), not messages: a batch handler called with five orders counts once. A delivery that did not decode counts too: the record holds it although the body never ran. It returns the assertions, so with, with_raw and settled chain after it and read that one call. On failure it panics with the number of calls it found. assert_called(n) checks any other number, and assert_not_called checks that there was no call.

assert_called(n) checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly n times, counting a batch as one call. n is the number of handler calls. A single-message handler is called once per delivery, and once more for each redelivery. A batch handler is called once per batch, so here n counts batches; assert_batch_sizes shows how big each one was. A publish through the harness runs to completion before it returns, so three publishes make three calls. On failure it panics with the number of calls it found. assert_called_once is the same check for one call, and outcomes shows how each call settled. A destination's assert_called(n) counts publishes instead.

assert_last_failed_to_decode() checks that the latest delivery did not decode into the handler's input type. The verdict comes from the codec, or from the broker when its client reports a decode error itself. The record holds the delivery as a call although the body never ran, so assert_called_once counts it. The decode policy settles it: the default drops the message and keeps the service running, which assert_running states. The test injects the bad bytes through a #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] newtype, which publishes them as they are. It returns nothing, so it ends a chain. assert_outcome gives the same verdict as Outcome::DecodeFailed, and panicked checks the other failure a call can end in.

assert_not_called checks that a subscriber's handler never ran. It passes when the record of that subscription, subscriber(name), is empty. A name no handler subscribes to has an empty record as well, so a misspelled name passes. A positive check on a neighbour guards against that: here assert_called_once on "orders" shows the order did arrive. The handler sends only an order without an id on to "rejected", so a valid order leaves the review subscription untouched. It returns nothing, so it ends a chain. assert_called(n) expects any number of calls.

assert_outcome(..) checks the latest handler call by its classified Outcome, failures included. Outcome folds a call into five cases: Ack, Nack, Drop, DecodeFailed and Panicked. Nack covers both retry() and retry_after(..), so the delay plays no part. A panic or a decode failure wins over the settlement: such a call reads as Panicked or DecodeFailed, which panicked and assert_last_failed_to_decode check on their own. Here the delayed copy waits for tb.advance(..) on the paused clock, so the record holds one call. settled checks by HandlerOutcome instead, and outcomes returns the outcome of every call.

batches_raw() returns the bytes a batch handler received, one list per call. It is received_raw with the batch boundaries kept. A single-message handler yields lists of one. Here the handler takes raw frames, &[Frame<'_>], so no codec runs on the way in or in the check. The batches come from a replayed log, as on the batches page. A batch built from a bare publisher is driven with settle.

batches::<T>() returns what a batch handler received, one decoded list per call. Each inner list is one handler call, in call order, so the batch boundaries that received drops stay. It decodes with DefaultCodec; batches_with(&codec) decodes with another codec. A publish through the harness runs each message to completion on its own, so it reaches a batch handler as a batch of one. Fuller batches come from a log that already holds the messages: the test fills a retaining broker, the subscription opens at the start of its log, and tb.settle() drives the replay. The settle page shows a batch built from a bare publisher. The mount names the size, batch(nonzero!(2)), so three orders arrive as two and one. batches_raw returns the same batches as bytes, and assert_batch_sizes checks only the sizes.

outcomes() returns how every handler call settled, in call order. Each entry is an Outcome: Ack, Nack, Drop, DecodeFailed or Panicked. settled and assert_outcome read the latest call only; outcomes pins a sequence, such as a nack followed by the ack of its redelivery. A batch call has one entry, classified by its first delivery. Outcome is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it needs a wildcard arm.

panicked() checks that the handler panicked on its latest call. The harness runs dispatch under the app's real failure policy. Under the default policy, fail_fast, a panic shuts the service down, which tb.assert_shut_down() states. The delivery stays unsettled, so no settled(..) matches it; assert_outcome(Outcome::Panicked) is the same check by outcome. The test output carries the handler's panic message, and the test itself passes. assert_last_failed_to_decode checks the other failure a call can end in. The assert_shut_down and run_result pages show what the panic did to the service.

It fits a check that a chain of assertions cannot say: an order, a subset, a property of every element. with checks the latest payload only, and received_raw returns the same list as bytes.

settled(outcome) checks how the latest handler call settled, against the HandlerOutcome a handler returns. It takes the value a handler answers with: ack(), retry(), drop(), retry_after(..). It compares the settlement alone, so a hook attached with and_after plays no part. For a batch it checks every element of the latest call, which is what one answer for the whole slice produces. The record holds what the handler answered: on a transport that cannot requeue, a retry still reads as a retry, and the missing redelivery shows in assert_called. A fail-fast panic leaves the delivery unsettled, which matches no outcome. assert_outcome is the same check by Outcome, failures included, and outcomes returns every settlement in order.

Macros Manual examples/testing_subscriber_calls.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_without_an_id_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Order { id: 0 }) .to("orders") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_subscriber_calls.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_without_an_id_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Order { id: 0 }) .to("orders") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); Ok(()) }

with_raw(bytes) checks the exact bytes of the latest handler call, before any decoding. It compares the payload as the broker delivered it, so it pins the wire format: here the JSON the default codec wrote. It reads the most recent call only, and that call must hold one delivery. It is the check for a handler that reads bytes itself, where no codec has a value to compare. with checks the same call decoded, and received_raw returns the bytes of every call.

Macros Manual examples/testing_subscriber_payloads.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_order_arrived_as_json() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .to("orders") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with_raw(br#"{"id":7}"#); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_subscriber_payloads.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_order_arrived_as_json() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Order { id: 7 }) .to("orders") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with_raw(br#"{"id":7}"#); Ok(()) }

with_value(&value) checks the value the latest delivery lent its handler, on a broker whose deliveries already hold one. Some brokers decode a delivery in their client and lend the handler that value, such as a database row; the delivery implements Carries<T>. That value never was bytes, so with has nothing to decode; the harness keeps a clone of the lent value instead. The value type needs Clone, PartialEq and Debug. It panics when the latest delivery lent no T: the handler takes another type, or the delivery carried nothing. The row subscription here stands in for such a broker crate: it reads id:name payloads of the in-memory broker as rows (examples/support/carried_rows.rs). received_values returns every lent value, not only the latest.

Macros Manual examples/testing_subscriber_carried.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_handler_got_the_row() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Wire(b"7:alice".to_vec())) .to("users") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("users") .assert_called_once() .with_value(&Row::new(7, "alice")) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_subscriber_carried.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_handler_got_the_row() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&Wire(b"7:alice".to_vec())) .to("users") .publish() .await?; broker .subscriber("users") .assert_called_once() .with_value(&Row::new(7, "alice")) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) }

with(&value) checks that the latest handler call received this value, decoded with the default codec. It reads the most recent call only; the earlier ones are in received. It decodes the recorded payload with DefaultCodec, the codec the enabled features select (json first). A handler mounted with another codec is checked with with_codec(&codec, &value), which decodes with that codec. The value type needs Deserialize, PartialEq and Debug. The latest call must hold one delivery: on a batch of several it panics, and the batch is read with batches. with_raw checks the same call as bytes, and with_value the value a carrying delivery lent the handler. A destination's with checks the value a publish carried.

Macros Manual examples/testing_subscriber_payloads.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_latest_call_got_the_second_order() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); for id in [7, 8] { broker.message(&Order { id }).to("orders").publish().await?; } broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called(2) .with(&Order { id: 8 }); Ok(()) } examples/manual/testing_subscriber_payloads.rs #[tokio::test] async fn the_latest_call_got_the_second_order() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); for id in [7, 8] { broker.message(&Order { id }).to("orders").publish().await?; } broker .subscriber("orders") .assert_called(2) .with(&Order { id: 8 }); Ok(()) }

The asyncapi feature generates the AsyncAPI 3.1 document of a service from its app value, with build_spec. The document is read from what the app registers, so it describes the handlers the service mounts and nothing else. It lists the channels and operations, the message schemas, the servers and who owns the service. It is built on demand, from a test, a command or an HTTP route, and costs the running service nothing.

How the document is produced, serialized and served, and where its payload schemas come from. build_spec reads the document from the app value, and the document serializes to JSON or YAML. The main that the app attribute generates prints it, and a self-contained page renders it. Payload schemas come from a JsonSchema derive on each message type.

build_spec reads the AsyncAPI document of a service from its app value, the same value main runs. The document follows AsyncAPI 3.1. It is read from what the app registers, so it describes the handlers the service mounts and nothing else. Each subscriber becomes a channel named after its subscription, a receive operation, and a message component for its input type. The handler's doc comment is the operation's description, and the input type's doc comment is the message's. A reply rides the receive operation, and each message an Out slot declares gets a send operation. The result is a Spec: plain data with public fields, which a test reads and a tool may complete before it is serialized. The document is built when the function is called, so it costs the running service nothing. The asyncapi feature turns it on. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Accepts every order placed in the shop. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } /// The document of the service, read from the same app value `main` runs. fn document() -> Spec { build_spec(&app()) } examples/manual/asyncapi_generation.rs /// The handler `#[subscriber("orders")]` writes for the body. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Accept) .describe("Accepts every order placed in the shop.") .build(), ); }) } /// The document of the service, read from the same app value `main` runs. fn document() -> Spec { build_spec(&app()) }

asyncapi gen prints the document of a service from the main that #[ruststream::app] generates. The command builds the app with the builder the attribute names and prints what build_spec returns. It prints JSON by default; --yaml prints YAML, and -o <file> writes to a file instead of standard output. The service crate enables the asyncapi feature; without it the command fails with an error that names the feature. The ruststream command runs it through cargo run against a crate, and cargo run -- asyncapi gen does the same without it. A main written by hand gets the same commands from run_main.
In the service crate: cargo run -- asyncapi gen cargo run -- asyncapi gen --yaml -o asyncapi.yaml With the ruststream command installed: ruststream asyncapi gen -o asyncapi.json

.describe(text) gives a manual registration the operation description the attribute takes from the handler's doc comment. describe is a step of the subscriber(..) chain, before .build(); after .reply() it is still available. The text becomes the description of the registration's receive operation. A message's description comes from its own type. A message whose type has no description takes the handler's. On the attribute path the doc comment of the handler function is the description, and the step has no use. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Accepts every order placed in the shop. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_generation.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Accept) .describe("Accepts every order placed in the shop.") .build(), ); }) }

MessageInfo names the component of a message in the document and describes it, whatever the Rust type is called. Channels and operations refer to a message by its component name. Without MessageInfo that name is the schema's title, which schemars takes from the type's name, so renaming the type renames the published message. An impl of MessageInfo keeps the name: NAME is the component's name and DESCRIPTION its description. #[derive(MessageInfo)] writes the impl from the type's name and doc comment. With #[message(headers(Meta))] the derive also declares the type's header contract. #[derive(Outgoing)] implements MessageInfo for the types it derives. Without the macros a registration names the component by the schema's title, so #[schemars(rename = "..")] keeps the published name there. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// A refund a customer asked for. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct RefundRequestV2 { order_id: u64, } /// The component keeps the name the contract was published under, whatever the type is called. impl MessageInfo for RefundRequestV2 { const NAME: &'static str = "RefundRequest"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some("A refund a customer asked for."); } #[subscriber("refunds")] async fn refund(request: &RefundRequestV2) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(request.order_id, "refund requested"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// A refund a customer asked for. // The schema's title names the component: the rename keeps the name the contract was published // under, whatever the type is called. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(rename = "RefundRequest")] struct RefundRequestV2 { order_id: u64, } struct Refund; impl Handle<RefundRequestV2> for Refund { fn handle( &self, request: &RefundRequestV2, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(request.order_id, "refund requested"); ready(Ok(())) } }

messages_without_schema lists the messages the document describes with no payload schema, for a check to fail on. A message without a schema documents its channel but not its shape, and a client generator has no type to produce from it. build_spec logs one warning per gap when it builds the document; this method returns the same list as component names. A test or a release check asserts on it. Messages whose bytes are their own format, on a byte lane, are left out: they have no schema by design. On the attribute path a gap is a message type without a JsonSchema derive. A subscriber(..) registration has one only after undocumented. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } #[subscriber("audit")] async fn record(entry: &AuditRecord) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The release check: every message in the document has a schema, or the check names the ones /// that do not. fn check_schemas(spec: &Spec) -> Result<(), String> { match spec.messages_without_schema().as_slice() { [] => Ok(()), gaps => Err(format!("no payload schema for {}", gaps.join(", "))), } } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } struct Record; impl Handle<AuditRecord> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditRecord, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The release check: every message in the document has a schema, or the check names the ones /// that do not. fn check_schemas(spec: &Spec) -> Result<(), String> { match spec.messages_without_schema().as_slice() { [] => Ok(()), gaps => Err(format!("no payload schema for {}", gaps.join(", "))), } }

A message type that derives JsonSchema gives its message a payload schema in the document. The crate re-exports schemars as ruststream::schemars, so a service needs no dependency of its own for the derive. The schema is JSON Schema draft 07, the draft the AsyncAPI Schema Object extends. Doc comments on the type and its fields become descriptions in the schema, and the type's doc comment is the message's description. serde attributes shape the schema as they shape the wire: a renamed field or an Option reads the same in both. On the attribute path the derive is optional. A type without it still mounts, and its message carries no payload schema. build_spec then logs a warning naming the subscription and the type, and messages_without_schema lists the message. A subscriber(..) registration demands the derive at compile time; undocumented lifts the demand from one registration. A type that carries its own bytes, on a byte lane, has no schema by design and is not listed as missing one. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { /// The order number, unique per shop. id: u64, /// What was ordered. item: String, /// How many items; one when absent. quantity: Option<u32>, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, quantity = ?order.quantity, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { /// The order number, unique per shop. id: u64, /// What was ordered. item: String, /// How many items; one when absent. quantity: Option<u32>, } /// The handler `#[subscriber("orders")]` writes for the body. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, quantity = ?order.quantity, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } }

to_json and to_yaml serialize the document in the two formats AsyncAPI tools read. to_json writes pretty-printed JSON, and to_yaml writes YAML. Each returns its serializer's error; a document build_spec built serializes without one. Servers, channels, operations and components are maps sorted by name, so the output is the same on every run and a change reads as a plain diff in review. The command the generated main understands prints the same text. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Writes the document next to the service's code, in both formats AsyncAPI tools read. fn write_document(dir: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let spec = build_spec(&app()); fs::write(dir.join("asyncapi.json"), spec.to_json()?)?; fs::write(dir.join("asyncapi.yaml"), spec.to_yaml()?)?; Ok(()) }

.undocumented() takes the schemas of one manual registration out of the document and lifts its JsonSchema demand. Under the asyncapi feature a subscriber(..) registration is documented by default. Mounting it demands JsonSchema of its message types, and a type without the derive is a compile error at the mount. undocumented is the exit for one registration, such as one whose message type comes from a crate that ships no schema. The registration stays in the document: its channel and its operation remain, and its messages carry no payload schema. messages_without_schema lists those messages. The step is written once; a second one does not compile. On the attribute path a type without the derive already mounts and contributes no schema, so the attribute has no such step. Without the asyncapi feature a registration demands nothing. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } #[subscriber("audit")] async fn record(entry: &AuditRecord) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); b.include(subscriber("refunds", Refund).build()); // `AuditRecord` has no `JsonSchema`: without this step the mount does not compile. b.include(subscriber("audit", Record).undocumented().build()); }) }

render_viewer_html returns a self-contained HTML page that renders the document with the AsyncAPI React component. The page loads the document from the URL it is given, so the service serves two routes: the document and the page. The function renders a string; serving it is the job of the HTTP stack the service already runs. examples/asyncapi_http.rs in the repository serves both routes with axum. The component and its stylesheet load from jsDelivr, at a pinned version. ViewerOptions sets the page title and another asset base with cdn_base: a mirror, or the service's own assets where the network has no way out. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// The page the service serves at `/docs`: it renders the document served at `/asyncapi.json`. fn docs_page() -> String { let options = ViewerOptions::default().title("Orders events"); render_viewer_html("/asyncapi.json", &options) }

What the document says about a service beyond its channels: replies, channel parameters, headers, content types and retries. Each of them comes from a declaration the runtime already acts on, so the document and the service's behaviour do not drift apart.

A destination declared as a name template becomes a channel whose address keeps its placeholders, each one declared as a parameter. #[outgoing(name = "orders.{tenant}.accepted")] declares a name template. The template is the channel's id and its address. Each {placeholder} is an entry of the channel's parameters. The document names the segments; what a service puts in them is run-time data and is not listed. A type reaches the document where it is published: each type of an Out slot's #[publishes(..)] list gets a send operation on its channel. A type with no declared destination contributes no channel, since each call site names its own. Without the macros the slot's OutSlot::outgoing returns the list, and OutgoingMessageMetadata::with_parameters names the placeholders. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// An order accepted for one tenant: the tenant is a segment of the channel's name. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.{tenant}.accepted")] struct Accepted { id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Accepted)] struct Tenants; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order, Out(tenants): Out<impl Publisher, Tenants>) -> HandlerOutcome { let accepted = Accepted { id: order.id }; match tenants .message(&accepted) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// An order accepted for one tenant: the tenant is a segment of the channel's name. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Accepted { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Accepted { type Form = NameTemplate; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.{tenant}.accepted"; const PARAMETERS: &'static [&'static str] = &["tenant"]; } impl MessageHeaders for Accepted { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl<Cont> TemplateAddress<Cont> for Accepted { type Builder = AcceptedAt<Cont, MissingSegment<Tenant>>; fn begin(cont: Cont) -> Self::Builder { AcceptedAt { cont, tenant: MissingSegment::new(), } } } /// The slot the handler publishes through, and the dictionary the document reports for it. struct Tenants; impl OutSlot for Tenants { const NAME: &'static str = "Tenants"; type Destination = Reads; fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { <Accepted as OutMessages<Self>>::outgoing() } } impl PublishedThrough<Tenants> for Accepted {} impl<M: OutSlot> OutMessages<M> for Accepted { fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { vec![ OutgoingMessageMetadata::new(Self::DESTINATION, type_name::<Self>()) .with_parameters(Self::PARAMETERS) .with_payload_schema(<Self as Documentable>::schema_json()), ] } } struct Accept; impl<O> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(O,)>> for Accept where O: OutEntry<Tenants, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(O,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let accepted = Accepted { id: order.id }; let tenants = outs.get(Tenants); match tenants .message(&accepted) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } }

Each message names the media type of the codec that reads or writes it; the root defaultContentType appears only when all of them agree. The media type is the codec's CONTENT_TYPE: application/json, application/cbor or application/msgpack. It follows the codec chosen for the mounting, at whichever level chose it. A message that no codec reads or writes names none: a type that carries its own bytes, on a byte lane. A reader applies the root defaultContentType to each message that names no media type. So it stands only while every message names the same one; a second format, or a message without one, leaves it out. A message shared by several registrations takes the media type of the first.

The example needs the cbor feature: cargo test --example asyncapi_content_type --features macros,memory,asyncapi,cbor Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_content_type.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) // The default codec: `Order` is `application/json`. .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) // The scope's codec: `Reading` is `application/cbor`. .with_broker_codec(MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| { b.include(record); }) } examples/manual/asyncapi_content_type.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) // The default codec: `Order` is `application/json`. .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); }) // The scope's codec: `Reading` is `application/cbor`. .with_broker_codec(MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("readings", Record).build()); }) }

A header contract becomes the headers schema of its message, from a Headers<T> parameter or from #[outgoing(headers = ..)]. The contract struct derives JsonSchema, as a payload does. The schema describes the logical contract; on the wire each header value is a string (see Headers). On the receive side the contract is a Headers<T> parameter, or the header half of a Message<H, P> input. On the publish side it is the type's #[outgoing(headers = Meta)] declaration. A message component carries one contract. Two handlers that read one type with different contracts keep the first, and generation logs a warning. Without the macros a Message<H, P> input reports its contract. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// What travels in the headers of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentMeta { /// The trace the shipment belongs to. trace_id: String, /// The carrier's attempt number. attempt: u32, } /// A parcel handed to the carrier. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Shipment { id: u64, } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment, Headers(meta): Headers<ShipmentMeta>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.id, trace_id = %meta.trace_id, meta.attempt, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// What travels in the headers of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentMeta { /// The trace the shipment belongs to. trace_id: String, /// The carrier's attempt number. attempt: u32, } /// A parcel handed to the carrier. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Shipment { id: u64, } /// The pair input carries the header contract, so the registration reports its schema. struct Ship; impl Handle<Message<ShipmentMeta, Shipment>> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Message<ShipmentMeta, Shipment>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let meta = &shipment.headers; tracing::info!(shipment.body.id, trace_id = %meta.trace_id, meta.attempt, "shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A reply is the reply of the receive operation it answers: the document names its channel and its message. A request-reply registration's receive operation carries a reply object. It points at the reply's channel and at the reply type's message component. The reply gets no send operation of its own. Its channel is the destination the reply resolves to: the reply type's #[outgoing(name = "..")], or the name the mount site gives (see Replies). A reply that a naming transform addresses per delivery has no fixed address, and its channel's address is null. The reply's address then says where a client reads it, as a runtime expression such as $message.header#/reply-to. The broker states that expression through PublishPolicy::reply_address_location, and a broker that cannot state it leaves the address out. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// The confirmation an order request gets back. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } /// Confirms every order request. #[subscriber("order-requests", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmed { Confirmed { id: order.id } } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// The confirmation an order request gets back. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the chain names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Confirmed { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Confirmed { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmed> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmed, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmed { id: order.id })) } }

The attempt cap and the dead-letter destination of a registration appear on its receive operation as the x-ruststream-retry extension. max_attempts(n) is maxAttempts, and dead_letter(name) is deadLetter. AsyncAPI has a field for neither: a binding models a dead-letter queue only for SQS and SNS, and nothing models an attempt cap. So the document carries them as an extension of the operation. The dead-letter destination is a channel of its own, with a send operation, since the registration publishes there. Retry copies sent to a named destination add retryDestination, with its channel (see Retry slot). Copies that return to the subscription's own address add nothing: that channel is already in the document. A registration that declares none of this has no extension. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(confirm); b.include(accept).out(Tenants, Publish).build(); b.include(ship); // The cap and the dead-letter destination reach the document with the registration. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead"); }) } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("order-requests", Confirm) .describe("Confirms every order request.") .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ); b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) .out(Tenants, Publish) .build(); b.include(subscriber("shipments", Ship).build()); // The cap and the dead-letter destination reach the document with the registration. b.include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead"); }) }

The servers section: the brokers a service connects to, how clients authenticate, and the protocol bindings. A broker registered under a label describes its own server. The service declares the others, and states how clients authenticate to each.

Bindings carry what one protocol says about a server, a channel, an operation or a message, in that protocol's AsyncAPI vocabulary. A Binding is one protocol's object. Binding::new takes the protocol key, the binding's version and a serde body, and writes bindingVersion into the body itself. A key outside the specification's list fails construction with a BindingError, at startup rather than in a published file. Binding::extension carries an x- object for a transport the specification has no binding for. Bindings holds one body per protocol, and an empty set leaves the object out of the document. Broker crates fill most bindings: a server through DescribeServer, a subscription through its descriptor's channel_bindings and its siblings, a publish position through its PublishPolicy. A service attaches a server binding itself with ServerSpec::bindings. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// The Kafka server binding: where the cluster's schema registry is. #[derive(Serialize)] struct KafkaServer { #[serde(rename = "schemaRegistryUrl")] schema_registry_url: &'static str, } /// Adds the binding; a protocol the specification does not list fails here, at startup. fn with_registry(server: ServerSpec) -> Result<ServerSpec, BindingError> { let registry = KafkaServer { schema_registry_url: "https://registry.example.com", }; let binding = Binding::new("kafka", "0.5.0", &registry)?; Ok(server.bindings(Bindings::new().with(binding))) }

ServerSpec::security attaches a SecurityScheme that says how clients authenticate; each scheme becomes a component the server references. Security is the service author's statement, never the broker's: one broker runs with different authentication in different deployments. To secure a server a labeled broker describes, the service declares it again under the same label with the scheme attached. Each call of security adds an alternative, in order. The first scheme's component takes the server's name as its key, the next ones -1, -2 and on. SecurityScheme has a constructor per scheme the specification lists: user_password, api_key with an ApiKeyLocation, x509, plain, scram_sha256, scram_sha512, gssapi, http, http_api_key with an HttpApiKeyLocation, open_id_connect and oauth2. custom takes a scheme object as JSON, and description adds a note. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// How clients authenticate: SCRAM over TLS, or a client certificate. fn secured(server: ServerSpec) -> ServerSpec { server .security(SecurityScheme::scram_sha512().description("SASL over TLS")) .security(SecurityScheme::x509()) }

RustStream::server declares a server the document lists, from a ServerSpec that says how clients reach the broker. server is for a broker no registration of the process describes, or to replace what a labeled broker says. The name is the server's key in the document. ServerSpec::new takes the host and the protocol. ServerSpec::from_url takes a broker URL and keeps only its host and port, so credentials in the URL never reach the document, which is published. protocol_version names the version clients speak, where one protocol name covers incompatible versions, as AMQP 0.9.1 and 1.0 do. description adds a note for the reader. A server spec holds coordinates, never configuration. How clients authenticate is security, and what the protocol adds is bindings. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// The cluster the service is deployed against, as its clients reach it. fn production() -> ServerSpec { ServerSpec::new("kafka.example.com:9093", "kafka") .protocol_version("3.9") .description("The production cluster") } Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); })) } examples/manual/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); })) }

with_broker_labeled registers a broker under a label that is its server name in the document, and the broker describes the server. with_broker_labeled takes a broker that implements DescribeServer; every shipped broker does. The broker fills the server entry in its protocol's vocabulary: host, protocol, protocol version and bindings. The in-memory broker describes an in-process server over the memory protocol, with no host. The label is also the broker's identity in the service; a test addresses the broker by it with broker_named. The registration's channels list the server, and its operations carry the server's protocol as a tag, so a document with several brokers reads by transport. A document with one server puts every channel on it. With several, the channels of an unlabeled registration list none, which AsyncAPI reads as "on every server". An explicit server under the same label takes precedence over what the broker says. with_broker_labeled_codec also names the scope's codec. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); })) } examples/manual/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); })) }
The info section: what the service is, who owns it and under which license. It comes from the AppInfo the app is built with, and the service's id sits at the root of the document.

AppId is the identifier of the service at the root of the document, a URI parsed when it is built. AsyncAPI requires the id to be a URI. AppId checks the part a URI scheme must have: a letter, then letters, digits, +, - or ., then a colon. What follows the colon is the scheme's business. A bare title fails with AppIdError::NoScheme, and a malformed scheme with MalformedScheme. AppInfo::id sets it, and only a parsed AppId fits there. An id from the deployment's configuration therefore fails where the app is built, never in a published document. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The id comes from the deployment's configuration, so a value that is not a URI stops the /// build of the app. fn app(id: &str) -> Result<impl App, AppIdError> { let id: AppId = id.parse()?; Ok(RustStream::new(info().id(id))) }

AppInfo is the info section of the document: the title and the version, a description and the terms of service. AppInfo::new takes the title and the version, which every document carries. description and terms_of_service fill two optional fields. The contact, the license, the tags and the external docs are pages of their own. A field left empty is left out of the document. The app is built from the same AppInfo, so the service's logs and its document name it the same way. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// What the service is, who owns it, and under what terms it runs. fn info() -> AppInfo { AppInfo::new("payments", "1.4.0") .description("Everything the payment domain publishes.") .terms_of_service("https://example.com/terms") .contact(contact()) .license(license()) .tag(tag()) .external_docs(external_docs()) }
