Contact names who answers for the service: a person or a team, a URL and an e-mail address, each optional. AppInfo::contact sets it. Contact::new starts empty, and name, url and email fill the fields. A contact with no field filled is left out of the document. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// Who answers for the service; every field is optional. fn contact() -> Contact { Contact::new() .name("Payments team") .url("https://example.com/teams/payments") .email("payments@example.com") }

ExternalDocs points at documentation kept outside the document: a URL and what the reader finds there. AppInfo::external_docs sets it for the service, and Tag::external_docs for a tag. ExternalDocs::new takes the URL. description says what is there. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.
examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// Where the prose about the service lives. fn external_docs() -> ExternalDocs { ExternalDocs::new("https://example.com/runbooks/payments").description("The runbook") }

License names the license the service is published under, with an optional URL of its text. AppInfo::license sets it. License::new takes the name, an SPDX identifier by convention. url points at the license text. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.
examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The license, by its SPDX identifier and where its text is. fn license() -> License { License::new("Apache-2.0").url("https://spdx.org/licenses/Apache-2.0.html") }

A Tag is a label that groups the service among its neighbours, with an optional description and link. AppInfo::tag adds one; each call adds another. Tag::new takes the label. description says what it means, and external_docs where it is documented. The document also tags each operation with the protocol of its server. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The domain the service belongs to among its neighbours. fn tag() -> Tag { Tag::new("payments") .description("Everything that moves money") .external_docs(ExternalDocs::new("https://example.com/domains/payments")) }

MemoryBroker is a complete broker inside the service's process, and the reference implementation of the broker contract. It comes with the memory feature and needs no server. It suits a queue that belongs to one process, a prototype, or local development; the default cargo generate template starts on it. MemoryBroker::new does no I/O, like every broker constructor. A broker built with it keeps nothing: a message lives until the last subscriber has read it, so memory holds the work the handlers have yet to do. A broker that keeps the newest messages for replay is built with retaining. A mount site imports ruststream::memory::prelude, one glob with the core prelude, the broker's own types, and its publish policies under the names every broker crate uses: Publish, TransactionalPublish and Request. Partitioned stays out of the glob, because in scope it makes msg.partition_key() ambiguous; a service that reads partition keys imports it. A handler body that names capabilities, not policies, keeps ruststream::prelude::*. A subscription by name reads messages published to that exact name, from the moment it opens. Every subscription of a name receives every message published to it. MemorySource is the broker's subscription descriptor, and MemoryPattern reads every name a pattern matches. An ack or a drop consumes a delivery; a retry, or a delivery left without a settlement, comes back to the same subscriber. A retry_after delivery comes back to the same subscriber after its delay, and nothing is republished. Every delivery reports how many times the broker has handed it to that subscriber, so a registration's attempt cap counts these redeliveries. MemoryBroker is a shared handle: its clones work on one bus. After shutdown, a publish, a commit or a request through a handle taken earlier returns an error.

The dependency line: ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } Two subscriptions to orders each receive the order, and one of them replies over the same bus. Macros Manual examples/memory_broker.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(confirm); b.include(audit); }) } examples/manual/memory_broker.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ); b.include(subscriber("orders", Audit).build()); }) }

The broker implements the optional capabilities on its own in-process semantics. Request and reply: broker.requester() gives a MemoryRequester, which names a unique reply name in the reply-to header and waits for the first message delivered there. Request is its policy. Batches: a batch is the first delivery to arrive plus everything already buffered, up to the size the registration names. Transactions: the publisher behind Publish implements TransactionalPublisher and OwnedTransactions. A commit delivers the buffered messages at once, in publish order; an abort discards them. Partition keys: a MemoryMessage reads its key from the partition-key header. Replay: on a retaining broker, a subscription opens at a start position and a handler seeks. The TestApp harness runs an application on this broker as it runs one on a networked broker, and its publishes wait on exactly the subscriptions the broker's routing picks.

A MemoryPattern subscription reads every name its pattern matches, and the broker's Routing decides who receives a shared match. Patterns use the NATS subject syntax. A name splits into tokens at .. * matches exactly one token, and > as the last token matches one or more. So orders.* reads orders.eu and orders.us, and orders.> also reads orders.eu.created. The broker checks a pattern when the subscription opens; a bad one stops the service at startup with MemoryError::InvalidPattern, which names it. A subscription by name reads one name, and a wildcard token in it stops the service with MemoryError::WildcardName. MemoryBroker::routing sets the rule for a publish that several subscriptions match. Routing::EveryMatch, the default, delivers it to every match, as NATS does: a pattern reads beside the handlers of single names, as an audit trail or a metrics tap. Routing::MostSpecific delivers it to the subscriptions of the exact name, or, where there are none, to the most specific matching pattern: a pattern is the fallback for names without a handler of their own. Patterns are compared token by token from the left, and at the first difference a literal beats *, and * beats >. For orders.eu.created, orders.eu.* beats orders.*.created, which beats orders.>, which beats *.eu.created. A broker with no pattern subscription routes by the exact name alone and pays nothing for patterns. A pattern subscription does not replay, even on a retaining broker.

orders.eu goes to its own handler alone, and the pattern takes every other region. Macros Manual examples/memory_patterns.rs #[subscriber("orders.eu")] async fn europe(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "european order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads every `orders.<region>` name. #[subscriber(MemoryPattern::new("orders.*"))] async fn other_regions(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order from another region"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // `orders.eu` goes to `europe` alone; the pattern takes the names nobody else reads. let broker = MemoryBroker::new().routing(Routing::MostSpecific); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(europe); b.include(other_regions); }) } examples/manual/memory_patterns.rs struct Europe; impl Handle<Order> for Europe { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "european order"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct OtherRegions; impl Handle<Order> for OtherRegions { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order from another region"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // `orders.eu` goes to `Europe` alone; the pattern takes the names nobody else reads. let broker = MemoryBroker::new().routing(Routing::MostSpecific); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.eu", Europe).build()); // Reads every `orders.<region>` name. b.include(subscriber(MemoryPattern::new("orders.*"), OtherRegions).build()); }) }

A retaining MemoryBroker keeps the newest messages of every name within a bound, and its subscriptions replay over them. MemoryBroker::retaining takes a Retention bound, applied to each name on its own. Retention::Messages(n) keeps the newest n messages. Retention::Bytes(n) keeps the newest payloads that fit in n bytes. Retention::MessagesAndBytes { .. } applies both. A broker that publishes under a thousand names keeps up to that much for each of them. The newest message always stays, so a payload larger than a byte bound is kept alone. The retaining broker is a type of its own, MemoryBroker<Retaining>, and only its subscriptions implement Seekable. A start_at or a seek therefore does not compile on MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps nothing. A MemoryPosition names a place in the log of one name: start() is the oldest message still kept, sequence(n) the n-th message ever published to the name, and end() the tip. A sequence number keeps naming the same message as the bound evicts older ones. A sequence the bound has already evicted is refused with MemoryError::PositionEvicted, which names the oldest position left. A pattern subscription does not replay, because the log is kept per name.

The broker keeps two messages of each name; three published before the service starts leave the last two to replay. Macros Manual examples/memory_retention.rs /// Keeps the newest two messages of every name. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(2))) } /// Opens at the oldest message still kept, so it reads what came before the service. #[subscriber("audit", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn record(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(record); }) } examples/manual/memory_retention.rs /// Keeps the newest two messages of every name. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(2))) } struct Record; impl Handle<Entry> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Opens at the oldest message still kept, so it reads what came before the service. b.include( subscriber("audit", Record) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ); }) }

Logs, metrics and traces of a running service: each comes from a layer on the app and a feature that exports it. RustStream reports what it does through tracing events, and the logging feature prints them on the console. The per-delivery signals come from layers that wrap every handler, so a handler body holds only its own logic. A layer added to the app wraps the handlers of its routers too. Prometheus metrics need the metrics feature; trace propagation and OpenTelemetry export need the otel feature.

The logging feature prints the service's tracing events on the console, colored, at the verbosity RUST_LOG sets. RustStream emits tracing events while it dispatches, publishes and starts or stops the service, and a handler emits its own with tracing::info! and its siblings. Nothing is printed until a tracing subscriber is installed. logging::init installs the bundled one. It writes to stderr, so stdout stays clean for the output of a command such as asyncapi gen. Levels are colored when stderr is a terminal. RUST_LOG sets the filter in the usual directive syntax; without it, the filter is info. The main that #[ruststream::app] generates calls init on run, so a service with the attribute needs no setup. A hand-written main calls init itself, or builds a Logging to change the defaults: the fallback filter, colors, and whether each line names its target. try_init installs it, and returns LoggingInitError when the filter does not parse or a subscriber is already installed. A subscriber installed first stays in place: the generated main leaves a service's own stack alone, a JSON formatter or an OpenTelemetry bridge for one. The events of each delivery and its outcome come from TracingLayer.

The example runs with the logger on: RUST_LOG=ruststream=debug,info cargo run --example logging --features testing,macros,memory,json,logging -- run Macros Manual examples/logging.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } examples/manual/logging.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); }) } fn main() -> Result<ExitCode, LoggingInitError> { // `RUST_LOG` still wins; this filter applies when it is unset. Logging::new() .with_default_filter("ruststream=debug,info") .try_init()?; // `run_main` finds the logger installed and leaves it in place. Ok(run_main(app)) }

The metrics feature counts and times deliveries and counts publishes in a Prometheus registry that the service serves on /metrics. A Metrics value owns the collectors and the registry they are registered in. Metrics::new registers them in the process's default registry, so a process builds one. Metrics::with_registry registers them in a registry of your own, and registry hands the registry out for collectors of your own. consume_layer is a layer for the app: it times every handler and counts its outcome. publish_layer is a publish layer: it counts every publish a handler makes, replies included, and the failed ones too. Metrics is cheap to clone, and every clone writes into the same collectors. Metric Type Labels ruststream_messages_consumed_total counter name, status: ack or nack ruststream_consume_duration_seconds histogram name ruststream_messages_published_total counter name, status: ok or error name is the subscription on the consume side and the destination on the publish side. With the poll-diagnostics feature, observe_poll_diagnostics adds the time handlers spend in one poll, as described in Diagnostics. export renders the registry in the Prometheus text format. Serving it is the service's part: a route of its HTTP server, or a push to a gateway.

The example serves /metrics on port 8080: cargo run --example metrics --features testing,macros,memory,json,metrics Macros Manual examples/metrics.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, } } fn app(metrics: &Metrics, broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Counts and times every delivery, by subscription and outcome. .layer(metrics.consume_layer()) // Counts every publish, the replies included, by destination and outcome. .publish_layer(metrics.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } examples/manual/metrics.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, })) } } fn app(metrics: &Metrics, broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Counts and times every delivery, by subscription and outcome. .layer(metrics.consume_layer()) // Counts every publish, the replies included, by destination and outcome. .publish_layer(metrics.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ); }) } The route that serves the registry is an ordinary axum handler. examples/metrics.rs /// The `/metrics` route: the registry in the Prometheus text format. async fn scrape(State(metrics): State<Metrics>) -> Result<String, StatusCode> { metrics .export() .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) }

Otel sends the service's spans and metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector over OTLP, the dispatch metrics included. Otel::builder starts an OtelBuilder. It takes the service.name, the OTLP endpoint, the messaging.system the dispatch metrics carry, and extra resource attributes such as the environment. An endpoint left unset comes from the standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* environment, http://localhost:4317 by default. init builds the exporters and installs the tracer and meter providers as the process's globals. It also installs a tracing subscriber that bridges spans into the tracer, so the spans of Propagation are exported with no further wiring. A service with a subscriber of its own turns the bridge off with tracing_bridge(false) and adds it to its own stack. consume_layer and publish_layer record the dispatch metrics, named by the messaging semantic conventions and labelled per subscription or destination: Instrument What it measures messaging.client.consumed.messages deliveries received messaging.process.duration handler time ruststream.messages.processed settlements, by outcome: ack, nack_requeue, nack_drop, retry_after ruststream.messages.in_flight deliveries inside handlers ruststream.message.queue_time time from publish to handler, from the publish-time header the publish layer stamps ruststream.messages.decode_failures, ruststream.messages.panics payloads the codec rejected, handlers that panicked messaging.client.sent.messages, messaging.client.operation.duration publishes and their time ruststream.message.payload.size published payload sizes ruststream.batch.size decoded batch sizes, recorded by batch dispatch once init has run The duration histograms use the buckets the conventions advise, 5 ms to 10 s; view changes them per instrument. observe_health adds the ruststream.app.state gauge over the app's health probe. The service's own instruments come from opentelemetry::global::meter and go out through the same pipeline; the example builds them once at startup and shares them as state. Spans and metric points are batched in the background. shutdown flushes them, after the app has stopped; dropping Otel does not. A hand-written main makes that call, which is why the example keeps one with and without the macros. attach takes providers built by the caller and installs no globals: an exporter of your own, or an in-memory one in a test. A Grafana dashboard over these instruments is in ruststream-grafana.

The example exports to a collector on localhost:4317; without one, the exporter retries in the background and the service keeps working: cargo run --example otel_export --features testing,macros,memory,json,otel -- run main installs the exporters, runs the app, and flushes at the end. examples/otel_export.rs // Written by hand rather than by `#[ruststream::app]`: the exporters batch in the background, // so `main` flushes them once the app has drained. fn main() -> Result<ExitCode, Box<dyn Error>> { let otel = Otel::builder() .service_name("orders") .otlp_endpoint("http://localhost:4317") .messaging_system("memory") .attribute("deployment.environment", "dev") .init()?; let code = run_main(|| app(&otel)); // Ships the last spans and metric points; dropping `Otel` does not. otel.shutdown()?; Ok(code) } The app takes both layers and builds the service's own instrument at startup. Macros Manual examples/otel_export.rs // `use<>`: the app keeps its own handles to the instruments, not a borrow of `otel`. fn app(otel: &Otel) -> impl App + use<> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Per delivery: consumed, processing time, outcomes, in flight, queue time. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) // Per publish: sent, operation time, payload size, the publish-time stamp. .publish_layer(otel.publish_layer()) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics { accepted: global::meter("orders") .u64_counter("orders_accepted") .build(), }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } examples/manual/otel_export.rs // `use<>`: the app keeps its own handles to the instruments, not a borrow of `otel`. fn app(otel: &Otel) -> impl App + use<> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Per delivery: consumed, processing time, outcomes, in flight, queue time. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) // Per publish: sent, operation time, payload size, the publish-time stamp. .publish_layer(otel.publish_layer()) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics { accepted: global::meter("orders") .u64_counter("orders_accepted") .build(), }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); }) } The handler records the instrument it reads from the state. Macros Manual examples/otel_export.rs /// The service's own instruments, built once at startup against the global meter, so they /// export through the same pipeline as the dispatch metrics. #[derive(Clone)] struct OrderMetrics { accepted: Counter<u64>, } #[derive(Clone, FromRef)] struct AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(_order: &Order, State(metrics): State<OrderMetrics>) -> HandlerOutcome { metrics.accepted.add(1, &[KeyValue::new("region", "eu")]); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/otel_export.rs /// The service's own instruments, built once at startup against the global meter, so they /// export through the same pipeline as the dispatch metrics. #[derive(Clone)] struct OrderMetrics { accepted: Counter<u64>, } // A hand-written handler reads the state whole off the context, so it needs no `FromRef`. #[derive(Clone)] struct AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics, } struct Accept; // The state is the last axis of `Handle`; the mount checks it against the app's. impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), AppState> for Accept { fn handle( &self, _order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ctx.state() .metrics .accepted .add(1, &[KeyValue::new("region", "eu")]); ready(Ok(())) } }

The otel feature carries the W3C trace context from a delivery to its replies and opens a span for every delivery. OpenTelemetry hands out two pieces. consume_layer is a layer for the app. For each delivery it reads the traceparent and tracestate headers and continues that trace with a new span id: the consumer's span. A delivery without a valid traceparent starts a new sampled trace. The handler runs inside an INFO span named ruststream.consume, which records the subscription and both ids. The layer writes the consumer's context into the delivery's working headers, where a handler reads it: ctx.headers().get_str("traceparent"). propagation is a publish transform for a reply position. It copies traceparent and tracestate from the working headers onto every reply, so the next service continues the same trace with the consumer span as the parent. for_batch(otel.propagation()) puts it on a batch reply. The headers are parsed and written by the OpenTelemetry SDK's W3C propagator, which follows the specification strictly. Propagation works with any tracing subscriber, or none; Export sends the spans to a collector.

Macros Manual examples/otel_propagation.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let otel = OpenTelemetry::new(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // A span per delivery, a child of the trace the delivery carries. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply carries the consumer span's trace context. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(otel.propagation()); }) } examples/manual/otel_propagation.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let otel = OpenTelemetry::new(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // A span per delivery, a child of the trace the delivery carries. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply carries the consumer span's trace context. b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(otel.propagation()); }) }

TracingLayer logs every delivery and its outcome as tracing events, so handlers hold no logging code of their own. It is a layer bundled with the runtime. Added to the app with RustStream::layer, it wraps every handler, those of routers included. Each delivery gives a DEBUG event when it reaches the handler and one more event when the handler settles it. An ack is logged at INFO. A nack is logged at WARN with requeue=true or requeue=false, and a delayed retry at WARN with its delay. The events go under the ruststream::dispatch target, so RUST_LOG=ruststream::dispatch=debug shows them alone. The handler runs inside a TRACE span; TracingLayer::with_target records a name on that span. The layer never changes the outcome it logs. The events need a tracing subscriber to show, such as the one Logging installs. Batch handlers are not wrapped by app layers, so their deliveries are not logged here.

The handler acks an order and drops an empty one; the layer logs both outcomes. Macros Manual examples/tracing_layer.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { // The layer logs this outcome as a WARN with `requeue=false`. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Wraps every handler the app mounts, router handlers included. .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } examples/manual/tracing_layer.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.quantity == 0 { // The layer logs this outcome as a WARN with `requeue=false`. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Wraps every handler the app mounts, router handlers included. .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).build()); }) }

#[subscriber] turns an async fn over a reference to the message into a handler that include mounts on a broker. The first parameter is the message: &T handles one message, &[T] a whole batch. The runtime decodes the payload with the scope's codec before the body runs; a serde type is all the input needs. A payload that does not decode never reaches the body: the decode failure policy settles it, and drops it by default. An optional &mut Context comes second, and any further parameter is an extractor resolved before the body runs: the context page covers both. What the body returns settles the delivery: HandlerOutcome, () (ack), Result<(), E> (ack on Ok, drop on Err) or Result<HandlerOutcome, E>, as the outcomes page shows. The attribute expands into a definition value named after the function, and include on a broker scope of the application or a router mounts it. The attribute's first argument is the subscription source; settings it leaves out are chained at the mount site. The manual form writes the body as an impl Handle<T> of a named type, binds it with subscriber(source, body) and closes the chain with .build(). There Ok(()) acks and Err(outcome) settles by that outcome.

Macros Manual examples/subscriber_handler.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } examples/manual/subscriber_handler.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); }) }

A handler over &[T] runs once per batch the broker delivers; the mount site names the batch size, and the body settles the batch or each element. The slice parameter is the whole declaration: a &[T] handler is a batch handler, and a &T handler is the single-message form of #[subscriber]. batch(n), one of the mount-site settings, caps each batch at n messages, and a batch handler does not mount without it. The broker builds the batches, natively or through the framework's client-side buffer, and the body sees each batch as delivered. A batch may hold fewer than n messages. The batch's return value settles every element with one of the outcomes: HandlerOutcome, (), Result<(), E> or Result<HandlerOutcome, E>. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles each element on its own, retry_after included; a vector of the wrong length is logged, and the elements it leaves unsettled are retried. An element that fails to decode is settled by the decode failure policy and never reaches the body. The body gets one context per batch, with the broker's subscription-scoped fields only. Per-message headers come with the elements when the parameter is &[Message<H, T>]. App-wide and router middleware wrap single-message handlers and do not apply to batch handlers. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>; Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles element by element. A test reads the batches with batches and checks their sizes with assert_batch_sizes.

One outcome settles the whole batch. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_batch.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } /// One call per batch; the one outcome settles every order in it. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn store(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(store.batch(nonzero!(64))); }) } examples/manual/subscriber_batch.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "orders")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// One call per batch; `Ok` settles every order in it. struct Store; impl Handle<[Order]> for Store { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(subscriber("orders", Store).batch(nonzero!(64)).build()); }) }

A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles element i with outcome i. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_batch.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, cleared: bool, } /// One outcome per element, in slice order: only the uncleared payments come back. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.cleared { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } examples/manual/subscriber_batch.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Payment { id: u64, cleared: bool, } // `#[outgoing(name = "payments")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// One outcome per element, in slice order: only the uncleared payments come back. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.cleared { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ); }) }

A codec turns a payload into a message type and back; it is a compile-time type, chosen at the mount site, and JSON is the default. A Codec decodes the bytes of a delivery into the type the handler reads, and encodes what the handler publishes. It belongs to the mounting, not to the message type, so one type can arrive in JSON on one subscription and in CBOR on another. The codec is resolved when the app is built, so choosing one costs nothing per message. A handler decodes with the codec of the most specific level that names one: Level Macros Manual registration Router::new().with_codec(codec).include(def) subscriber(..).codec(codec) scope with_broker_codec(broker, codec, |b| ..) the same default DefaultCodec the same with_broker_codec names the codec for every handler of a broker scope. A router names one for the handlers it mounts with Router::with_codec. DefaultCodec is the first enabled of the json, cbor and msgpack features, in that order. With no codec feature, a mounting that needs the default does not compile, and the error lists the ways out. The publish side names its codec at its own position. A reply takes the default codec unless .out_reply(policy).codec(codec) names another, so a request and its reply may use different formats. An Out slot takes .out(marker, policy).codec(codec); without it a slot encodes with the codec of the router or scope it is mounted in, not the default codec a reply falls back to. A single publish takes .with_codec(codec) on the builder. A payload that does not decode never reaches the body. The subscriber's on_failure(decode = ..) policy settles it, a drop by default. A type that carries its own bytes skips the codec: Protobuf and the byte lanes need no codec feature.

Macros Manual examples/codecs.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("codecs", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), // Every handler of this scope decodes CBOR. CborCodec, |b| { b.include(bill); // A router names the codec of the handlers it mounts. b.include_router(Router::new().with_codec(JsonCodec).include(audit)); // A reply takes the default codec, JSON, unless its position names one. b.include(checkout).out_reply(Publish).codec(CborCodec); }, ) } examples/manual/codecs.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("codecs", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), // Every registration of this scope decodes CBOR. CborCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).build()); // A registration names its own codec. b.include(subscriber("audit", Audit).codec(JsonCodec).build()); // A reply takes the default codec, JSON, unless its position names one. b.include( subscriber("checkout", Checkout) .reply() .to("receipts") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .codec(CborCodec); }, ) }

A handler that reads the delivery's bytes as they arrived, and a reply that leaves as the bytes it holds, skip the codec. A newtype over &'a [u8] deriving Deserialized is a view of the payload, borrowed from the broker's buffer. A handler over &Frame<'_> receives it with no copy and no decode step, and &[Frame<'_>] is the batch form. A bare &[u8] parameter does not compile: the newtype names what the bytes are. A newtype over Vec<u8> deriving Serialized publishes its bytes as they are, as a reply, an Out slot or a publish from the builder. The two lanes mix freely with codecs: a handler can decode its input with the scope codec and reply in bytes, or the other way round. A service whose messages are all on the lanes builds with no codec feature. A type that holds fields and writes its own format uses the same derives with #[wire(..)], as Protobuf does. In the manual form the impls the derives write are spelled out.

The example builds with no codec feature: cargo test --example byte_lanes --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory Macros Manual examples/byte_lanes.rs /// The delivery's bytes, borrowed from the broker's buffer. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Frame<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// Bytes that leave as they are. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] struct Export(Vec<u8>); #[subscriber("frames", reply("exports"))] async fn reverse(frame: &Frame<'_>) -> Export { tracing::info!(len = frame.0.len(), "reversed"); let mut bytes = frame.0.to_vec(); bytes.reverse(); Export(bytes) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("frames", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(reverse); }) } examples/manual/byte_lanes.rs /// The delivery's bytes, borrowed from the broker's buffer. struct Frame<'a>(&'a [u8]); // `#[derive(Deserialized)]` by hand: the view borrows the payload, and `&Frame<'_>` takes the // lane that reads no codec. impl Deserialized for Frame<'_> { type Output<'a> = Frame<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Frame<'_>, Self::Error> { Ok(Frame(payload)) } } impl Input for Frame<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Frame<'static>>; } /// Bytes that leave as they are. struct Export(Vec<u8>); // `#[derive(Serialized)]` by hand: the bytes, the wire of a typed publish, the shape of a reply. impl Serialized for Export { type Error = Infallible; fn wire_bytes(&self, _buf: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<WireBytes<'_>, Infallible> { Ok(WireBytes::Own(&self.0)) } } impl MessageWire for Export { type Wire = SerializedWire; } impl ReplyShape for Export { type Body = Self; type Headers = (); type Wire = SerializedReply; } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the call site names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Export { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Export { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Reverse; impl<'p> Handle<Frame<'p>, Export> for Reverse { fn handle( &self, frame: &Frame<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Export, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(len = frame.0.len(), "reversed"); let mut bytes = frame.0.to_vec(); bytes.reverse(); ready(Ok(Export(bytes))) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("frames", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("frames", Reverse).reply().to("exports").build()); }) }

CborCodec reads and writes CBOR through ciborium, a compact binary format with the data model of JSON; it is on with the cbor feature. A message type derives the same serde traits as for JSON, and a struct keeps its field names on the wire. The media type is application/cbor. The example names the codec on the scope with with_broker_codec, so it holds whichever other codec features are on. With cbor as the only codec feature, DefaultCodec is CborCodec, and a mounting needs to name nothing. A payload in another format is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's failure policy.

The example builds with CBOR as the only codec: cargo test --example codec_cbor --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory,cbor Macros Manual examples/codec_cbor.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // Every handler of this scope decodes CBOR. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| { b.include(bill); }, ) } examples/manual/codec_cbor.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // Every registration of this scope decodes CBOR. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).build()); }, ) }

A codec of your own implements the Codec trait over any serde format and mounts wherever a built-in codec does. The trait has two required methods: encode writes a value into a new buffer, and decode reads a value from the delivery's bytes. encode_into writes into a buffer the caller passes. The publish path calls it for a broker that only reads the payload, and inside a dispatch loop that buffer is reused, so a codec that implements it allocates nothing per publish. Its default encodes into a buffer of its own and copies. Both sides return a CodecError: the format's error goes in CodecError::Decode or CodecError::Encode as the source. CONTENT_TYPE is the media type the generated AsyncAPI document reports. A codec generic over another composes with it: the inner codec decides the format, and the wrapper changes the bytes around it, such as a version byte in front. Both methods are synchronous, so a codec can only use what it holds and the bytes at hand. Work that needs I/O, such as a schema registry lookup, goes around the codec: in the broker's delivery path on the way in, and in a PublishLayer on the way out. The example writes MessagePack with field names: a struct travels as a map, the form a peer in a dynamic language reads, where the built-in MessagePack codec writes an array. It uses rmp-serde, the crate behind the msgpack feature.

The example builds with msgpack as the only codec feature: cargo test --example custom_codec --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory,msgpack examples/custom_codec.rs /// `MessagePack` that writes a struct as a map of field names, not as an array of values. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] struct NamedMsgpack; impl Codec for NamedMsgpack { const CONTENT_TYPE: &'static str = "application/msgpack"; fn encode<T: Serialize>(&self, value: &T) -> Result<BytesMut, CodecError> { let mut buf = BytesMut::new(); self.encode_into(value, &mut buf)?; Ok(buf) } fn encode_into<T: Serialize>(&self, value: &T, buf: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<(), CodecError> { // Straight into the publish path's buffer: nothing else is allocated. rmp_serde::encode::write_named(&mut buf.writer(), value) .map_err(|err| CodecError::Encode(Box::new(err))) } fn decode<T: DeserializeOwned>(&self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<T, CodecError> { rmp_serde::from_slice(bytes).map_err(|err| CodecError::Decode(Box::new(err))) } } The codec mounts at the scope and at the reply position, like a built-in one. Macros Manual examples/custom_codec.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), NamedMsgpack, |b| { b.include(checkout).out_reply(Publish).codec(NamedMsgpack); }, ) } examples/manual/custom_codec.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), NamedMsgpack, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Checkout) .reply() .to("receipts") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .codec(NamedMsgpack); }, ) }

JsonCodec reads and writes JSON through serde_json; it is the default codec, on with the json feature. The json feature is a default feature of the crate. While it is on, DefaultCodec is JsonCodec, so a handler mounted with no codec named decodes JSON, and a reply is encoded in JSON. A message type derives serde::Deserialize; a type the handler publishes derives Serialize as well. The media type is application/json, and the generated AsyncAPI document reports it for each message. A payload that is not JSON, or JSON of another shape, is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's failure policy. To name JSON where another codec is the scope's, mount through a router or a registration that names it, as on Codecs.

The example builds with JSON as the only codec: cargo test --example codec_json --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory,json Macros Manual examples/codec_json.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // No codec named anywhere: the handler decodes with the default codec, JSON. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(bill); }) } examples/manual/codec_json.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // No codec named anywhere: the registration decodes with the default codec, JSON. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).build()); }) }

MsgpackCodec reads and writes MessagePack through rmp-serde; a struct travels as an array of its field values. It is on with the msgpack feature. A message type derives the same serde traits as for JSON. A struct is written as an array, in the order of its fields, so both ends must declare the fields in the same order. Decoding accepts a struct written as a map of field names too. A peer that expects maps, such as a service in a dynamic language, needs a codec of your own; its example is that codec. The media type is application/msgpack. The example names the codec on the scope with with_broker_codec; with msgpack as the only codec feature, DefaultCodec is MsgpackCodec. A payload in another format is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's failure policy.

The example builds with MessagePack as the only codec: cargo test --example codec_msgpack --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory,msgpack Macros Manual examples/codec_msgpack.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // Every handler of this scope decodes MessagePack. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), MsgpackCodec, |b| { b.include(bill); }, ) } examples/manual/codec_msgpack.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // Every registration of this scope decodes MessagePack. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), MsgpackCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).build()); }, ) }

A message generated by prost carries its own bytes with #[wire(prost)]: no serde, no codec feature, encoded once into the buffer that leaves. The message derives Serialized and Deserialized next to prost::Message, and #[wire(prost)] tells both derives to call prost's encoder and decoder. The type then rides the byte lanes: a handler reads &Order, decoded by prost before the call, and a publish or a reply writes the value with prost into the publish path's own buffer. No codec is resolved for the type anywhere, so the service builds with no codec feature. In a real service prost-build generates the type: its message_attribute setting adds the derives and the #[wire(prost)] line to every message it emits. The example writes the generated struct out by hand. Another format uses the general form, #[wire(encode = <path>, decode = <path>)], which names the format's own writer and reader: Cap'n Proto, FlatBuffers and a hand-rolled frame fit it. A payload that prost cannot decode is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's failure policy. In the manual form the impls the derives write are spelled out, and wire_bytes and from_payload call prost directly.

The example builds with no codec feature: cargo test --example protobuf --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory Macros Manual examples/protobuf.rs #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Outgoing, Serialized, Deserialized)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] #[wire(prost)] struct Order { #[prost(uint64, tag = "1")] id: u64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] sku: String, } examples/manual/protobuf.rs /// What `prost-build` emits from the schema. On the macro path a `message_attribute` line adds /// `#[derive(Outgoing, Serialized, Deserialized)]` and `#[wire(prost)]` to it; here the impls /// below take their place, and the struct is what the generator wrote and nothing more. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message)] struct Order { #[prost(uint64, tag = "1")] id: u64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] sku: String, } // `#[derive(Serialized)]` under `#[wire(encode = ..)]`: the format's own encoder writes into the // buffer the publish path already carries, and the value lends what it wrote - so the message is // encoded once and nothing intermediate is allocated. The error is the format's, named here // because a hand-written impl can see it (the derive cannot, and erases it instead). impl Serialized for Order { type Error = prost::EncodeError; fn wire_bytes(&self, buf: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<WireBytes<'_>, Self::Error> { prost::Message::encode(self, &mut *buf)?; Ok(WireBytes::InBuffer) } } // The two spellings that route the type onto the serialized wire. They carry no bytes of their // own: what differs between a byte bag and a generated message is `wire_bytes`, not where the // value may be used, so the derive writes these two the same way for both. impl MessageWire for Order { type Wire = SerializedWire; } impl ReplyShape for Order { type Body = Self; type Headers = (); type Wire = SerializedReply; } // `#[derive(Deserialized)]` under `#[wire(decode = ..)]`, plus the `Input` spelling that routes // `&Order` onto the self-deserializing lane. `Output<'a>` is `Self` because a generated message // owns its fields; a zero-copy reader names its own borrowing view there instead. impl Deserialized for Order { type Output<'a> = Self; type Error = prost::DecodeError; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> { prost::Message::decode(payload) } } impl Input for Order { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Self>; } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "orders")]`: where the type goes, what header // contract it declares, and what it contributes to the generated document. `with_serialized` // records the lane, which is what the derive's probe reports for a type carrying its own bytes. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl<M: OutSlot> OutMessages<M> for Order { fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { vec![ OutgoingMessageMetadata::new(Self::DESTINATION, std::any::type_name::<Self>()) .with_serialized(true), ] } } The handler reads the message type, and the publish names no codec. Macros Manual examples/protobuf.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(handle); // The outgoing half of the same declaration: the value encodes itself on the way out // too, so this publish names no codec either. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Order { id: 7, sku: "widget".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }) } examples/manual/protobuf.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()); // The outgoing half of the same declaration: the value encodes itself on the way out // too, so this publish names no codec either. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Order { id: 7, sku: "widget".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }) }
A handler's parameters after the message: the per-delivery Context and the values extracted from it.

Ctx<K> passes one field of the broker's per-delivery context to the handler as a parameter. K is the broker's key for the field, the same key ctx.context(key) reads, so the body needs no &mut Context. Ctx takes any CtxKey: a broker's context key, or MainRuntime. The #[subscriber] attribute infers the context type from the key. A key only reads a context that the broker provides: Ctx<Position> compiles on a retaining memory broker, not on a plain one. Ctx<MainRuntime> is the one key that reads no broker field: it binds the application's runtime for a handler on dedicated threads. Ctx<K> is an extractor, resolved before the body runs.

Macros Manual examples/context.rs /// Where an order sits in the broker's log, published on `located`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "located")] struct Located { order: u64, sequence: usize, } /// `Ctx<Position>` hands the body this delivery's position: one field of the broker's /// per-delivery context, with no `&mut Context` parameter. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn locate(order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> Result<Located, HandlerOutcome> { let MemoryPosition::Sequence(sequence) = at else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; Ok(Located { order: order.id, sequence, }) } fn app() -> impl App { // A retaining broker numbers its messages; its deliveries carry the position. let broker = MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(16))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(locate); }) } examples/manual/context.rs /// Where an order sits in the broker's log, published on `located`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Located { order: u64, sequence: usize, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "located")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Located { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "located"; } impl MessageHeaders for Located { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// The broker's per-delivery context is the fourth parameter of `Handle`; the body reads /// one field of it by its key. struct Locate; impl Handle<Order, Located, (), MemoryContext> for Locate { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MemoryContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Located, HandlerOutcome>> { let MemoryPosition::Sequence(sequence) = ctx.context(Position) else { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); }; ready(Ok(Located { order: order.id, sequence, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { // A retaining broker numbers its messages; its deliveries carry the position. let broker = MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(16))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Locate).reply().build()); }) }

Context carries one delivery's channel, headers, state and broker fields to the middleware and the handler. The runtime builds one Context per delivery and lends it to the middleware and then to the handler. A #[subscriber] function takes it as &mut Context<'_> after the message; a manual handler gets it as the last argument of handle. name() is the channel the message arrived on. headers() reads the delivery's headers; headers_mut() gives a working copy that middleware can enrich for the handler. The working copy stays inside the delivery: a reply or a publish from the handler starts with fresh headers. state() is the application state that on_startup produced. The context's first type parameter is the broker's per-delivery context: () for most subscriptions, MemoryContext for a retaining memory broker. The broker exports keys for its fields, and ctx.context(key) reads one; Ctx<K> does the same read as a handler parameter. A key implements ContextField, which names the context it reads, and Field, which reads the value out of it with no lookup at run time. The memory broker's seek handle is one such field. The context also schedules work for after the settlement: the post-settle hooks.

Macros Manual examples/context.rs /// What the service read off one delivery, published on `receipts`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, channel: String, request: Option<String>, } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn receive(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Receipt { let request = ctx .headers() .get("x-request-id") .map(|id| String::from_utf8_lossy(id).into_owned()); Receipt { order: order.id, channel: ctx.name().to_owned(), request, } } examples/manual/context.rs /// What the service read off one delivery, published on `receipts`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Receipt { order: u64, channel: String, request: Option<String>, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "receipts")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// The context is the last parameter of `handle`, always in reach. struct Receive; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let request = ctx .headers() .get("x-request-id") .map(|id| String::from_utf8_lossy(id).into_owned()); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id, channel: ctx.name().to_owned(), request, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).reply().build()); }) }

A type that implements FromContext becomes a handler parameter, resolved from the delivery before the body runs. Every parameter of a #[subscriber] function after the message and the optional &mut Context is an extractor. The generated handler resolves the extractors in the order they are declared, then runs the body. from_context reads the context mutably, so an extractor can read headers, broker fields and the state. It is async, so it may also do I/O, such as a lookup. An error is the Rejection, which converts into a HandlerOutcome: the delivery settles with that outcome, and the body does not run. HandlerOutcome itself is a valid rejection; an extractor that cannot fail uses Infallible. A manual handler calls from_context at the top of handle and returns a rejection as its error. The impl is generic over the context type C and the state S, so the extractor works on any subscription. An extractor that reads a broker field or a typed state implements the trait for those types instead. State<T>, the extractor of the application state, and Ctx<K> are extractors of this kind that the crate provides.

Macros Manual examples/from_context.rs /// The tenant an order belongs to, read off its `x-tenant` header. struct Tenant(String); impl<C: Send, S: Sync> FromContext<C, S> for Tenant { type Rejection = HandlerOutcome; fn from_context( ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Self, HandlerOutcome>> + Send { let tenant = ctx.headers().get("x-tenant"); let tenant = tenant.map(|tenant| Self(String::from_utf8_lossy(tenant).into_owned())); // No tenant, no work: the delivery is dropped and the body does not run. ready(tenant.ok_or_else(HandlerOutcome::drop)) } } /// An accepted order and its tenant, published on `accepted`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "accepted")] struct Accepted { order: u64, tenant: String, } /// The tenant arrives as a parameter, resolved before the body runs. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn accept(order: &Order, Tenant(tenant): Tenant) -> Accepted { Accepted { order: order.id, tenant, } } examples/manual/from_context.rs /// The tenant an order belongs to, read off its `x-tenant` header. struct Tenant(String); impl<C: Send, S: Sync> FromContext<C, S> for Tenant { type Rejection = HandlerOutcome; fn from_context( ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Self, HandlerOutcome>> + Send { let tenant = ctx.headers().get("x-tenant"); let tenant = tenant.map(|tenant| Self(String::from_utf8_lossy(tenant).into_owned())); // No tenant, no work: the delivery is dropped and the body does not run. ready(tenant.ok_or_else(HandlerOutcome::drop)) } } /// An accepted order and its tenant, published on `accepted`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Accepted { order: u64, tenant: String, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "accepted")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Accepted { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "accepted"; } impl MessageHeaders for Accepted { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// The body resolves the tenant first; a rejection settles the delivery in its place. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, Accepted> for Accept { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<Accepted, HandlerOutcome> { let Tenant(tenant) = Tenant::from_context(ctx).await?; Ok(Accepted { order: order.id, tenant, }) } }

How many deliveries of one subscription run at once, and on which threads. A subscription handles one delivery at a time by default. The next delivery is read only after the previous one has settled, so the handler sees the stream in order. The handler runs on the runtime the app runs on, beside the broker clients' I/O, the timers and every other subscription. Workers run several deliveries of one subscription at once, for a handler that waits on I/O. Threads give a subscription threads of its own, for a handler that computes. Both are a setting of the subscription, and a subscription takes one of them.

The poll-diagnostics feature times the polls of every handler and names the handlers that compute on the app's runtime. With the feature on, every subscription is sampled. One poll of its handler in 64 is timed with two reads of the CPU's cycle counter. The time measured is the time inside one poll, between two .await points. A handler that waits on I/O or a timer is not slow here; only one that computes is. Each subscription keeps an exponential moving average and a histogram of that time. When the average crosses 100 microseconds, the runtime logs one warning naming the subscription, its average and p99, and the fix: threads. It warns after 16 samples, and once per crossing. A subscription already on threads(n) is measured the same way, and no warning names it. PollDiagnostics changes the threshold and the sample_every interval, and reads the reports. RustStream::poll_diagnostics hands it to the app; a clone the caller keeps reads the same reports. Metrics::observe_poll_diagnostics and Otel::observe_poll_diagnostics export them, labelled per subscription. The cost is a countdown per poll and, on a timed poll, two counter reads and a few atomic updates. The example runs with cargo test --example poll_diagnostics --features testing,macros,memory,json,poll-diagnostics.

Macros Manual examples/poll_diagnostics.rs /// The app gets the settings; the caller keeps a clone of `diagnostics` to read the reports. fn app(diagnostics: &PollDiagnostics) -> impl App { let diagnostics = diagnostics .clone() .threshold(Duration::from_millis(1)) .sample_every(nonzero!(8u32)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .poll_diagnostics(diagnostics) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); b.include(summarize); }) } examples/manual/poll_diagnostics.rs /// The app gets the settings; the caller keeps a clone of `diagnostics` to read the reports. fn app(diagnostics: &PollDiagnostics) -> impl App { let diagnostics = diagnostics .clone() .threshold(Duration::from_millis(1)) .sample_every(nonzero!(8u32)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .poll_diagnostics(diagnostics) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()); b.include(subscriber("reports", Summarize).build()); }) }

reports returns a PollReport for every subscription that has opened, and report the one of a given name. A report holds the number of samples, the average and the p99 of the time in one poll. examples/poll_diagnostics.rs /// A periodic task beside the app: the handlers whose average poll is over `limit`. fn slow_handlers(diagnostics: &PollDiagnostics, limit: Duration) -> Vec<PollReport> { diagnostics .reports() .into_iter() .filter(|report| report.average() > limit) .collect() }

threads(n) gives a subscription n threads of its own, so a handler that computes leaves the app's runtime free for I/O. A handler that computes holds up the thread it runs on. On the app's runtime, that thread also serves the broker clients' I/O, the timers and every other subscription. threads(n) starts n threads with the subscription, each running a current-thread runtime. The subscription's loop stays on the app's runtime and hands deliveries to the threads in turn, through a bounded ring per thread. It stops reading the broker only when every ring is full. Decoding, the handler, encoding a reply and settling run on the thread that got the delivery, and only there. So does everything the delivery leaves behind: a timer, a plain tokio::spawn, a continuation, the timer of a retry_after copy. MainRuntime is the way back to the app's runtime: Ctx<MainRuntime> as a parameter, or main_runtime() on the context of a manual body. spawn starts a task there, and run runs one there and returns its output; what they send must be Send. threads(n, by_key) sends each key to a fixed thread, so a key keeps its order, as with workers. At the mount site the setting is .threads(n) or .threads_by_key(n); it fills the position workers fills, so a subscription takes one of them. A delivery allocates nothing on its way to a thread. On shutdown the loop stops reading, the threads finish their rings and wait for what the deliveries left behind, all within the app's shutdown_timeout. A plain tokio::spawn is not waited for and ends with its thread; work that must outlive the subscription goes through MainRuntime::spawn. The threads pay from about ten microseconds of computation per delivery; on lighter handlers they cost more CPU than they save. Diagnostics find the handlers that need them. Under TestApp the threads run as n workers on the test's runtime.

Macros Manual examples/threads.rs /// Runs on one of the subscription's eight threads, from the first poll to the end; the app's /// runtime stays free for I/O and for the other subscriptions. #[subscriber("images.resize", threads(8), reply)] async fn resize(job: &Resize, Ctx(main): Ctx<MainRuntime>) -> Resized { let checksum = render(job); // The explicit way back to the app's runtime; what it sends must be `Send`. main.spawn(notify(job.id)); Resized { id: job.id, checksum, } } examples/manual/threads.rs /// Runs on one of the subscription's eight threads, from the first poll to the end; the app's /// runtime stays free for I/O and for the other subscriptions. struct ResizeImage; impl Handle<Resize, Resized> for ResizeImage { fn handle( &self, job: &Resize, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Resized, HandlerOutcome>> { let checksum = render(job); // The explicit way back to the app's runtime; what it sends must be `Send`. ctx.main_runtime().spawn(notify(job.id)); ready(Ok(Resized { id: job.id, checksum, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("images.resize", ResizeImage) .threads(nonzero!(8)) .reply() .build(), ); }) }

The dedicated threads and the app runtime's threads share the machine's cores, and Tokio starts one worker per core by default. A service with threads(n) sizes the app's runtime for its I/O. #[ruststream::app] takes the runtime arguments of #[tokio::main]: flavor = "current_thread" or worker_threads = n. A current-thread runtime beside dedicated threads gives the rest of the service the lowest latency. In the manual form, main passes an AppRuntime to run_main_on. Macros Manual examples/threads.rs /// The dedicated threads carry the computation, so the app's runtime needs one thread for I/O. #[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(resize); }) } examples/manual/threads.rs /// What `#[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")]` writes: the dedicated threads carry the /// computation, so the app's runtime needs one thread for I/O. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main_on(AppRuntime::CurrentThread, app) }

workers(n) handles up to n deliveries of one subscription at once; workers(n, by_key) keeps the deliveries of one key in order. The subscription starts n long-lived workers, tasks of the runtime the app runs on. A free worker takes the next delivery. While n deliveries are in flight, the subscription does not read the broker, so back-pressure holds. Deliveries finish in any order: the subscription's global order is lost. Workers suit a handler that waits on I/O; a handler that computes belongs on threads. The setting is a clause of the attribute, or .workers(n) among the mount-site settings. The count is a NonZeroUsize, and nonzero! writes one. A router chain takes a Workers value through Router::workers. Handing a delivery to a worker allocates nothing. A batch handler gets a pool of batches, each batch in a task of its own. On shutdown, the deliveries in flight finish within the app's shutdown_timeout.

Four charges that each wait a second on a payment provider take one second together. Macros Manual examples/workers.rs /// Up to four orders are charged at once; the next one waits for a free worker. #[subscriber("orders", workers(4))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { charge(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/workers.rs /// Up to four orders are charged at once; the next one waits for a free worker. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).workers(nonzero!(4)).build()); }) }

workers(n, by_key) makes the same n workers into n sequential lanes. A delivery goes to the lane picked by hashing its partition key, which the broker's message reports through Partitioned. Deliveries with one key never reorder, and deliveries with different keys run at once. A delivery without a key rotates over the lanes. The in-memory broker reads the key from the partition-key header. At the mount site the setting is .workers_by_key(n). Macros Manual examples/workers.rs /// Four lanes by the message's partition key: one customer's orders are charged in order, /// different customers' at once. #[subscriber("orders", workers(4, by_key))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { charge(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/workers.rs /// Four lanes by the message's partition key: one customer's orders are charged in order, /// different customers' at once. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Bill) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ); }) }

What a subscriber does when its handler panics or a payload cannot decode, set per subscriber with on_failure. A subscriber carries two policies: one for a handler panic, one for a delivery that cannot decode. A panic fails fast by default, and a test reads it with panicked: a loud error names the subscription, the service shuts down gracefully, and run returns an error, so an orchestrator restarts it. Fail fast takes effect under an unwinding panic profile; with panic = "abort" the process is already gone. A decode failure drops the delivery by default: one malformed payload does not stop the consumer, and assert_last_failed_to_decode checks it in a test. A decode failure is a payload the codec rejects, a header contract that does not parse, a missing carried value, or a delivery the broker reports unreadable. Each policy is a FailurePolicy: fail_fast, drop, retry, retry_after(delay) or skip. drop, retry and retry_after(delay) settle the way the handler outcomes of the same name do. skip acks the delivery to move past it; the message is gone and was never handled. retry and retry_after bring the delivery back, so a payload that never decodes keeps coming back. The attribute takes on_failure(panic = .., decode = ..), with either key alone; the manual form takes a FailurePolicies value.

Macros Manual examples/failure_policy.rs /// No clause: a payload that cannot decode is dropped, and a panic stops the service. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn fulfil(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached fulfilment"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs /// No settings step: a payload that cannot decode is dropped, and a panic stops the service. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached fulfilment"); ready(Ok(())) } }

Macros Manual examples/failure_policy.rs /// An audit trail moves past anything it cannot process: both failures ack the delivery. #[subscriber("orders", on_failure(panic = skip, decode = skip))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached the audit"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs /// An audit trail moves past anything it cannot process: both failures ack the delivery. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached the audit"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Audit) .on_failure( FailurePolicies::default() .with_panic(FailurePolicy::Skip) .with_decode(FailurePolicy::Skip), ) .build(), ); }) }

Macros Manual examples/failure_policy.rs const SCHEMA_ROLLOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// Producers roll a schema change out first: a payload this version cannot read yet comes /// back in a minute instead of being dropped. A panic still stops the service. #[subscriber("orders", on_failure(decode = retry_after(SCHEMA_ROLLOUT)))] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs const SCHEMA_ROLLOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// Producers roll a schema change out first: a payload this version cannot read yet comes /// back in a minute instead of being dropped. A panic still stops the service. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Accept) .on_failure( FailurePolicies::default() .with_decode(FailurePolicy::RetryAfter(SCHEMA_ROLLOUT)), ) .build(), ); }) }
What a handler returns settles its delivery: ack, retry, retry after a delay, or drop, as a HandlerOutcome.

and_after attaches a continuation to an outcome: work that runs on a task of its own once the delivery is settled. HandlerOutcome::ack().and_after(fut) settles the delivery first, then runs fut. A continuation attaches to any of the outcomes, drop() and retry() included; a second and_after replaces the first. On a batch each element carries its own continuation, so only the elements that asked for one run it. Post-settle work is at most once: the delivery is already settled, so a lost or panicking continuation never brings it back. Work whose loss must redeliver the message belongs in the body, before the settlement. A graceful shutdown waits for running continuations within the app's shutdown_timeout. A test waits for them with drain. A hook on the context runs after the settlement too, gated by which settlement it was.
