The publisher capabilities a broker offers, one trait each, starting with Publisher. A handler names the capability its slot needs, never the broker's publisher type. A slot bound to a policy whose live publisher lacks that capability does not compile. A broker offers only the capabilities its transport has: Kafka-like brokers carry one transaction per producer, and request and reply need a broker that correlates answers.

OwnedTransactions opens independent transactions that own their buffers, so a handler keeps several open on one slot at once. A broker whose transactions are client buffers flushed at commit offers this kind: an AMQP confirms buffer, a Redis pipeline, the memory broker. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Marker> and calls transaction(). Each call returns a TypedTransaction of its own, and settling one never touches another. Publishes go through the transaction's builder and stay in its buffer until commit() flushes them together. commit() and abort() consume the value, so a publish after settling does not compile. A transaction dropped unsettled discards its buffer, the way an abort does, and logs a warning. The transaction sends from its own buffer: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages, and a test reads them on the destination record, published, rather than the slot's. Kafka-like brokers offer only the borrowed kind, TransactionalPublisher.

A transfer books its entries in one transaction and its audit record in another, so an empty transfer keeps the audit record and books nothing. Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit, Audited)] struct Ledger; /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. #[subscriber("transfers")] async fn book( transfer: &Transfer, Out(ledger): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Audited {} /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Transfer, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let ledger = outs.get(Ledger); let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } return Ok(()); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(book).out(Ledger, Publish).build(); }) } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("transfers", Book).build()) .out(Ledger, Publish) .build(); }) }

Publisher is the capability every slot names; a publish policy at the mount site becomes one when startup pairs it with the connected broker. A handler bounds its slot on the capability, Out<impl Publisher>, and never on a broker's publisher type. The same handler then mounts on a production broker and on its in-process test transport unchanged. A policy holds no connection, so it is built anywhere: a broker's prelude names its plain one Publish. Startup pairs each policy with the connected broker, so a handler never holds a publisher that is not connected. A reply with no policy named leaves through the broker's default one, DefaultPublish. A startup hook such as after_startup takes a policy and gets its live publisher, for a publish outside any handler. A bare publisher starts a publish with the same builder, under the default codec. A publisher declares three types. Payload says how its client takes the bytes: Lend when it only reads them, so the runtime lends one reused buffer, and Take when it keeps them. Options are its per-message settings, and Error is what a failed publish returns. Its base_headers go on every message it sends, under the headers of the call site. The narrower capabilities extend it: TransactionalPublisher, OwnedTransactions and RequestReply.

The handler names the capability; the mount site and the startup hook name the policy. Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn archive(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if out .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. struct Archive; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Archive where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. b.include(archive).out(DefaultSlot, Publish).build(); // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }); }) } examples/manual/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. b.include(subscriber("orders", Archive).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) .build(); // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }); }) }

RequestReply sends a request from a handler and awaits the correlated answer, on a broker that correlates replies natively. NATS-style brokers correlate replies, and the memory broker does too; Kafka and classic queues do not offer this capability. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply, Marker>, and the mount site binds the broker's request policy, which its prelude names Request. request(message, timeout) publishes the message and resolves on the first answer, or fails once the time runs out. The request is an OutgoingMessage of bytes the handler encoded, and the answer is the broker's incoming message, which the handler decodes. The request goes to the broker directly, past the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers. The broker names an inbox for the answer: the memory broker puts it in the reply-to header. The responder is an ordinary reply handler whose reply goes to that inbox, through a naming transform. The slot also publishes with the builder, what its #[publishes(..)] list admits.

The handler asks the quote service for a price, then publishes the priced order through the same slot. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Priced)] struct Pricing; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn price(order: &Order, Out(pricing): Out) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(ask) = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let Ok(answer) = pricing.request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(quote) = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; if pricing.message(&priced).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/requester.rs struct Pricing; impl OutSlot for Pricing { const NAME: &'static str = "Pricing"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough for Priced {} struct Price; impl

Handle> for Price where P: OutEntry, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(P,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pricing = outs.get(Pricing); let ask = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }).map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let answer = pricing .request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; let quote = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; pricing .message(&priced) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } The responder answers on the inbox the request named. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(price).out(Pricing, Request).build(); b.include(quote_price).out_reply(Publish).transform(ToInbox); }) } examples/manual/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).build()) .out(Pricing, Request) .build(); b.include( subscriber("quotes.ask", QuoteAsk) .reply() .to("quotes.answers") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox); }) }

TransactionalPublisher puts several publishes in one broker transaction: every reply of a batch, or a scope a handler opens on its slot. Messages published inside a transaction become visible together on commit, or not at all. A batch handler whose reply chain ends with .transactional() publishes every reply of the batch in one transaction, and acks the batch after the commit. A policy whose live publisher has no transactions does not compile there. A broker's prelude names its transactional policy TransactionalPublish. By hand, a handler bounds its slot Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Marker> and calls begin(). It returns a TransactionScope that owns the transaction, and publishes go through the scope's builder. commit() and abort() consume the scope, so a second commit or a publish after settling does not compile. A scope dropped unsettled logs a warning and leaves the broker transaction open, so a handler settles every scope it opens. The scope sends straight into the transaction: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages. This is the borrowed kind of transaction: the publisher carries one broker transaction, and one scope is open on it at a time. Kafka-like brokers, whose client holds one transaction per producer, offer this kind only. Brokers whose transactions are client buffers also offer OwnedTransactions.

Every confirmation of a batch in one transaction. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn confirm(orders: &[Order]) -> Vec<Confirmed> { orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect() } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. struct Confirm; impl Handle<[Order], Vec<Confirmed>> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Confirmed>, Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect())) } } A scope opened on a slot: both entries of a payment, or neither. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit)] struct Ledger; /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn book( payment: &Payment, Out(ledger): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = ledger.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let (id, amount) = (payment.id, payment.amount); let debit = scope.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = scope.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() { if let Err(err) = scope.abort().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "payments: aborting the ledger transaction failed"); } return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } match scope.commit().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ok(scope) = outs.get(Ledger).begin().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let (id, amount) = (payment.id, payment.amount); let debit = scope.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = scope.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() { if let Err(err) = scope.abort().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "payments: aborting the ledger transaction failed"); } return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } scope.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transaction per batch, committed before the batch is acked. b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(64))) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional(); b.include(book).out(Ledger, TransactionalPublish).build(); }) } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transaction per batch, committed before the batch is acked. b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional(); b.include(subscriber("payments", Book).build()) .out(Ledger, TransactionalPublish) .build(); }) }

A handler answers a message by returning a value; the reply type or the mount site says where the answer goes. Every reply type derives Outgoing. A type with #[outgoing(name = "..")] fixes its destination, and the handler carries the bare clause #[subscriber("src", reply)]. A type that names nothing takes the destination from the clause, reply("dest"). A destination declared on the type wins over a name at the mount site, and startup logs a warning for such a registration. The forms of a destination are on the Destinations page. Result<Reply, HandlerOutcome> keeps the settlement in the handler's hands: Ok publishes the reply and acks, Err publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. A reply whose publish fails nacks the delivery with requeue, so a replying handler has to be safe to run twice. A batch handler returns one Vec of replies per batch. With nothing else said, the reply leaves through the broker's default policy under the default codec. .out_reply(policy) names the publish policy, and the steps after it complete the reply's wiring. .codec(..) names the codec of the reply, while the request still decodes with the scope's codec. .transform(..) adds a publish transform, and .transactional() puts every reply of a batch in one broker transaction. A broker that only reads the payload is lent the dispatch loop's own encode buffer, so a reply allocates nothing per delivery.

The reply type fixes its destination. Macros Manual examples/replies.rs /// The reply type fixes its destination, so the clause is the bare `reply`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// `Ok` publishes the receipt and acks; `Err` publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { if order.id == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id }) } examples/manual/replies.rs /// The reply type fixes its destination, so the chain names none. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "receipts")]` by hand. impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// `Ok` publishes the receipt and acks; `Err` publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { if order.id == 0 { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } The clause names the destination of a type that declares none. Macros Manual examples/replies.rs /// The reply type declares no destination, so the clause names one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Quote { order_id: u64, price: u64, } #[subscriber("quote-requests", reply("quotes"))] async fn quote(order: &Order) -> Quote { Quote { order_id: order.id, price: order.id * 10, } } examples/manual/replies.rs /// The reply type declares no destination, so the chain names one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Quote { order_id: u64, price: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Quote { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Quote { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct QuoteOrder; impl Handle<Order, Quote> for QuoteOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Quote, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Quote { order_id: order.id, price: order.id * 10, })) } } Macros Manual examples/replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's default policy, under the default codec. b.include(issue_receipt); // The policy the reply leaves through, named at the mount site. b.include(quote).out_reply(Publish); }) } examples/manual/replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's default policy, under the default codec. b.include(subscriber("orders", IssueReceipt).reply().build()); // The destination the type leaves open, and the policy the reply leaves through. b.include( subscriber("quote-requests", QuoteOrder) .reply() .to("quotes") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish); }) }

A publish transform changes an outgoing message at one publish position, before it reaches the publisher. A transform belongs to one position: a reply, one slot, or the replies of a batch. It is static, so the chain of transforms is one type and costs only its own code. What it reads, which settings it writes and whether it names the destination are part of its type, so a transform mounted where it does not fit does not compile. The app-wide counterpart, which wraps every publish of the app, is the publish layer.

A batch publish transform is a step on the replies of a batch handler: each reply passes it on its own, with the batch's context. A batch handler with a reply returns one Vec of replies per batch, and those replies pass their own steps. .batch_transform(..) adds one after .out_reply(policy), and a single-message mount rejects it at compile time. The per-message publish transforms do not run on batch replies, and batch transforms do not run on single replies. for_batch lifts a per-message transform onto the batch path, so one impl serves both. All replies of a batch see one PublishContext, the batch's: its name is the subscription, its headers are empty, and its context fields are the broker's batch context. A transform that reads the message it answers belongs on a single-message handler. A batch reply never offers the naming right. A batch transform has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs.

examples/batch_transform.rs /// Marks every reply of a batch. It sees the batch's context, not one delivery's. struct Batched; impl<C, Options> BatchPublishTransform<C, Options> for Batched { fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut().insert("batched", "true"); } } /// A per-message transform, reused on the batch path through `for_batch`. struct Service(&'static str); impl<K: ContextKind, Options> PublishTransform<K, Options> for Service { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &K::View<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("service", self.0); } } Macros Manual examples/batch_transform.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(64))) .out_reply(Publish) .batch_transform(Batched) .batch_transform(for_batch(Service("billing"))); }) } examples/manual/batch_transform.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("receipts") .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .batch_transform(Batched) .batch_transform(for_batch(Service("billing"))); }) }

A naming transform sets the destination of each message, on a position where nothing else declared it: a reply to the inbox a request named. A transform that declares type Destination = Names may call set_name on the outgoing message. A position offers that right only where nothing declared the destination: a reply type with no #[outgoing(name = ..)], or a slot whose whole #[publishes(..)] list leaves it open. It offers it once, so a second naming transform on one position does not compile, and neither does one on a declared reply or on a batch reply. DefaultSlot and a slot that lists a declared destination never offer it. The name at the mount site stays the declared fallback: the generated document reports it, and a delivery the transform leaves alone is answered there. A name read off the delivery costs no copy: get_shared hands over the header's own buffer, and Str checks it is UTF-8. The reply side of RequestReply is the usual case. A naming transform is a publish transform in every other way: it has no macro form, and only the mounting differs.

examples/naming_transform.rs /// Answers on the inbox the question named in its `reply-to` header. The header's bytes become /// the destination as they are: one UTF-8 check, no copy. struct ToInbox; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToInbox { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(inbox) = cx.headers().get_shared("reply-to") && let Ok(name) = Str::try_from(inbox) { out.set_name(name); } } } Macros Manual examples/naming_transform.rs /// `"answers"` is the fallback, and what the generated document reports. #[subscriber("questions", reply("answers"))] async fn answer(question: &Question) -> Answer { Answer { id: question.id } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("answers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(answer).out_reply(Publish).transform(ToInbox); }) } examples/manual/naming_transform.rs struct AnswerQuestion; impl Handle<Question, Answer> for AnswerQuestion { fn handle( &self, question: &Question, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Answer, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Answer { id: question.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("answers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // `"answers"` is the fallback, and what the generated document reports. b.include( subscriber("questions", AnswerQuestion) .reply() .to("answers") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox); }) }

A publish transform is a static step on one publish position: it reads the delivery or the slot, and changes the outgoing message. .transform(..) adds one after the position it belongs to: after .out_reply(policy) for a reply, after .out(marker, policy) for a slot. Its apply gets the outgoing message, the broker's per-message settings and a view of the position, and returns nothing: it cannot refuse a publish. An impl declares three things. The kind is what it reads. ForReply<C> reads the delivery being answered through a PublishContext: its channel, headers and the broker's context fields. ForSlot reads a SlotContext, the slot's name and nothing else, because the body that publishes has already read its delivery. The Options parameter is the settings it writes: (), or the broker's own type, which mounts it only over that broker's publisher. type Destination is what it may do to the destination: Reads leaves it alone, and Names sets it. A transform that reads and sets nothing is generic over both, impl<K: ContextKind, Options>, and mounts anywhere. Transforms run in the order the chain writes them, then the app's publish layers, then the send. The chain is one type, built when the code compiles, so a transform costs only its own code. A reply of a batch handler takes batch transforms instead. A transform has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs.

A reply transform carries the request's correlation id onto the reply. examples/publish_transform.rs /// Carries the request's correlation id onto its reply. `ForReply` reads the delivery being /// answered, so this transform mounts on a reply position. struct Correlate; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for Correlate { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { // The delivery's own buffer, shared rather than copied. if let Some(id) = cx.headers().get_shared("correlation-id") { out.headers_mut().insert("correlation-id", id); } } } A slot transform stamps a constant on what leaves the slot. examples/publish_transform.rs /// Stamps the schema version on what leaves a slot. `ForSlot` reads the slot's name and nothing /// else: the body that publishes has already read its delivery. struct SchemaVersion(&'static str); impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForSlot, Options> for SchemaVersion { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &SlotContext<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("schema-version", self.0); } } Macros Manual examples/publish_transform.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A transform follows the position it belongs to. b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish).transform(Correlate); b.include(audit) .out(Trail, Publish) .transform(SchemaVersion("2")) .build(); }) } examples/manual/publish_transform.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A transform follows the position it belongs to. b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().to("receipts").build()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(Correlate); b.include(subscriber("payments", AuditPayment).build()) .out(Trail, Publish) .transform(SchemaVersion("2")) .build(); }) }
A subscription over a replayable log opens at a position of your choice, and its handler can move it.

A handler moves its own subscription to another position of the log through the broker's seek handle. The in-memory broker's per-delivery context carries the handle under the key SeekHandle. A handler reads it with the Ctx<SeekHandle> parameter; the manual form declares MemoryContext on its Handle and reads ctx.context(SeekHandle). seek takes a MemoryPosition, the same type start_at takes. Once seek resolves, the next delivery comes from the new position, and entries already queued before it are skipped. A sequence the retention bound has already evicted is refused with an error, and the example retries the delivery then. The handle implements Seeker, the trait a broker with a replayable log provides. Ctx<SeekHandle> does not compile against MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps no log.

The handler meets a poison marker and moves its subscription past the entries behind it. Macros Manual examples/seek.rs /// The id that marks a poisoned region: the entries up to the resume point are skipped. const POISON: u64 = 999; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "jobs")] struct Job { id: u64, } /// The seek handle is a field of the broker's per-delivery context, read with `Ctx`. #[subscriber("jobs", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { if job.id == POISON { // Resume at the fourth entry of the log. if seeker.seek(MemoryPosition::sequence(3)).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!(job.id, "processed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/seek.rs /// The id that marks a poisoned region: the entries up to the resume point are skipped. const POISON: u64 = 999; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Job { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "jobs")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Job { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "jobs"; } impl MessageHeaders for Job { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Work; // Declaring the broker's `MemoryContext` is what puts the seek handle in the context. impl Handle<Job, (), (), MemoryContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MemoryContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if job.id == POISON { // Resume at the fourth entry of the log. let seeker = ctx.context(SeekHandle); if seeker.seek(MemoryPosition::sequence(3)).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } return Ok(()); } tracing::info!(job.id, "processed"); Ok(()) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("jobs", Work) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ); }) }

start_at opens a replayable subscription at a position: the start of the log, a sequence number, or the tip. A broker over a replayable log owns its position type; for the in-memory broker it is MemoryPosition. start_at(position) seeks the subscription before its first delivery, on every startup. It is one of the mount-site settings, and the attribute takes it as a clause too. Without it, the subscription opens at the broker's default; the in-memory broker's default is the tip of the log, so earlier entries are not delivered. MemoryPosition::start() is the oldest entry the broker still keeps, sequence(n) the n-th entry published to the name, counted from zero, and end() the tip. The in-memory broker keeps a log only when it is built with MemoryBroker::retaining. start_at does not compile against MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps nothing. A broker's subscription accepts a position when it implements Seekable.

The subscription opens at the start of the log and replays what was published before the service started. Macros Manual examples/seek.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "audit")] struct Entry { id: u64, } /// The audit trail opens at the start of the log, so it also reads what came before it. #[subscriber("audit", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn record(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Replaying reads what the broker kept, so this one keeps the last 64 entries of every name. /// `MemoryBroker::new()` keeps nothing, and a mount that seeks does not compile on it. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(64))) } examples/manual/seek.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Entry { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "audit")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "audit"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Record; impl Handle<Entry> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Replaying reads what the broker kept, so this one keeps the last 64 entries of every name. /// `MemoryBroker::new()` keeps nothing, and a mount that seeks does not compile on it. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(64))) } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The audit trail opens at the start of the log, so it also reads what came before it. b.include( subscriber("audit", Record) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ); }) }

max_attempts(n) ends a message that keeps coming back, and dead_letter(name) is where it goes then. max_attempts(n) counts the deliveries one message gets, the first one included. The delivery that reaches the cap is not retried: it is published to the dead_letter destination with its payload and headers. A cap without a destination rejects the delivery instead, and a warning names the subscription. The count is the broker's own where the transport keeps one, read through redelivery_count, and the framework's RETRY_COUNT_HEADER where it keeps none. The in-memory broker counts its deliveries, so the cap there counts its redeliveries. A retry() and a retry_after(delay) are both capped. Where the broker moves a spent delivery itself (a queue with a delivery limit and a dead-letter exchange), the declaration reaches the subscription descriptor at startup, and the broker applies it. The two steps come right after include, before .out_retry(..), the slot the dead-letter copy leaves through, and each is written once.

Macros Manual examples/retry.rs /// The gateway rejects this payment every time, so on its own it would never stop coming back. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Three deliveries, then the payment goes to the dead-letter subject. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead"); }) } examples/manual/retry.rs /// The gateway rejects this payment every time, so on its own it would never stop coming back. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Three deliveries, then the payment goes to the dead-letter subject. b.include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead"); }) }

The Retry slot is the publisher a copy of a delivery leaves through; .out_retry(policy) replaces it and .to(name) names its destination. The runtime publishes a copy of a delivery in two cases: a delayed retry_after on a broker without native delayed redelivery, and a delivery sent to its dead_letter destination. Every registration has a publisher for those copies, paired from the broker's default publish policy. .out_retry(policy) replaces it; it is the Out slot Retry, so .codec(..) and .transform(..) follow it as on any slot. A copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so no codec encodes it, and its PublishTransforms read the delivery being retried. A copy sent back to the subscription carries the RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, incremented. On the in-memory broker the delay is native, so only the dead-letter copy leaves through this slot. A subscription whose source descriptor declares AddressedCopies reports where it is reached again, and copies go there. One that declares NamedCopies reads many destinations and addresses none: a wildcard, a filter, a pattern. On it the mount site names the destination with .to(name), or a transform names one per delivery. Without either, a router chain does not compile, and a mount in a broker scope refuses to start. A name given with .to(name) is a channel the registration sends to, and the generated document reports it. A broker that moves a spent delivery itself declares BrokerMoves, and .out_retry(..) does not compile there.

Macros Manual examples/settle_retry_destination.rs /// Stamps every copy with the subscription its delivery came from. struct RetriedFrom; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for RetriedFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } #[subscriber("payments")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(2u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") // Replaces the broker's default publisher for the copies of this registration. .out_retry(Publish) .transform(RetriedFrom); }) } examples/manual/settle_retry_destination.rs /// Stamps every copy with the subscription its delivery came from. struct RetriedFrom; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for RetriedFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(2u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") // Replaces the broker's default publisher for the copies of this registration. .out_retry(Publish) .transform(RetriedFrom); }) }

A Router groups one module's handlers with their own middleware and codec, and include_router mounts the group on a broker. A router is a group of registrations bound to a broker type, not to a broker value, so a module builds it without a connection. include adds a #[subscriber] handler to the router the same way it adds one to a broker scope, settings included. A router's full type names every registration in a RouterDef, so a builder function returns impl RouterDef<B>, or Router<B, impl RouterDef<B>> when the caller still merges it. merge appends another router's registrations, and each router keeps its own codec and layers. include_router on a broker scope of the application mounts the group. layer adds middleware and is called before the router's first include; after one, .layer(..) applies to that registration alone. A router's layer must be a BlanketLayer, because the router hides its handlers' types. The app's own layers wrap outside the router's layers. Router layers wrap single-message handlers; batch handlers are not wrapped. with_codec switches the codec mid-chain: registrations already added keep the codec they were added with. Without it, a router decodes with the default codec, JSON when the json feature is on.

Each module returns its router, and the service merges them and mounts the result. Macros Manual examples/routing.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn dispatch(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The orders module's handlers. fn orders() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(accept) } /// The shipping module's handlers. fn shipping() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(dispatch) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders().merge(shipping())); }) } examples/manual/routing.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Dispatch; impl Handle<Shipment> for Dispatch { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The orders module's handlers. fn orders() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) } /// The shipping module's handlers. fn shipping() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(subscriber("shipments", Dispatch).build()) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders().merge(shipping())); }) }

Router::layer wraps every handler of the router, and nothing mounted outside it. Macros Manual examples/routing.rs /// Counts the deliveries of the handlers it wraps. #[derive(Clone)] struct Count(Arc<AtomicUsize>); struct Counted<H> { inner: H, count: Arc<AtomicUsize>, } // A router hides its handlers' types, so its layer wraps a handler of any type. impl BlanketLayer for Count { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { Counted { inner: handler, count: Arc::clone(&self.0), } } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Counted<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { self.count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.inner.handle(msg, ctx).await } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn dispatch(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(orders_seen: Arc<AtomicUsize>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The layer comes first and wraps every handler of this router. b.include_router(Router::new().layer(Count(orders_seen)).include(accept)); // Mounted on the scope, outside the router's layer. b.include(dispatch); }) } examples/manual/routing.rs /// Counts the deliveries of the handlers it wraps. #[derive(Clone)] struct Count(Arc<AtomicUsize>); struct Counted<H> { inner: H, count: Arc<AtomicUsize>, } // A router hides its handlers' types, so its layer wraps a handler of any type. impl BlanketLayer for Count { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { Counted { inner: handler, count: Arc::clone(&self.0), } } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Counted<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { self.count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.inner.handle(msg, ctx).await } } struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Dispatch; impl Handle<Shipment> for Dispatch { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(orders_seen: Arc<AtomicUsize>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The layer comes first and wraps every handler of this router. b.include_router( Router::new() .layer(Count(orders_seen)) .include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()), ); // Mounted on the scope, outside the router's layer. b.include(subscriber("shipments", Dispatch).build()); }) }

Router::with_codec sets the codec the registrations after it decode with. Macros Manual examples/routing.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The registrations after `with_codec` decode CBOR. fn orders() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker> { Router::new().with_codec(CborCodec).include(accept) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders()); }) } examples/manual/routing.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The registrations after `with_codec` decode CBOR. fn orders() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker> { Router::new() .with_codec(CborCodec) .include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders()); }) }

A subscriber reads a subscription named by a string or by the broker's descriptor, fixed in the attribute or left to the mount site. The attribute fixes the kind of subscription and may leave its value to the mount site: Attribute Kind Value #[subscriber("orders")] by name fixed here #[subscriber] by name .name(..) at the mount site #[subscriber(MemorySource::new("orders"))] the broker's descriptor fixed here #[subscriber(MemorySource)] the broker's descriptor .name(..) at the mount site A name is a Name source and works on any broker that implements Subscribe, which opens its default subscription kind for that name. A descriptor is a type of the broker crate that implements SubscriptionSource and carries the broker's own settings, such as a consumer group or a durable name; the in-memory broker's is MemorySource. The macro reads the descriptor's type off the constructor call, so the expression ends in Type::new(..) and every step after it returns Self. A descriptor kind that the mount site names implements FromName. A source left open must be named: a mount without .name(..) does not compile. .name(..) is one of the mount-site settings and takes any string, so the name may come from configuration read before the app is built. A descriptor kind that needs more than a name, such as a Pulsar topic with its subscription, is written out in full in the attribute. In the manual form the first argument of subscriber is the source: a string, a descriptor, or Unnamed::<Kind>::new() for a source the mount site names, an Unnamed value.

The bare attribute leaves the name to the mount site. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_source.rs /// The attribute leaves the name open: the mount site gives it. #[subscriber] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(shard: u32) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(audit.name(format!("audit-{shard}"))); }) } examples/manual/subscriber_source.rs struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(shard: u32) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // `Unnamed<Name>` is no source yet: the mount does not compile until `.name(..)`. b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<Name>::new(), Audit) .name(format!("audit-{shard}")) .build(), ); }) }

A descriptor is fixed in the attribute, or only its kind is, and the name comes at the mount site. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_source.rs /// The broker's descriptor, fixed in the attribute. #[subscriber(MemorySource::new("orders"))] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The descriptor's kind in the attribute, its name at the mount site. #[subscriber(MemorySource)] async fn archive(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); b.include(archive.name("archive")); }) } examples/manual/subscriber_source.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Archive; impl Handle<Order> for Archive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's descriptor, built here. b.include(subscriber(MemorySource::new("orders"), Accept).build()); // The descriptor's kind, named at the mount site. b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<MemorySource>::new(), Archive) .name("archive") .build(), ); }) }

A serde struct is the header contract a handler reads and a publish writes, checked in both directions. A contract is a flat struct: each field names a header, and its value travels as a string. Fields are numbers, booleans, strings, bytes, unit-only enums, or Options of those. An Option field reads as None when its header is absent; any other missing field fails the contract. Header names are matched without regard to case; #[serde(rename = "..")] gives a wire name that is not a Rust identifier. Headers<T> parses the contract before the body runs. A contract that does not parse is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's on_failure(decode = ..) policy. In a manual body Headers::<T>::from_context(ctx) parses it, and a failure there drops the delivery. The raw HeaderMap of a delivery stays on its context. What the handler publishes carries a contract of its own, declared on the outgoing type.

Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// What travels in the headers of a chunk: each field is one header, its value a string. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct ChunkMeta { task_id: u64, chunk_no: u32, chunks_total: u32, } /// What travels in the headers of a finished chunk. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct DoneMeta { task_id: u64, chunk_no: u32, } examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// What travels in the headers of a chunk: each field is one header, its value a string. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct ChunkMeta { task_id: u64, chunk_no: u32, chunks_total: u32, } /// What travels in the headers of a finished chunk. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct DoneMeta { task_id: u64, chunk_no: u32, } Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// The contract is parsed before the body runs; what the body publishes carries its own. #[subscriber("chunks")] async fn convert( chunk: &Chunk, Headers(meta): Headers<ChunkMeta>, Out(events): Out<impl Publisher, Events>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no, chunk.size, "converting"); let done = ChunkDone { output_key: format!("chunks/{}/{}.part", meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no), }; let done_meta = DoneMeta { task_id: meta.task_id, chunk_no: meta.chunk_no, }; match events .message(&done) .with_headers(&done_meta) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// The contract is parsed before the work starts; what the body publishes carries its own. struct Convert; impl<Entry> Handle<Chunk, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Convert where Entry: OutEntry<Events, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, chunk: &Chunk, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Headers(meta) = Headers::<ChunkMeta>::from_context(ctx).await?; tracing::info!(meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no, chunk.size, "converting"); let done = ChunkDone { output_key: format!("chunks/{}/{}.part", meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no), }; let done_meta = DoneMeta { task_id: meta.task_id, chunk_no: meta.chunk_no, }; let sent = outs .get(Events) .message(&done) .with_headers(&done_meta) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

HeaderMap::insert_typed writes a header contract into a header map, the way a publish transform stamps every message of a slot. A field becomes one header named after it, its value written as a string. A None field writes nothing, and a header of the same name is overwritten. A field that holds a nested struct, a sequence or a map is an error. The example's transform is a publish transform on an Out slot, so every message the slot sends carries the contract.

Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// Where the service runs, as a contract stamped on everything the slot sends. #[derive(Clone, Serialize)] struct Origin { region: &'static str, canary: bool, } struct Stamp(Origin); impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForSlot, Options> for Stamp { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &SlotContext<'_>, ) { if let Err(error) = out.headers_mut().insert_typed(&self.0) { tracing::warn!(%error, "origin headers left out"); } } } fn app() -> impl App { let origin = Origin { region: "eu-west", canary: false, }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("transcoder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(convert) .out(Events, Publish) .transform(Stamp(origin)) .build(); }) } examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// Where the service runs, as a contract stamped on everything the slot sends. #[derive(Clone, Serialize)] struct Origin { region: &'static str, canary: bool, } struct Stamp(Origin); impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForSlot, Options> for Stamp { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &SlotContext<'_>, ) { if let Err(error) = out.headers_mut().insert_typed(&self.0) { tracing::warn!(%error, "origin headers left out"); } } } fn app() -> impl App { let origin = Origin { region: "eu-west", canary: false, }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("transcoder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("chunks", Convert).build()) .out(Events, Publish) .transform(Stamp(origin)) .build(); }) }

Message<H, T> hands a handler the decoded payload and its parsed header contract as one input. chunk.headers is the contract and chunk.body the payload. The contract parses the way Headers<T> parses it, and a contract that does not parse is a decode failure. A batch handler takes &[Message<H, T>], so each element keeps its own headers. A reply typed Message<H, T> carries its headers the same way.

Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// The payload and its contract arrive decoded together. #[subscriber("chunks")] async fn store(chunk: &Message<ChunkMeta, Chunk>) -> HandlerOutcome { let meta = &chunk.headers; if meta.chunk_no >= meta.chunks_total { // A chunk past the end of its task. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no, chunk.body.size, "stored"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// The payload and its contract arrive decoded together. struct Store; impl Handle<Message<ChunkMeta, Chunk>> for Store { fn handle( &self, chunk: &Message<ChunkMeta, Chunk>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let meta = &chunk.headers; if meta.chunk_no >= meta.chunks_total { // A chunk past the end of its task. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(meta.task_id, meta.chunk_no, chunk.body.size, "stored"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A message type names its header contract, so publishing it does not compile without the headers. #[outgoing(headers = Meta)] makes the contract part of the message type, the type's MessageHeaders contract. Its publish does not compile without .with_headers(&meta). The manual form implements MessageHeaders by hand and names the contract as its Contract; a type with none names NoHeaders. An Out slot lists the types it may publish in #[publishes(..)], and each keeps its own contract, as on the Slots page. The handler on the Headers page publishes a ChunkDone through such a slot.

Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// A chunk: publishing one does not compile without its `ChunkMeta`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "chunks", headers = ChunkMeta)] struct Chunk { size: u64, } /// A finished chunk: publishing one does not compile without its `DoneMeta`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "chunks.done", headers = DoneMeta)] struct ChunkDone { output_key: String, } examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// A chunk: publishing one does not compile without its `ChunkMeta`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Chunk { size: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Chunk { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "chunks"; } impl MessageHeaders for Chunk { type Contract = WithHeaders<ChunkMeta>; } /// A finished chunk: publishing one does not compile without its `DoneMeta`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct ChunkDone { output_key: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for ChunkDone { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "chunks.done"; } impl MessageHeaders for ChunkDone { type Contract = WithHeaders<DoneMeta>; } Macros Manual examples/typed_headers.rs /// The slot the converter publishes through, and what it may publish. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(ChunkDone)] struct Events; examples/manual/typed_headers.rs /// The slot the converter publishes through, and what it may publish. struct Events; impl OutSlot for Events { const NAME: &'static str = "Events"; type Destination = Reads; fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { <ChunkDone as OutMessages<Self>>::outgoing() } } impl PublishedThrough<Events> for ChunkDone {} impl<M: OutSlot> OutMessages<M> for ChunkDone { fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { vec![OutgoingMessageMetadata::new( Self::DESTINATION, type_name::<Self>(), )] } }

Guides take you from an empty crate to a running RustStream service. Installation: the crate, its cargo features and a broker crate. Quick start: a running service scaffolded with cargo generate. Tutorial: an orders service with a message type, a handler, a reply and a router, on the in-memory broker. Agent skills: skills that teach a coding agent to write services, tests and broker crates the recommended way. Build a service, step by step: one shop service grown chapter by chapter, from its first subscriber to a networked broker. Brokers: the broker crates, and moving a service to another broker.

Eleven chapters grow one RustStream service, a small shop, from its first subscriber to a networked broker. The shop takes an order, charges it, ships it and tells the customer. Each step is a subscriber, and the steps talk to each other through topics. The shop runs on the in-memory broker, so every chapter runs with nothing to install. Each chapter adds the components it needs and links to their pages in Components. Every code block has two tabs: Macros with the attributes and derives, Manual with the same code written by hand. The finished shop lives in examples/guide in the repository, and its manual twin in examples/manual/guide. CI builds both and runs their tests on every change. Each side of the shop is a module: orders.rs, payments.rs, shipping.rs and notifications.rs. state.rs holds what the subscribers share, observability.rs a middleware of the shop's own, and service.rs assembles the app. main.rs is the command-line entry point, and http.rs runs the same shop beside an HTTP server.
documents.s: Build a service, step by step

documents.t: asyncapi gen prints the shop's AsyncAPI document: every topic, who reads and writes it, the schemas, the retry cap, and the description the app gives itself. The document is built from the app itself, so it cannot describe a topic the code does not use. Each subscription is a receive operation, each reply and slot a send operation. A payload's schema comes from its JsonSchema derive, and a doc comment becomes a description. max_attempts and dead_letter appear on the operation, so a reader sees where a failing message ends up. AsyncAPI covers servers, security schemes and serving the document over HTTP. The document needs the crate's asyncapi feature.

main.rs builds the shop on the in-memory broker. #[ruststream::app] gives the binary its commands: run starts the shop, asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual main.rs /// `run` starts the shop; `asyncapi gen` prints its AsyncAPI document. #[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")] fn app() -> impl App<State = Shop> { service::shop(MemoryBroker::new()) } main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Shop> { service::shop(MemoryBroker::new()) } /// What `#[ruststream::app]` writes: `run` starts the shop; `asyncapi gen` prints its AsyncAPI /// document. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main_on(AppRuntime::CurrentThread, app) }

AppInfo is the document's info block: the title, the version, a description, a contact, a license and tags. Macros Manual service.rs /// What the AsyncAPI document says about the shop. fn info() -> AppInfo { AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0") .description("Takes orders, charges them, ships them and tells the customer.") .contact(Contact::new().name("Shop team").email("shop@example.com")) .license(License::new("Apache-2.0")) .tag(Tag::new("orders")) } service.rs /// What the AsyncAPI document says about the shop. fn info() -> AppInfo { AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0") .description("Takes orders, charges them, ships them and tells the customer.") .contact(Contact::new().name("Shop team").email("shop@example.com")) .license(License::new("Apache-2.0")) .tag(Tag::new("orders")) }
documents.s: What the shop says about itself

documents.t: cargo run --example guide --features testing,macros,memory,json,cbor,asyncapi -- asyncapi gen --yaml The operation of charge reads the topic, answers on payments.settled, and declares the cap: receive_payments_requested: action: receive channel: $ref: '#/channels/payments.requested' messages: - $ref: '#/channels/payments.requested/messages/PaymentRequest' description: Charges an order through the payment provider. reply: channel: $ref: '#/channels/payments.settled' messages: - $ref: '#/channels/payments.settled/messages/Paid' x-ruststream-retry: maxAttempts: 5 deadLetter: payments.dead Both forms of the shop produce the same document. A test in each compares the document with examples/guide/asyncapi.json, so a change to a topic shows up in review.

Packing computes, so it gets two threads of its own; booking a courier waits on the network, so four bookings run at once. A subscription handles one delivery at a time by default, in the order the broker hands them over. Workers let it handle several at once on the app's runtime: the right tool for a handler that waits on I/O. Threads give it threads of its own: the right tool for a handler that computes, since it would otherwise hold up the runtime that serves every other subscription. Both are settings of the subscription, and the handler's body does not change. A subscription with workers or threads no longer keeps its deliveries in order; workers(n, by_key) keeps the order of each key.

pack splits a paid order into parcels and answers with the plan. A paid order past the shop's bounds is dropped before any parcel is planned. threads(2) starts two threads with the subscription; the deliveries go to them in turn. Decoding, the body, the reply and the settlement all run on the thread that got the delivery. Macros Manual shipping.rs /// Packs a paid order into parcels. // Packing is computation: two threads of its own keep it off the app's runtime, which serves I/O. #[subscriber("payments.settled", threads(2), reply)] async fn pack(paid: &Paid) -> Result<Packed, HandlerOutcome> { if !within_bounds(&paid.lines) { tracing::warn!( order = paid.order, "a paid order past the shop's bounds, dropped" ); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(Packed { order: paid.order, customer: paid.customer.clone(), parcels: plan(&paid.lines), }) } shipping.rs /// Packs a paid order into parcels. struct Pack; impl Handle<Paid, Packed, (), (), Shop> for Pack { fn handle( &self, paid: &Paid, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Packed, HandlerOutcome>> { if !within_bounds(&paid.lines) { tracing::warn!( order = paid.order, "a paid order past the shop's bounds, dropped" ); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(Packed { order: paid.order, customer: paid.customer.clone(), parcels: plan(&paid.lines), })) } }

dispatch books a courier for a packed order and tells the customer the tracking code. workers(4) keeps up to four bookings in flight; the next delivery waits for a free worker. Macros Manual shipping.rs /// Books a courier for a packed order and tells the customer. // Booking waits on the courier's API, so four bookings run at once. #[subscriber("shipping.packed", workers(4))] async fn dispatch(packed: &Packed, Out(notices): Out<impl Publisher, Notices>) -> HandlerOutcome { let tracking = book_courier(packed).await; let notice = Notice { customer: packed.customer.clone(), text: format!("Order {} is on its way: {tracking}.", packed.order), }; match notices.message(&notice).publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } shipping.rs /// Books a courier for a packed order and tells the customer. struct Dispatch; impl<Entry> Handle<Packed, (), Outs<(Entry,)>, (), Shop> for Dispatch where Entry: OutEntry<Notices, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, packed: &Packed, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let tracking = book_courier(packed).await; let notice = Notice { customer: packed.customer.clone(), text: format!("Order {} is on its way: {tracking}.", packed.order), }; let sent = outs.get(Notices).message(&notice).publish().await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

The shipping router reads the shop's own topics, so it decodes CBOR. A reply takes the default codec unless its position names one, so pack's reply names CBOR. A slot takes the router's codec unless it names one, so the notices name JSON. In the manual form the two settings are steps of the mount chain: threads and workers. With the computing step on threads of its own, the app's runtime only waits on I/O, so the shop runs it on the thread that calls main: #[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")], or run_main_on(AppRuntime::CurrentThread, app) in the manual form. The HTTP entry point of a later chapter does the same with #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]. Macros Manual shipping.rs /// The shipping side's subscribers. Both read the shop's own topics, so both decode CBOR. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .with_codec(INTERNAL) .include(pack) // A reply encodes with the default codec unless its position names one. .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .build() .include(dispatch) // A slot encodes with the router's codec unless it names one; notices stay JSON. .out(Notices, Publish) .codec(JsonCodec) .build() } shipping.rs /// The shipping side's subscribers. Both read the shop's own topics, so both decode CBOR. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .with_codec(INTERNAL) .include( subscriber(Paid::DESTINATION, Pack) .describe("Packs a paid order into parcels.") // Packing is computation: two threads of its own keep it off the app's runtime. .threads(nonzero!(2)) .reply() .build(), ) // A reply encodes with the default codec unless its position names one. .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .build() .include( subscriber(Packed::DESTINATION, Dispatch) .describe("Books a courier for a packed order and tells the customer.") // Booking waits on the courier's API, so four bookings run at once. .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ) // A slot encodes with the router's codec unless it names one; notices stay JSON. .out(Notices, Publish) .codec(JsonCodec) .build() } Threads pay off from about ten microseconds of computation per delivery; on a lighter handler they cost more than they save. Poll diagnostics find the handlers that hold up the runtime.

The storefront takes orders over HTTP and stores them with their events; a relay hands the events to the broker, and the shop runs beside the server. When the service also serves HTTP, the HTTP server owns the process and the shop runs beside it. start starts the shop in the background and returns once it is running, so a broker that refuses to connect stops the process before the server takes a request. An HTTP request should not publish to the broker itself: a broker outage would fail the request, and an order stored without its event would never reach the shop. A transactional outbox solves both. The request writes the order and its event in one transaction, and a relay publishes the stored events later. A broker outage only delays the events, and none is lost; a crash between a publish and its removal publishes the event again, so the shop sees each order at least once.
documents.s: Running beside an HTTP server, outbox

documents.t: With a real database, the orders and the outbox are two tables written in one transaction. The mutex over the pair plays that role here. Only a real database lets the events survive a crash: these rows live in memory, and a crash loses the ones not yet published. Macros Manual http.rs /// The orders the storefront took, and the events the shop still owes the broker. With a real /// database both writes run in one transaction; the mutex over the pair plays that role here. #[derive(Default)] struct Store { orders: Vec<Order>, outbox: VecDeque<(RequestMeta, Order)>, } http.rs /// The orders the storefront took, and the events the shop still owes the broker. With a real /// database both writes run in one transaction; the mutex over the pair plays that role here. #[derive(Default)] struct Store { orders: Vec<Order>, outbox: VecDeque<(RequestMeta, Order)>, } The HTTP side and the outbox are plain functions, so both tabs show the same code.

POST /orders takes the order as JSON and the request id from the x-request-id header. It only writes to the store, so it answers 202 Accepted without waiting on the broker. An order past the shop's bounds answers 400 Bad Request and is not stored. Macros Manual http.rs /// Takes an order over HTTP. The request only writes to the store, so no broker I/O can fail or /// stall the response. async fn place_order( State(store): State<Arc<Mutex<Store>>>, headers: HeaderMap, Json(order): Json<Order>, ) -> (StatusCode, &'static str) { let request_id = headers .get("x-request-id") .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok()) .unwrap_or("unknown") .to_owned(); if total_cents(&order.lines).is_none() { return ( StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "the order is past the shop's bounds
", ); } { let mut store = store.lock().await; store.orders.push(order.clone()); store.outbox.push_back((RequestMeta { request_id }, order)); } (StatusCode::ACCEPTED, "accepted
") } http.rs /// Takes an order over HTTP. The request only writes to the store, so no broker I/O can fail or /// stall the response. async fn place_order( State(store): State<Arc<Mutex<Store>>>, headers: HeaderMap, Json(order): Json<Order>, ) -> (StatusCode, &'static str) { let request_id = headers .get("x-request-id") .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok()) .unwrap_or("unknown") .to_owned(); if total_cents(&order.lines).is_none() { return ( StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "the order is past the shop's bounds
", ); } { let mut store = store.lock().await; store.orders.push(order.clone()); store.outbox.push_back((RequestMeta { request_id }, order)); } (StatusCode::ACCEPTED, "accepted
") }

The relay publishes the oldest event first, with its header contract, and removes it only after the publish succeeded. A refused publish leaves the row for the next round. The relay runs until the process stops it, then runs one last round. The publisher is any Publisher, so the relay does not change with the broker. Macros Manual http.rs /// Hands the outbox to the broker, oldest event first. A row leaves the outbox only after its /// publish succeeded, so a broker outage delays events and loses none. async fn relay_pending(store: &Mutex<Store>, egress: &impl Publisher) { loop { let Some((meta, order)) = store.lock().await.outbox.front().cloned() else { return; }; let sent = egress .message(&order) .with_headers(&meta) .with_codec(JsonCodec) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { // The row stays for the next round. return; } store.lock().await.outbox.pop_front(); } } /// Runs the relay every 200 milliseconds until `stop` completes, then runs it once more. async fn relay_outbox( store: Arc<Mutex<Store>>, egress: impl Publisher, stop: impl Future<Output = ()>, ) { let mut rounds = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_millis(200)); tokio::pin!(stop); loop { tokio::select! { biased; () = &mut stop => break, _ = rounds.tick() => relay_pending(&store, &egress).await, } } // The last round runs once no request writes a row any more, so it empties the outbox. relay_pending(&store, &egress).await; } http.rs /// Hands the outbox to the broker, oldest event first. A row leaves the outbox only after its /// publish succeeded, so a broker outage delays events and loses none. async fn relay_pending(store: &Mutex<Store>, egress: &impl Publisher) { loop { let Some((meta, order)) = store.lock().await.outbox.front().cloned() else { return; }; let sent = egress .message(&order) .with_headers(&meta) .with_codec(JsonCodec) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { // The row stays for the next round. return; } store.lock().await.outbox.pop_front(); } } /// Runs the relay every 200 milliseconds until `stop` completes, then runs it once more. async fn relay_outbox( store: Arc<Mutex<Store>>, egress: impl Publisher, stop: impl Future<Output = ()>, ) { let mut rounds = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_millis(200)); tokio::pin!(stop); loop { tokio::select! { biased; () = &mut stop => break, _ = rounds.tick() => relay_pending(&store, &egress).await, } } // The last round runs once no request writes a row any more, so it empties the outbox. relay_pending(&store, &egress).await; }

bindable lets the process take a publisher token before the shop starts, and publisher turns it into a live publisher once the broker is connected. The server stops on Ctrl+C, or when stopping reports that the shop stopped on its own. Once HTTP has drained, the process stops the relay, and its last round hands over the rows still pending while the shop runs. The shop then drains with shutdown. MemoryBroker keeps its queues in the process's memory as well: an order the last round hands over that the shop has not taken by the time it drains is lost with the process, and a broker that stores its messages keeps it for the next start. A hand-written main installs the logger itself with ruststream::logging::init().
