Macros Manual http.rs #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { ruststream::logging::init()?; let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); // A token now, a live publisher once the shop has connected the broker. let egress = broker.bind(Publish); // The shop starts first: a broker that refuses to connect stops the process before HTTP // takes a request. let running = shop(broker).start().await?; let egress = running.publisher(egress).await?; let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Store::default())); let stop_relay = CancellationToken::new(); let relay = tokio::spawn(relay_outbox( Arc::clone(&store), egress, stop_relay.clone().cancelled_owned(), )); let router = axum::Router::new() .route("/orders", post(place_order)) .with_state(store); let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?; tracing::info!("storefront on http://127.0.0.1:8080/orders"); // HTTP stops on Ctrl+C, or when the shop stops on its own; the shop then drains. let stopping = running.stopping(); axum::serve(listener, router) .with_graceful_shutdown(async move { tokio::select! { _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {} () = stopping => {} } }) .await?; // HTTP has drained, so no request writes a row any more: the relay's last round hands the // pending rows over while the shop still runs, and only then does the shop drain. stop_relay.cancel(); relay.await?; running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } http.rs #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { ruststream::logging::init()?; let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); // A token now, a live publisher once the shop has connected the broker. let egress = broker.bind(Publish); // The shop starts first: a broker that refuses to connect stops the process before HTTP // takes a request. let running = shop(broker).start().await?; let egress = running.publisher(egress).await?; let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Store::default())); let stop_relay = CancellationToken::new(); let relay = tokio::spawn(relay_outbox( Arc::clone(&store), egress, stop_relay.clone().cancelled_owned(), )); let router = axum::Router::new() .route("/orders", post(place_order)) .with_state(store); let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?; tracing::info!("storefront on http://127.0.0.1:8080/orders"); // HTTP stops on Ctrl+C, or when the shop stops on its own; the shop then drains. let stopping = running.stopping(); axum::serve(listener, router) .with_graceful_shutdown(async move { tokio::select! { _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {} () = stopping => {} } }) .await?; // HTTP has drained, so no request writes a row any more: the relay's last round hands the // pending rows over while the shop still runs, and only then does the shop drain. stop_relay.cancel(); relay.await?; running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } Run it and place an order: cargo run --example guide_http --features testing,macros,memory,json,cbor,asyncapi,logging curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/orders -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H 'x-request-id: req-1' \ -d '{"id":1,"customer":"ada@example.com","lines":[{"sku":"mug","quantity":12,"price_cents":1200}]}' The log of chapter 5 follows the order through the shop. A health endpoint reports the shop's state to an orchestrator from the same server.

An order grows into a payload with lines, a header contract every publish must carry, and a codec chosen per topic. The payload is any serde type; the codec turns it into bytes and back. The headers travel beside the payload, and a header contract is a serde struct with one field per header. A message type that names a contract cannot be published without it: the publish does not compile. A subscriber reads the contract with a Headers<T> parameter, parsed before the body runs. A delivery whose headers do not parse never reaches the body and is dropped, like a payload that does not decode. The codec belongs to the mount site, not to the type, so one type can travel as JSON on one topic and as CBOR on another.

From here on, the shop's code lives in modules. orders.rs holds the order: its lines, the total, and the contract it travels with. The bounds cap what one order may ask for, and the total adds up with checked arithmetic, so an order past them has no total. Macros Manual orders.rs /// How many lines an order may hold. pub(crate) const MAX_LINES: usize = 100; /// How many items one line may order. pub(crate) const MAX_QUANTITY: u32 = 1_000; /// The highest price of one item, in cents. pub(crate) const MAX_PRICE_CENTS: u64 = 1_000_000; /// One line of an order: what the customer buys, how many, and at what price. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Line { pub(crate) sku: String, pub(crate) quantity: u32, pub(crate) price_cents: u64, } /// An order placed in the storefront. It travels with the headers of the request that placed it. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.placed", headers = RequestMeta)] pub(crate) struct Order { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, } /// Whether `lines` stay within the shop's bounds. pub(crate) fn within_bounds(lines: &[Line]) -> bool { lines.len() <= MAX_LINES && lines .iter() .all(|line| line.quantity <= MAX_QUANTITY && line.price_cents <= MAX_PRICE_CENTS) } /// What `lines` cost together, or `None` past the shop's bounds. pub(crate) fn total_cents(lines: &[Line]) -> Option<u64> { if !within_bounds(lines) { return None; } lines.iter().try_fold(0_u64, |total, line| { total.checked_add(u64::from(line.quantity).checked_mul(line.price_cents)?) }) } orders.rs /// How many lines an order may hold. pub(crate) const MAX_LINES: usize = 100; /// How many items one line may order. pub(crate) const MAX_QUANTITY: u32 = 1_000; /// The highest price of one item, in cents. pub(crate) const MAX_PRICE_CENTS: u64 = 1_000_000; /// One line of an order: what the customer buys, how many, and at what price. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Line { pub(crate) sku: String, pub(crate) quantity: u32, pub(crate) price_cents: u64, } /// An order placed in the storefront. It travels with the headers of the request that placed it. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Order { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "orders.placed", headers = RequestMeta)]` // writes: the destination, the headers a publish must carry, and the name in the document. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.placed"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = WithHeaders<RequestMeta>; } impl MessageInfo for Order { const NAME: &'static str = "Order"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some( "An order placed in the storefront. It travels with the headers of the request that \ placed it.", ); } /// Whether `lines` stay within the shop's bounds. pub(crate) fn within_bounds(lines: &[Line]) -> bool { lines.len() <= MAX_LINES && lines .iter() .all(|line| line.quantity <= MAX_QUANTITY && line.price_cents <= MAX_PRICE_CENTS) } /// What `lines` cost together, or `None` past the shop's bounds. pub(crate) fn total_cents(lines: &[Line]) -> Option<u64> { if !within_bounds(lines) { return None; } lines.iter().try_fold(0_u64, |total, line| { total.checked_add(u64::from(line.quantity).checked_mul(line.price_cents)?) }) } headers = RequestMeta makes the contract part of the type. The manual form says the same with type Contract = WithHeaders<RequestMeta>, and gives the message its name in the AsyncAPI document with a MessageInfo impl.

Each field of the contract is one header. request_id names the storefront request that placed the order, so every step can log it. Macros Manual orders.rs /// The headers of a placed order: each field is one header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct RequestMeta { pub(crate) request_id: String, } orders.rs /// The headers of a placed order: each field is one header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct RequestMeta { pub(crate) request_id: String, }

audit is a second subscriber on orders.placed: it writes every order to the audit log with the request that placed it. Each subscription gets every message of its topic, so audit and the accept of the next chapter both see each order. The manual form takes the pair Message<RequestMeta, Order> as its input: both parts decode before the body runs, and the AsyncAPI document shows the header schema. Macros Manual orders.rs /// Writes every placed order to the audit log, with the request that placed it. #[subscriber("orders.placed")] async fn audit(order: &Order, Headers(meta): Headers<RequestMeta>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!( request = %meta.request_id, order = order.id, total_cents = total_cents(&order.lines), "order placed", ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } orders.rs /// Writes every placed order to the audit log, with the request that placed it. struct Audit; // The input is the pair of headers and payload: both decode before the body runs, and the // document shows the header schema, as a `Headers<RequestMeta>` parameter does with the macros. impl Handle<Message<RequestMeta, Order>, (), (), (), Shop> for Audit { fn handle( &self, placed: &Message<RequestMeta, Order>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let (meta, order) = (&placed.headers, &placed.body); tracing::info!( request = %meta.request_id, order = order.id, total_cents = total_cents(&order.lines), "order placed", ); ready(Ok(())) } }

JSON is the default codec, and the shop keeps it for orders.placed and notices, which other teams read. The topics between the shop's own steps travel as CBOR: smaller, and read by no one else. One constant names that codec, so the routers of the next chapters cannot disagree about it. Macros Manual payments.rs /// The codec of the topics between the shop's own steps: CBOR is smaller than JSON, and no /// other team reads them. pub(crate) const INTERNAL: CborCodec = CborCodec; payments.rs /// The codec of the topics between the shop's own steps: CBOR is smaller than JSON, and no /// other team reads them. pub(crate) const INTERNAL: CborCodec = CborCodec; A router decodes with the codec with_codec names, and each publish position names its own with .codec(..). The next chapter puts both to use. CBOR needs the crate's cbor feature.
documents.s: The codec of the shop's own topics

documents.t: The app wraps every subscriber in two layers: one logs each delivery and its outcome, one of the shop's own warns about slow handlers. A Layer wraps a handler in another handler. It runs code before the body, after it, or instead of it, and passes the outcome on. A layer on the app wraps every subscriber the app mounts; a layer on a router wraps that router's subscribers only. RustStream emits its own events through tracing: the service starting, each subscription opening, the service stopping. TracingLayer adds an event for every delivery: delivery received at DEBUG, then its outcome, an ack at INFO, a retry or a drop at WARN. The logging feature prints them, as chapter 1 showed; any other tracing subscriber works in its place. Observability covers Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry export, which mount as layers the same way.

SlowHandlers times each handler and warns when one runs longer than its threshold. The warning names the subscription, read off the delivery's context. A layer has no macro form: it is the same plain type in both tabs. BlanketLayer is what lets the app apply it to handlers whose types it hides. Macros Manual observability.rs /// Warns about every delivery whose handler ran longer than the threshold. #[derive(Clone)] pub(crate) struct SlowHandlers { threshold: Duration, } impl SlowHandlers { pub(crate) const fn over(threshold: Duration) -> Self { Self { threshold } } } /// The handler `SlowHandlers` makes of the one it wraps. pub(crate) struct Timed<H> { inner: H, threshold: Duration, } impl<H> Layer<H> for SlowHandlers { type Handler = Timed<H>; fn layer(&self, inner: H) -> Timed<H> { Timed { inner, threshold: self.threshold, } } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Timed<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { let started = Instant::now(); let outcome = self.inner.handle(msg, ctx).await; let took = started.elapsed(); if took > self.threshold { tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), ?took, "slow handler"); } outcome } } // The app wraps handlers whose types it hides, through this generic method. impl BlanketLayer for SlowHandlers { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { self.layer(handler) } } observability.rs /// Warns about every delivery whose handler ran longer than the threshold. #[derive(Clone)] pub(crate) struct SlowHandlers { threshold: Duration, } impl SlowHandlers { pub(crate) const fn over(threshold: Duration) -> Self { Self { threshold } } } /// The handler `SlowHandlers` makes of the one it wraps. pub(crate) struct Timed<H> { inner: H, threshold: Duration, } impl<H> Layer<H> for SlowHandlers { type Handler = Timed<H>; fn layer(&self, inner: H) -> Timed<H> { Timed { inner, threshold: self.threshold, } } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Timed<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { let started = Instant::now(); let outcome = self.inner.handle(msg, ctx).await; let took = started.elapsed(); if took > self.threshold { tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), ?took, "slow handler"); } outcome } } // The app wraps handlers whose types it hides, through this generic method. impl BlanketLayer for SlowHandlers { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { self.layer(handler) } }
documents.s: A layer of the shop's own

documents.t: service.rs assembles the shop. layer adds a layer to the app; the first one added is the outermost. Each module's router mounts with include_router, and the app's layers wrap its subscribers. on_startup opens the shared state of chapter 7, and info() is the description of chapter 9. The function takes the broker as a parameter, so the command-line entry point and the HTTP host of chapter 10 build the same shop. Macros Manual service.rs /// The whole shop on `broker`. The command-line entry point and the HTTP host both build it here. pub(crate) fn shop( broker: impl BrokerRegistration<Broker = MemoryBroker>, ) -> impl App<State = Shop> { RustStream::new(info()) .on_startup(async move |()| Shop::open().await) .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .layer(SlowHandlers::over(Duration::from_millis(250))) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include_router(orders::routes()); b.include_router(payments::routes()); b.include_router(shipping::routes()); b.include_router(notifications::routes()); }) } service.rs /// The whole shop on `broker`. The command-line entry point and the HTTP host both build it here. pub(crate) fn shop( broker: impl BrokerRegistration<Broker = MemoryBroker>, ) -> impl App<State = Shop> { RustStream::new(info()) .on_startup(async move |()| Shop::open().await) .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .layer(SlowHandlers::over(Duration::from_millis(250))) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include_router(orders::routes()); b.include_router(payments::routes()); b.include_router(shipping::routes()); b.include_router(notifications::routes()); }) }

An order placed with the request id req-1 leaves one line per step: INFO guide_http::orders order placed request=req-1 order=1 total_cents=14400 INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO guide_http::notifications mail sent server=smtp://mail.internal:25 to="ada@example.com" text="We have your order 1." INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack INFO guide_http::notifications mail sent server=smtp://mail.internal:25 to="ada@example.com" text="Order 1 is on its way: TRK-1-2." INFO ruststream::dispatch handler ack RUST_LOG tunes what is printed, for example RUST_LOG=ruststream=debug,info.

The shop moves to NATS by changing the broker it is built on; the subscribers and the routers' settings stay as they are. The broker is chosen in one place: the value passed to shop. A broker crate brings the broker type and a prelude with the same names the in-memory prelude has, Publish among them. So a router reads the same on every broker, and only the type it names changes. The subscriber bodies import nothing from the broker, so they do not change at all. Every broker has its own crate; this chapter uses ruststream-nats.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "cbor", "asyncapi", "logging"] } ruststream-nats = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The memory feature is no longer needed. The testing features of both crates go into [dev-dependencies].

The entry point builds the shop on a NatsBroker, which, like the in-memory broker, connects only when the service starts. Macros Manual main.rs use ruststream_nats::prelude::*; use crate::state::Shop; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Shop> { service::shop(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222")) } main.rs use std::process::ExitCode; use ruststream::runtime::cli::run_main; use ruststream_nats::prelude::*; use crate::state::Shop; fn app() -> impl App<State = Shop> { service::shop(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The other files change in two ways. Each imports ruststream_nats::prelude::* in place of ruststream::memory::prelude::*. Each router returns RouterDef<NatsBroker, Shop>, and shop takes a broker whose type is NatsBroker. The codecs, the slots, the attempt cap and the dead-letter topic stay as they are. http.rs binds its publisher token on NatsBroker::new(..).bindable() the same way.

NatsBroker has an in-process mode, so TestApp runs the shop without a server, as it did on the in-memory broker. The tests take their broker from test_broker in service.rs, which now builds a NatsBroker: service.rs #[cfg(test)] pub(crate) fn test_broker() -> NatsBroker { NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222") } In process, the address is only parsed, never dialled. The tests ask for the broker by its type, tb.broker::<NatsBroker>(). Nothing else in them changes, the delay of chapter 8 and the AsyncAPI document included.

docker run --rm -p 4222:4222 nats:2-alpine cargo run -- run A topic name is a subject on Core NATS. Core NATS keeps no messages: one published while no subscriber listens is gone, and a delivery has no acknowledgement. A retry or a retry_after publishes a copy back to the subject, and the attempt cap counts the copies. A topic whose messages must survive a restart reads a JetStream stream instead: JetStreamSubject in the attribute, with a durable consumer. The crate's nats_jetstream example shows one, and nats_retry shows how each kind of subscription retries.

accept answers each order with a payment request and tells the customer through an Out slot; a router says how both leave. A subscriber publishes in two ways. A reply is the value the body returns: the runtime encodes it and publishes it after the body succeeds. An Out slot is a publisher the body receives as a parameter and calls itself, as many times as it needs. Where a message goes is a property of its type: #[outgoing(name = ..)] fixes the topic, so neither the body nor the mount site repeats it. A slot lists the types that may leave through it, so publishing anything else does not compile. The mount site binds each position to a publish policy, here the broker's plain Publish.
documents.s: Replies and publishing to other topics

documents.t: Payments receives a PaymentRequest; Paid is what it answers in the next chapter. Macros Manual payments.rs /// What the orders side asks payments to charge. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.requested")] pub(crate) struct PaymentRequest { pub(crate) order: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, pub(crate) amount_cents: u64, pub(crate) request_id: String, } /// A charged order, on its way to shipping. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.settled")] pub(crate) struct Paid { pub(crate) order: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, } payments.rs /// What the orders side asks payments to charge. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct PaymentRequest { pub(crate) order: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, pub(crate) amount_cents: u64, pub(crate) request_id: String, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "payments.requested")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for PaymentRequest { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments.requested"; } impl MessageHeaders for PaymentRequest { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for PaymentRequest { const NAME: &'static str = "PaymentRequest"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some("What the orders side asks payments to charge."); } /// A charged order, on its way to shipping. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Paid { pub(crate) order: u64, pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) lines: Vec<Line>, } impl OutgoingDestination for Paid { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments.settled"; } impl MessageHeaders for Paid { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Paid { const NAME: &'static str = "Paid"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some("A charged order, on its way to shipping."); } A Notice is what the shop tells a customer, and the OutSlot marker Notices is the slot it leaves through. The manual form writes what #[derive(OutSlot)] generates: the slot's name, the types it publishes, and their entries in the AsyncAPI document. Macros Manual notifications.rs /// What the shop tells a customer. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "notices")] pub(crate) struct Notice { pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) text: String, } /// The slot a subscriber tells customers through, and what may leave through it. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Notice)] pub(crate) struct Notices; notifications.rs /// What the shop tells a customer. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Notice { pub(crate) customer: String, pub(crate) text: String, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "notices")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Notice { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "notices"; } impl MessageHeaders for Notice { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Notice { const NAME: &'static str = "Notice"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some("What the shop tells a customer."); } /// The slot a subscriber tells customers through, and what may leave through it. pub(crate) struct Notices; // What `#[derive(OutSlot)]` with `#[publishes(Notice)]` writes. impl OutSlot for Notices { const NAME: &'static str = "Notices"; // `Notice` fixes its destination, so no transform on this slot may name one. type Destination = Reads; fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { <Notice as OutMessages<Self>>::outgoing() } } impl PublishedThrough<Notices> for Notice {} impl<Slot: OutSlot> OutMessages<Slot> for Notice { fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { vec![OutgoingMessageMetadata::new( Self::DESTINATION, type_name::<Self>(), )] } }

accept drops an order with no lines, since there is nothing to charge, and an order past the shop's bounds, since it has no total. It tells the customer the order arrived, through the slot, and asks for a retry if that publish fails. Then it returns the payment request, which the runtime publishes as the reply. Ok publishes the reply and acks; Err publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. Macros Manual orders.rs /// Accepts an order: asks payments to charge it, and tells the customer it arrived. #[subscriber("orders.placed", reply)] async fn accept( order: &Order, Headers(meta): Headers<RequestMeta>, Out(notices): Out<impl Publisher, Notices>, ) -> Result<PaymentRequest, HandlerOutcome> { if order.lines.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order = order.id, "an order with no lines, dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let Some(amount_cents) = total_cents(&order.lines) else { tracing::warn!(order = order.id, "an order past the shop's bounds, dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let notice = Notice { customer: order.customer.clone(), text: format!("We have your order {}.", order.id), }; if notices.message(&notice).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(PaymentRequest { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), lines: order.lines.clone(), amount_cents, request_id: meta.request_id, }) } orders.rs /// Accepts an order: asks payments to charge it, and tells the customer it arrived. struct Accept; impl<Entry> Handle<Message<RequestMeta, Order>, PaymentRequest, Outs<(Entry,)>, (), Shop> for Accept where Entry: OutEntry<Notices, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, placed: &Message<RequestMeta, Order>, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> Result<PaymentRequest, HandlerOutcome> { let (meta, order) = (&placed.headers, &placed.body); if order.lines.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order = order.id, "an order with no lines, dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let Some(amount_cents) = total_cents(&order.lines) else { tracing::warn!(order = order.id, "an order past the shop's bounds, dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let notice = Notice { customer: order.customer.clone(), text: format!("We have your order {}.", order.id), }; if outs.get(Notices).message(&notice).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(PaymentRequest { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), lines: order.lines.clone(), amount_cents, request_id: meta.request_id.clone(), }) } } In the manual form the slot is an entry of Outs, and outs.get(Notices) hands out its publisher.

A Router collects one module's subscribers with the settings of their positions. out_reply binds the reply to a policy, and .codec(INTERNAL) encodes it as CBOR. out binds the slot; it keeps the router's codec, which is JSON here. The router names the broker and the app's state type in RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop>; chapter 7 introduces Shop. Macros Manual orders.rs /// The orders side's subscribers, with where their messages go. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .include(audit) .include(accept) // The payment request travels as CBOR, the codec of the shop's own topics. .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .out(Notices, Publish) .build() } orders.rs /// The orders side's subscribers, with where their messages go. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .include( subscriber(Order::DESTINATION, Audit) .describe( "Writes every placed order to the audit log, with the request that placed it.", ) .build(), ) .include( subscriber(Order::DESTINATION, Accept) .describe( "Accepts an order: asks payments to charge it, and tells the customer it \ arrived.", ) .reply() .build(), ) // The payment request travels as CBOR, the codec of the shop's own topics. .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .out(Notices, Publish) .build() } The manual form binds each subscriber to its topic with subscriber(..), and .describe(..) gives it the description the doc comment gives the macro. include_router mounts the router on the broker; chapter 5 shows the app that does it.

The shop starts as one subscriber that takes every placed order, mounted on the in-memory broker by a small app. A RustStream service is an application: a builder that names its brokers and mounts subscribers on them. A subscriber is an async fn whose first parameter is the message, and #[subscriber] names the topic it reads. The runtime decodes the payload before the body runs, with JSON by default. What the body returns settles the delivery: HandlerOutcome::ack tells the broker the message is done. The in-memory broker carries messages inside the process, so the shop needs nothing installed. Chapter 11 swaps it for a networked broker, and the subscribers stay as they are.
documents.s: The service and its first subscriber

documents.t: An order is a serde type. The Outgoing derive says where an order is published: orders.placed. The shop does not publish orders yet; a test does, and in chapter 10 the HTTP storefront does. Macros Manual examples/guide/first.rs /// An order placed in the storefront. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.placed")] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } examples/manual/guide/first.rs /// An order placed in the storefront. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "orders.placed")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.placed"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } The manual form writes the two impls the derive generates: the destination, and the headers an order carries (none yet).

accept reads orders.placed and logs each order through tracing. The manual form is a named type with an impl Handle<Order>: Ok(()) acks, and Err(outcome) settles by that outcome. Macros Manual examples/guide/first.rs /// Takes every placed order; for now it only logs it. #[subscriber("orders.placed")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order = order.id, customer = %order.customer, "order accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/guide/first.rs /// Takes every placed order; for now it only logs it. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = order.id, customer = %order.customer, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } }

RustStream is the app; with_broker registers a broker and mounts subscribers on it with include. The builder only records what it is given: the broker connects when the service starts. The #[ruststream::app] attribute turns the builder into main, with the run and asyncapi gen commands. The manual form writes that main by hand: run_main over the builder. Macros Manual examples/guide/first.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept); }) } examples/manual/guide/first.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.placed", Accept).build()); }) } /// What `#[ruststream::app]` writes: the `run` and `asyncapi gen` commands over `app`. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

cargo run --example guide_first --features testing,macros,memory,json,logging -- run The logging feature prints the service's log to the terminal. The service connects the broker, opens the subscription and runs until Ctrl+C: INFO ruststream::lifecycle starting service service=shop version=0.1.0 brokers=1 subscribers=1 INFO ruststream::lifecycle broker connected broker="ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker" INFO ruststream::dispatch subscriber started subscriber=orders.placed input="guide_first::Order" INFO ruststream::lifecycle service running subscribers=1 The rest of the guide grows this file into the shop of examples/guide.

charge answers each refusal of the payment provider with the outcome it needs: a retry now, a retry later, a drop, or the dead-letter topic. Every delivery ends in one outcome. ack finishes it, drop discards it, and retry asks the broker to deliver it again. retry_after delivers it again after a delay, without holding up the deliveries behind it. A retry that never succeeds would come back forever, so the mount site caps the attempts. Past the cap, the delivery goes to a dead-letter topic, where an operator or another service can look at it.

The payment provider refuses a charge in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up for now: an immediate retry would be refused again, so retry_after waits a second. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card does not cover the amount, and another try gets the same answer, so the payment is dropped. The provider's client comes from the app's state, which chapter 7 opens. Macros Manual payments.rs /// How long a busy provider asks its callers to wait. pub(crate) const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1); /// Charges an order through the payment provider. #[subscriber("payments.requested", reply)] async fn charge( request: &PaymentRequest, State(gateway): State<Arc<Gateway>>, ) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { match gateway.charge(request).await { Ok(()) => Ok(Paid { order: request.order, customer: request.customer.clone(), lines: request.lines.clone(), }), // Past the rate limit: a redelivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), // A refused card stays refused. Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(order = request.order, "card declined, payment dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } payments.rs /// How long a busy provider asks its callers to wait. pub(crate) const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1); /// Charges an order through the payment provider. struct Charge; // The state type is the last parameter of `Handle`; the mount checks it against the app's. impl Handle<PaymentRequest, Paid, (), (), Shop> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, request: &PaymentRequest, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { let State(gateway) = State::<Arc<Gateway>>::from_context(ctx).await?; match gateway.charge(request).await { Ok(()) => Ok(Paid { order: request.order, customer: request.customer.clone(), lines: request.lines.clone(), }), // Past the rate limit: a redelivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), // A refused card stays refused. Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(order = request.order, "card declined, payment dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } }

max_attempts counts every delivery of one message, the first included. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to payments.dead, payload and headers as they arrived. The router decodes the requests as CBOR and encodes the reply the same way. Macros Manual payments.rs /// The payments side's subscriber: five deliveries at most, then the dead-letter topic. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .with_codec(INTERNAL) .include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .build() } payments.rs /// The payments side's subscriber: five deliveries at most, then the dead-letter topic. pub(crate) fn routes() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker, Shop> { Router::new() .with_codec(INTERNAL) .include( subscriber(PaymentRequest::DESTINATION, Charge) .describe("Charges an order through the payment provider.") .reply() .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .out_reply(Publish) .codec(INTERNAL) .build() } The in-memory broker redelivers by itself, after the delay retry_after asks for. A broker that cannot delay a delivery gets a copy published back to the subscription; where a retry copy goes covers it. Chapter 8 tests all three paths, the delay included, without waiting for it.
documents.s: The cap and the dead-letter topic

documents.t: The payment client and the mailer open once at startup and reach every subscriber as State; the context tells a subscriber which delivery it holds. A service shares clients, pools and caches between its subscribers. The app opens them in on_startup, before the first subscription opens, and an error there stops the startup. What the hook returns is the app's state, one value for the whole service. A subscriber takes one field of it as a State<T> parameter. The context is the per-delivery half: the subscription's name, the headers, the broker's fields of this delivery. A subscriber takes it as a &mut Context parameter, right after the message.

Shop holds the payment client and the mailer, each behind an Arc so a clone is cheap. FromRef projects each field out of the state: State<Arc<Gateway>> resolves through it. open is the hook the app passes to on_startup in chapter 5. Macros Manual state.rs /// The app's state: each field reaches a subscriber as `State<FieldType>`. #[derive(Clone, FromRef)] pub(crate) struct Shop { pub(crate) gateway: Arc<Gateway>, pub(crate) mailer: Arc<Mailer>, } impl Shop { /// Opens the clients. The app runs it once, before the first subscription opens; an error /// stops the startup. pub(crate) async fn open() -> Result<Self, MailError> { Ok(Self { gateway: Arc::new(Gateway::new(CARD_LIMIT_CENTS, CHARGES_PER_SECOND)), mailer: Arc::new(Mailer::connect("smtp://mail.internal:25").await?), }) } } state.rs /// The app's state: each field reaches a subscriber as `State<FieldType>`. #[derive(Clone)] pub(crate) struct Shop { pub(crate) gateway: Arc<Gateway>, pub(crate) mailer: Arc<Mailer>, } // What `#[derive(FromRef)]` writes for each field: `State<Arc<Gateway>>` resolves through it. impl FromRef<Shop> for Arc<Gateway> { fn from_ref(shop: &Shop) -> Self { shop.gateway.clone() } } impl FromRef<Shop> for Arc<Mailer> { fn from_ref(shop: &Shop) -> Self { shop.mailer.clone() } } impl Shop { /// Opens the clients. The app runs it once, before the first subscription opens; an error /// stops the startup. pub(crate) async fn open() -> Result<Self, MailError> { Ok(Self { gateway: Arc::new(Gateway::new(CARD_LIMIT_CENTS, CHARGES_PER_SECOND)), mailer: Arc::new(Mailer::connect("smtp://mail.internal:25").await?), }) } } The manual form writes the two impls the derive generates, one per field.

send e-mails a notice through the mailer from the state. A mailbox that does not exist stays that way, so a refused notice is dropped, and the warning names the subscription from the context. Macros Manual notifications.rs /// E-mails a notice to the customer. // The mailer comes from the app's state; the context names the subscription in the warning. #[subscriber("notices")] async fn send( notice: &Notice, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, State(mailer): State<Arc<Mailer>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match mailer.send(&notice.customer, &notice.text).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(error) => { // A refused mailbox stays refused; another try would only repeat the warning. tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), %error, "notice not sent"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } notifications.rs /// E-mails a notice to the customer. struct Mail; // The mailer comes from the app's state; the context names the subscription in the warning. impl Handle<Notice, (), (), (), Shop> for Mail { async fn handle( &self, notice: &Notice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Shop>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let State(mailer) = State::<Arc<Mailer>>::from_context(ctx).await?; if let Err(error) = mailer.send(&notice.customer, &notice.text).await { // A refused mailbox stays refused; another try would only repeat the warning. tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), %error, "notice not sent"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } In the manual form the state type is the last parameter of Handle, and the mount checks it against the app's. The body reads the field with from_context, which is what the macro does for a State parameter. Custom extractors are types of your own read the same way.
documents.s: The state and the context in one subscriber

documents.t: TestApp runs the shop's own app in process: a test publishes an order and checks what each subscriber did and what each topic received. A test starts the app that main runs, unchanged, with TestApp::start. The broker connects in process, and every subscription runs on the test's runtime. A publish from the test returns once everything it set off has settled, so the next line can check the result. Assertions read two records: what each subscriber received and how it settled, and what was published to each topic. On a paused clock, advance moves time forward, so a delay of a second or an hour costs nothing. Testing needs the crate's testing feature, usually as a dev-dependency.

The test places an order with its request headers and follows it to the customer. The payment request travels as CBOR, so the assertion decodes it with with_codec. accept and dispatch each send a notice, and send acks both. Macros Manual main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_placed_order_is_charged_shipped_and_announced() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&order(7, mugs(12))) .with_headers(&meta("req-7")) .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.requested") .assert_called_once() .with_codec( &CborCodec, &PaymentRequest { order: 7, customer: "ada@example.com".to_owned(), lines: mugs(12), amount_cents: 14_400, request_id: "req-7".to_owned(), }, ); broker .published::<Notice>("notices") .assert_called(2) .with(&Notice { customer: "ada@example.com".to_owned(), text: "Order 7 is on its way: TRK-7-2.".to_owned(), }); broker .subscriber("notices") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_placed_order_is_charged_shipped_and_announced() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&order(7, mugs(12))) .with_headers(&meta("req-7")) .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.requested") .assert_called_once() .with_codec( &CborCodec, &PaymentRequest { order: 7, customer: "ada@example.com".to_owned(), lines: mugs(12), amount_cents: 14_400, request_id: "req-7".to_owned(), }, ); broker .published::<Notice>("notices") .assert_called(2) .with(&Notice { customer: "ada@example.com".to_owned(), text: "Order 7 is on its way: TRK-7-2.".to_owned(), }); broker .subscriber("notices") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) }
documents.s: An order from start to finish

documents.t: An order with no lines stops at accept: nothing is charged and no customer is told. Macros Manual main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_with_no_lines_goes_no_further() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&order(8, Vec::new())) .with_headers(&meta("req-8")) .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.requested") .assert_not_called(); broker.published::<Notice>("notices").assert_not_called(); Ok(()) } main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_with_no_lines_goes_no_further() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.message(&order(8, Vec::new())) .with_headers(&meta("req-8")) .publish() .await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.requested") .assert_not_called(); broker.published::<Notice>("notices").assert_not_called(); Ok(()) }
documents.s: An order that goes no further

documents.t: A provider that takes one charge a second refuses the second request with Busy. with_state starts the app with that provider instead of the one on_startup opens. test_broker in service.rs returns the broker the tests build the shop on, so they name it in one place. The clock starts paused, and advance(BACKOFF) brings the refused request back. Macros Manual payments.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_busy_provider_is_asked_again_after_the_backoff() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A provider that takes one charge a second. let state = Shop { gateway: Arc::new(Gateway::new(100_000, 1)), ..Shop::open().await? }; let tb = TestApp::with_state(shop(test_broker()), |_| state).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); for order in [1, 2] { broker .message(&request(order, 500)) .with_codec(CborCodec) .publish() .await?; } broker .subscriber("payments.requested") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)); tb.advance(BACKOFF).await?; broker .subscriber("payments.requested") .assert_called(3) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); broker .published::<Paid>("payments.settled") .assert_called(2); Ok(()) } payments.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_busy_provider_is_asked_again_after_the_backoff() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // A provider that takes one charge a second. let state = Shop { gateway: Arc::new(Gateway::new(100_000, 1)), ..Shop::open().await? }; let tb = TestApp::with_state(shop(test_broker()), |_| state).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); for order in [1, 2] { broker .message(&request(order, 500)) .with_codec(CborCodec) .publish() .await?; } broker .subscriber("payments.requested") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)); tb.advance(BACKOFF).await?; broker .subscriber("payments.requested") .assert_called(3) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); broker .published::<Paid>("payments.settled") .assert_called(2); Ok(()) }
documents.s: A delay, without waiting for it

documents.t: A provider that never answers makes every delivery fail. The fifth delivery goes to payments.dead, as it arrived. Macros Manual payments.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_silent_provider_sends_the_request_to_the_dead_letter_topic() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let state = Shop::open().await?; state.gateway.go_offline(); let tb = TestApp::with_state(shop(test_broker()), |_| state).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&request(3, 500)) .with_codec(CborCodec) .publish() .await?; broker.subscriber("payments.requested").assert_called(5); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.dead") .assert_called_once() .with_codec(&CborCodec, &request(3, 500)); Ok(()) } payments.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_silent_provider_sends_the_request_to_the_dead_letter_topic() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let state = Shop::open().await?; state.gateway.go_offline(); let tb = TestApp::with_state(shop(test_broker()), |_| state).await?; let broker = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>(); broker .message(&request(3, 500)) .with_codec(CborCodec) .publish() .await?; broker.subscriber("payments.requested").assert_called(5); broker .published::<PaymentRequest>("payments.dead") .assert_called_once() .with_codec(&CborCodec, &request(3, 500)); Ok(()) } Run the tests of both forms: cargo test --example guide --features testing,macros,memory,json,cbor,asyncapi cargo test --example manual_guide --no-default-features --features testing,memory,json,cbor,asyncapi The tests in both directories are the same, and they pass against both forms of the shop.

The repository ships agent skills: guidance a coding agent loads when a task needs it, so the code it writes follows the framework's recommended path. Install them in Claude Code with two commands: /plugin marketplace add powersemmi/ruststream /plugin install ruststream@ruststream The plugin brings five skills. An agent picks a skill by its description, so a request about a RustStream service loads the service skill without naming it. Skill When an agent uses it ruststream writing a service: handlers, the app, replies, publishing, retries, state, codecs ruststream-testing testing a service with TestApp ruststream-without-macros building a service without the macros feature ruststream-broker writing a broker crate ruststream-core contributing to the core repository

Each skill is a directory with a SKILL.md and its reference pages, under .agents/skills/ in the repository. Cursor and Codex read skills from .agents/skills/ of the project they work in. To give an agent the skills in your own service, copy the directories you need into that directory of your project, or into the skill directory your agent reads.

The skills describe the framework of the revision they come from. Install them from the same release line as the ruststream your service depends on. A skill is guidance, not a check: the compiler and the tests remain the judges of the result.

RustStream ships as a single crate, ruststream, whose surface is enabled by additive cargo features. Add it to your Cargo.toml: [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } serde is a direct dependency of your service because your message types derive Deserialize / Serialize. Edition and MSRV RustStream targets edition 2024 and a minimum supported Rust version of 1.95. Set edition = "2024" in your Cargo.toml. A broker crate may need a newer Rust than the core when its client library does. The broker crate's own rust-version field states the exact minimum version.

The core traits, the RustStream application object, the Router, middleware and message dispatch are always compiled. Everything else is an additive feature you enable when you need it. Feature Pulls in What it gives you json (default) serde_json JsonCodec msgpack rmp-serde MsgpackCodec cbor ciborium CborCodec memory - MemoryBroker, the in-memory reference broker macros ruststream-macros #[subscriber], #[ruststream::app], and the derives (Outgoing, OutSlot, OutMessages, Deserialized, Serialized, FromRef, MessageInfo) asyncapi schemars, serde_norway AsyncAPI generation and the HTML viewer metrics prometheus Prometheus middleware and exporter logging tracing-subscriber ruststream::logging, a colored console logger (Logging) otel opentelemetry, opentelemetry-otlp OTLP export for traces and metrics, and W3C trace-context propagation (OpenTelemetry) testing inventory TestApp and the assertion builders (Testing) conformance inventory the broker-author conformance harness cli clap, anyhow the ruststream binary You can enable several codecs at once (see Codecs). To drop the bundled JSON codec (for example in a broker crate that needs only the traits and the runtime), disable the default features: [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", default-features = false }

The ruststream binary ships with the crate behind the cli cargo feature. It runs cargo with the framework's subcommands (run, asyncapi gen); installation and commands are in the runtime::cli module. cargo generate scaffolds a new project from a template, covered in the quick start.

The memory broker is built into the crate and needs no external service. To reach a broker outside the process, depend on that broker's crate; it re-exports from ruststream everything it needs. Each broker has its own version and its own release cycle, so the exact dependency line, with the current version and the testing feature for handler tests, is in the broker's own documentation. The same documentation describes the broker's connection options and its capabilities. The available brokers are listed under Brokers; the link there leads to each broker's documentation and its installation instructions. To write your own broker, see the Broker trait.
The fastest way to a running service is to scaffold one with cargo generate.

cargo install cargo-generate cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream templates/memory --name my-service cd my-service Scaffolding needs only cargo generate. templates/memory is the starter template for the in-memory broker. A broker crate that ships a template is scaffolded the same way, naming that crate's repository and the template's path (for example --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-nats templates/nats); the broker's own documentation names the templates it has. cargo generate writes an idiomatic, multi-file project: my-service/ ├── Cargo.toml └── src/ ├── main.rs # #[ruststream::app] builds the service and mounts the router ├── orders.rs # handlers as #[subscriber] functions (one publishes a reply) └── routes.rs # collects the handlers into a Router

#[ruststream::app] generates main, so the binary already understands the framework commands: cargo run -- run # or: ruststream run, with the CLI installed cargo run -- run starts a tokio runtime. The service runs until you press Ctrl+C. It needs no external broker. The template turns on the logging feature, so the service prints its log to the terminal, and the handlers log through tracing.
cargo run -- asyncapi gen The command prints the AsyncAPI document as JSON. The output flags (-o, --yaml) and the document itself are covered in the asyncapi module.

Macros Manual src/main.rs mod orders; mod routes; use ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker; use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { let router = routes::orders(); b.include_router(router); }) } src/main.rs mod orders; mod routes; use std::process::ExitCode; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream::runtime::cli::run_main; fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { let router = routes::orders(); b.include_router(router); }) } // What `#[ruststream::app]` writes around the builder: the `run` and `asyncapi gen` commands. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } You write a function that builds the service; #[ruststream::app] turns it into main.
documents.s: What the entry point looks like

documents.t: Understand each piece in the tutorial. Learn the handler forms in Subscribers. Drive everything from the CLI.

By the end of this page you have a running orders service: a message type, a handler, a reply, and a router that collects them. It runs on the in-memory broker, so there is nothing external to start. Swapping in a real broker is a one-line change, and step 7 shows it.

cargo new orders-service cd orders-service Cargo.toml [package] name = "orders-service" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "memory", "json", "asyncapi", "logging"] } serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1"

A handler is an async fn whose first parameter is the decoded payload. The #[subscriber] macro turns it into a subscriber definition named after the function. Macros Manual src/orders.rs use ruststream::runtime::HandlerOutcome; use ruststream::schemars::JsonSchema; use ruststream::{Outgoing, subscriber}; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Order { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) quantity: u32, } #[subscriber("orders")] pub(crate) async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.quantity, "order received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/orders.rs use std::future::{Future, ready}; use ruststream::prelude::*; use ruststream::schemars::JsonSchema; use serde::Deserialize; /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Order { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) quantity: u32, } /// The handler: `#[subscriber("orders")]` generates this struct and this impl. The subject it /// carried is named where the handler is mounted instead. pub(crate) struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.quantity, "order received"); ready(Ok(())) } } A handler returns a HandlerOutcome: an ack, or a nack that drops or requeues the message. You can return () or Result<(), E> instead, where Ok acks and Err drops. The JsonSchema derive puts the payload's schema into the AsyncAPI document of step 6. The type's doc comment becomes the message description there. You need no extra dependency for it: the asyncapi feature re-exports schemars.
documents.s: 2. Define a message and a handler

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs mod orders; use ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker; use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use crate::orders::handle; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(handle); }) } src/main.rs mod orders; use std::process::ExitCode; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream::runtime::cli::run_main; use crate::orders::Receive; fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Codec defaults include decodes with the default codec, so it needs no codec argument. The default is json when the feature is enabled, otherwise cbor, otherwise msgpack. You can set one codec for all the broker's handlers at once with with_broker_codec(broker, codec, |b| ...). See Codecs for the full resolution rules. Run it: cargo run -- run The logging feature prints the service's log to the terminal: the startup lines, then a line for each order the handler logs with tracing::info!.

To publish a reply, return the reply value and write reply on the subscriber. The Outgoing derive on the reply type says where it goes: Macros Manual src/orders.rs /// The service's answer to an order. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "confirmations")] pub(crate) struct Confirmation { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) accepted: bool, } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] pub(crate) async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, } } src/orders.rs use serde::Serialize; /// The service's answer to an order, published on `confirmations`. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] pub(crate) struct Confirmation { pub(crate) id: u64, pub(crate) accepted: bool, } /// What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "confirmations")]` writes: the destination /// is fixed on the type, so nothing else names it. impl OutgoingDestination for Confirmation { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "confirmations"; } impl MessageHeaders for Confirmation { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// The reply form of the same trait: the second parameter of `Handle` is the reply type, so the /// body returns a `Confirmation`, and the mount site supplies the publisher it leaves through. pub(crate) struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, })) } } Mount confirm next to handle with the same include. The reply is published with the broker's default publish policy and encoded with the default codec. Macros Manual src/main.rs use crate::orders::{confirm, handle}; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(handle); b.include(confirm); }) } src/main.rs use crate::orders::{Confirm, Receive}; fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()); // The definition names the reply's destination; with no `.out_reply(..)` at the mount // site the reply leaves through the broker's default publisher. b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Publishing from inside a handler and the other ways to publish are in Publishing & replies.

As the number of handlers grows, keep them in their own module and collect them into a Router: Macros Manual src/routes.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use crate::orders; // The reply wiring is a publish policy: pure declaration, so the router needs no broker at all. pub(crate) fn orders() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker> { Router::new() .include(orders::handle) .include(orders::confirm) .out_reply(Publish) .build() } src/routes.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use crate::orders::{Confirm, Receive}; // Each handler is bound to its subject where it is mounted; the definition says what it replies // with, the reply type says where it goes, and the mount chain names who publishes it. The // publisher wiring is still a publish policy - pure declaration, so the router needs no broker // at all. pub(crate) fn orders() -> impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker> { Router::new() .include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()) .include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) .build() } include adds a plain handler to the router directly. A handler that publishes a reply hands back a mount chain instead: .out_reply(..) names the reply's publish policy, and .build() finishes the registration. Without .out_reply(..), .build() takes the broker's default publish policy - the same one include took in step 4. Routing covers the rest of the router surface. Macros Manual src/main.rs mod orders; mod routes; use ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker; use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { let router = routes::orders(); b.include_router(router); }) } src/main.rs mod orders; mod routes; use std::process::ExitCode; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream::runtime::cli::run_main; fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders-service", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { let router = routes::orders(); b.include_router(router); }) } // What `#[ruststream::app]` writes around the builder: the `run` and `asyncapi gen` commands. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

cargo run -- asyncapi gen Every subscriber adds a channel and a receive operation to the document. handle and confirm share the orders channel and get one operation each, because their subscriptions are separate. The reply adds a send operation on confirmations. The document keeps the payload schemas under components.messages. The output flags (-o, --yaml) and the document itself are covered in AsyncAPI.

Nothing above is tied to the in-memory broker: the broker is chosen at with_broker, so the swap is a one-line change. Add the broker crate as a dependency and construct it there instead of MemoryBroker::new(), for example NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"). The handlers, the router and the codecs stay as they are. Brokers lists the available brokers and the swap for each of them. The complete service is a compiled example Every snippet on this page comes from examples/tutorial in the repository, which CI builds on every change. first_app.rs and reply_app.rs are the service as steps 3 and 4 leave it, and main.rs is the finished one. Run it yourself with cargo run --example tutorial --features macros,memory,json,asyncapi,logging -- run.

Middleware - cross-cutting logic around handlers. Lifespan - shared state and startup/shutdown hooks. Testing - test the handlers you just wrote, in-process. Metrics - Prometheus counters and histograms.
